item.title: Max Verstappen takes pole for Las Vegas Grand Prix after Kimi Antonelli penalty
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Kimi Antonelli was quickest in qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix, but the newly-crowned world champion will not be on pole for Sunday’s race as he has a five-place grid penalty for taking a new engine for this meeting. Red Bull’s Max Verstappen, who was second, will take pole – his first in Las Vegas – and Mercedes’ George Russell will line up alongside him on the front row of the grid after finishing in third. Antonelli will start from sixth.

Lando Norris was fourth for McLaren and Isack Hadjar fifth for Red Bull. The Ferrari was not in good shape in Las Vegas however. Lewis Hamilton was struggling with a lack of grip throughout the session and could not hook up a good lap. Neither he nor his teammate Charles Leclerc could make it out of Q2, with Leclerc finishing in 11th and Hamilton in 12th. They will start from 10th and 11th after McLaren’s Oscar Piastri also has a 10-place penalty for taking a new engine.

Having won the title in Mexico, Antonelli had said he wanted to see out the season strongly as he and team look towards 2027 and the 20-year-old Italian was once more in immense form in Las Vegas, even if it did not yield pole. Had he done so it would have been his eighth of the season and second in four races despite the resurgence of Red Bull and with Ferrari and McLaren having been quick in recent rounds.

He and Mercedes will take great heart from having proved once more they are on top of their car and that the recent upgrades are working and prove the correct direction for next year’s model. For three rounds now the Mercedes, in Antonelli’s hands, has looked as strong as it did early in the season and is once more enjoying a slender advantage over their rivals.

With the pole, Verstappen and Red Bull continue a run of good form that will be a huge boost to the team and bodes well for a strong start next season. After their last tranche of upgrades proved so effective, Verstappen has taken pole in three of the last six rounds and won three of the last five. He has form in Nevada with two previous wins here and another cannot be ruled out. Verstappen felt he had extracted the best from his car, even if he was still over two tenths off Antonelli’s time in a car that has been something of a handful for the Dutchman this weekend.

With the low temperatures at night in Las Vegas, warming the tyres was key and the field did build laps to force heat into them, before putting in a quick run. In the first hot runs in Q3 it was clear that working as teammates to deliver a tow was proving hugely beneficial but, although Russell was behind Antonelli for his first effort, he was not close enough for the tow.

Russell did take the top spot with his run but was followed by Verstappen who had been squarely in the slipstream of his teammate Hadjar and the Dutchman went quicker by almost three-tenths. The benefit was clear and the British driver then specifically asked the team if he could have a tow from Antonelli given the Italian had a grid penalty.

There was jostling for position for the final runs with no driver wanting to be at the front of the field. Hadjar ultimately took on the mantle once more, leading out Verstappen but the Dutchman could not improve.

Similarly, Oscar Piastri was delivering a slipstream for Norris but he too could not improve. Russell had no tow from Antonelli who had backed out of the jostling and was ploughing his own furrow at the back. It was a close run thing for the Italian, but in dropping back he crossed the line to start his lap with just one second to spare.

Russell moved up to second but it was the Italian world champion who had kept the best for last, taking the top spot with a time of 1minute 33.893seconds. The slipstream had worked but the quickest man on track would not take pole, leaving Russell perhaps to wonder quite why the team did not favour him on this occasion. He said he would discuss it with Mercedes “offline”.

Verstappen and Russell were investigated by the stewards for an incident where they banged wheels at turn 14 in final practice. Verstappen had overtaken Russell on the way into the corner, and Russell reciprocated by ducking back up the inside and the pair clashed.

Verstappen accused Russell of trying to push him into the barriers, while the British driver’s race engineer Marcus Dudley said he had seen the Dutchman “cut in front of you”. Russell’s described it as “fun and games”. Verstappen was given a warning by the FIA stewards but no penalty.

Source: The Guardian US | Published: 2026-11-21 06:00 UTC

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/sport/2026/nov/21/max-verstappen-las-vegas-gp-f1-pole-position-qualifying-kimi-antonelli

item.title: Campaigners back call for scrutiny of consent laws by Joanne Young
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Campaigners have welcomed a call for scrutiny of consent laws by a survivor of drug-facilitated rape but said action must also focus on wider issues around sexual assault.

Joanne Young, who was drugged and raped by her husband and sexually abused by men he invited into their home, warned of “serious questions about how the law deals with consent”.

Philip Young, 50, advertised Joanne Young, his then wife, on dating and swinging websites, presenting it as a “kink” for both of them, Winchester crown court heard. In fact, he had been sedating her, plunging her into an “inanimate state” in which anything could be done to her by the men who answered the adverts, jurors were told.

The former Conservative councillor pleaded guilty earlier in the year to dozens of charges of abuse against his former wife, who has waived her right to anonymity.

As four men were convicted of sexual offences against her on Thursday, Young, 49, said: “No one should be able to give [consent] on your behalf.” Her daughter, Alex Young, also called for a change in the law to make it clear that third-party consent cannot ever be used as an argument in a court of law.

Barristers and campaigners said there was no law that stated third-party consent was a valid defence as they called for a public debate and further education about consent.

Kate Parker, a criminal barrister and founder of the charity Schools Consent Project, said: “The law currently has nothing in it which allows someone to point to another person and say: ‘Because of what they told me, I believed the other person to be consenting.’ You can’t effectively outsource consent to a third party, the law has never had that within it. The Sexual Offences Act 2003 certainly doesn’t have that in it.

“What is instead happening is defence counsel in this case, and in cases like this, are pointing to a defence you can run, which is to say that the defendant genuinely and reasonably thought that the victim was consenting.”

The trial heard that the four men, who were strangers to each other, failed to seek consent from Joanne Young before they engaged in sexual activity with her. The defendants claimed they had been duped by Philip Young and believed she was consenting.

Parker said it was right that a defendant should be able to say what was in his or her mind at the time of an alleged offence.

“I think that’s a sort of cornerstone of our law. But I hope that these arguments carry less and less traction with juries when generally there is more knowledge as to what the laws around consent are,” she said.

“I hope that as time goes by, juries become more aware and members of the public become more aware as to what the law on consent is, so no one can say: ‘Because a third party told me so and I acted on it, I thought I was legally safe.’”

Harriet Wistrich, a solicitor and the director of the Centre for Women’s Justice, said the jury in the Young case had ultimately rejected the defence.

“It should be obvious in the law that somebody can’t consent on somebody else’s behalf. But you could explicitly make it the case,” she said.

“Defence barristers should robustly defend their clients. That’s their job. But they shouldn’t overstep the mark by relying on myths and stereotypes.”

Ciara Bergman, the chief executive of Rape Crisis England & Wales, agreed the law on consent should be scrutinised. The Sexual Offences Act 2003 states: “A person consents if he agrees by choice, and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice.”

She said: “We can look at strengthening existing laws. But really we have to get to the root of the problem, which is about the understanding of consent.

“The existing law is already clear. This is about how that law is interpreted and it is regularly misinterpreted and misapplied. That happens all the time by defendants, by barristers, by juries, and so this is highlighting a lack of understanding that consent is specific: it’s not a one-time event, it’s ongoing, it’s highly dependent on the actual situation at the time. The fact that someone is unconscious necessarily means they can’t consent.

“The other thing about these cases is that drugging someone is the opposite of consent. What is emerging from these organised drug-facilitated sexual abuse cases is a growing recognition of the attraction that some people have to a woman not being able to consent.”

Prof Miranda Horvath, the director of the Institute for Social Justice and Crime at the University of Suffolk, said incorrect beliefs about consent should be “robustly challenged”.

“It is incredibly important that people understand that legally nobody can give consent on your behalf, and this underlines the importance of clear education on consent through society, from young people right through to adults,” she said.

“Rape and serious sexual offences are a direct choice made by perpetrators, and a lack of understanding on whether a sexual partner has given consent cannot be an acceptable excuse.”

The Labour MP Jess Phillips said the government should look at whether the law should be tightened. “It is absolutely right that the government should strength-test whether there is a way of really asserting in the law that consent cannot ever come from a third party – we need to be absolutely satisfied that that is the case,” she said.

“There is an argument that while the law states that consent cannot come from a third party, we still see it being used as a defence. Perhaps if we look at tightening the law, these men would have had to plead guilty and Joanne Young would have been spared this trial.”

A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said: “The law is clear: no one can consent on someone else’s behalf. Consent must come from the person themselves, and they must have the freedom and capacity to make that choice. We keep the criminal law under review, and we will always look at what more can be done to protect victims.”

Source: The Guardian World | Published: 2026-11-21 06:00 UTC

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026/nov/21/campaigners-back-call-for-scrutiny-of-consent-laws-by-joanne-young

item.title: Can Israel’s opposition bloc stay united against Netanyahu?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Can Israel’s opposition bloc stay united against Netanyahu?

Eisenkot’s fragile alliance must overcome deep ideological divisions to turn its opposition into a government.

As negotiations over the formation of Israel’s next government approach their first deadline of December 6, caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu appears to be seeking to exploit divisions within the opposition “change” alliance trying to oust him.

On Wednesday, he held an undeclared meeting with one of its leading figures, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett, in a move that has prompted accusations that Netanyahu is attempting to fracture the bloc from within.

The meeting, which lasted two and a half hours, was described by Netanyahu’s office as a “security briefing”. Sources within the opposition alliance led by Gadi Eisenkot, however, characterised it as a “strategic disaster”, according to Israeli media.

Bennett had not informed Eisenkot of the meeting in advance, sources told the outlet Ynet. During a subsequent gathering of opposition leaders, Bennett is reported to have argued that they should try to pursue the possibility of a unity government with Netanyahu, Channel 12 reported.

Bennett, a right-winger, is among several prominent figures in the opposition alliance who have previously served in Netanyahu-led governments. Eisenkot himself joined Netanyahu’s emergency unity government following the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, serving as a minister without portfolio and a member of the war cabinet.

Avigdor Lieberman, meanwhile – another right-wing member of the opposition bloc – served as Netanyahu’s foreign minister and defence minister.

“Netanyahu is trying to break up the [opposition] bloc for change through Bennett,” a senior figure in the Eisenkot-led alliance told Ynet in an article referencing the numerous pledges by opposition leaders, including Bennett, never to serve within a Netanyahu-led coalition again.

However, given the broad array of ideologies among the coalition leaders, stretching from the hard-right policies of Lieberman to the relatively left-wing platform of Democrats’ leader Yair Golan, and many having previously worked with Netanyahu, it remains unclear how long the bloc can maintain its unity.

Bennett himself was once among Netanyahu’s closest political allies, serving in several of his governments before breaking with him in 2021, when the opportunity arose to form an alternative administration with centrist Yair Lapid. Bennett and Lapid subsequently assembled a cross-party coalition that ended Netanyahu’s 12 consecutive years in office, with Bennett taking the premiership for the first half of its term. But he still shares many policy positions with Netanyahu.

So how cohesive is the opposition coalition, and what could be its potential breaking points?

Here’s what we know:

Is the change bloc united ideologically?

All of the bloc’s members supported Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza – at least at its start – as well as its attacks on several regional states, including Iran and Lebanon.

In terms of domestic policy, however, there are marked differences between members of the alliance.

Both the bloc’s leader, former Israeli military Chief of Staff Gadi Eisenkot, and Bennett’s electoral partner, Yair Lapid, are regarded as relatively centrist figures. By contrast, Bennett and Lieberman are firmly on the right, divided largely by their attitudes towards religion: Bennett is a religious nationalist, while Liberman is a staunchly secular politician with a background in Israel’s Russian-speaking community, increasingly at odds with Israel’s powerful religious political currents.

Standing apart is the left-wing Yair Golan, a supporter of a two-state solution with the Palestinians and an outspoken critic of settler pogroms in the occupied West Bank, which he has accused the government of encouraging or tolerating.

Is the alliance under strain?

Yes.

Beyond the prospect of Netanyahu – Israel’s longest-serving prime minister – continually attempting to undermine them, Eisenkot faces the formidable task of finding the additional 13 seats needed for a parliamentary majority. His bloc holds just 48 of the parliament’s 120 seats after the October 27 elections, leaving him dependent on bridging deep political divides among his allies if he is to form a government capable of governing.

Golan has already met political leaders from parties representing Palestinian citizens of Israel and spoken enthusiastically about forming a government with their support. However, that suggestion has been rejected by the rest of the bloc, and has provoked fierce opposition, with right-wing protesters even threatening civil war at the prospect.

Lieberman, whose Yisrael Beytenu party holds seven seats, has been particularly emphatic in rejecting any government dependent on Palestinian support. However, his longstanding and highly vocal opposition to the de facto exemption of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men from military service appears to be softening in the face of another possibility: the 13 seats held by the ultra-Orthodox parties, Shas and United Torah Judaism.

Lieberman’s willingness to compromise on conscription risks undermining one of his central electoral promises, as well as those of other opposition leaders, and could prompt a backlash from supporters.

Have the change bloc’s differences come out in the open?

In August, Bennett dismissed Eisenkot’s proposal to allow limited exemptions from military conscription that would cover the ultra-Orthodox as an “insane mistake”, warning that ultra-Orthodox politicians Aryeh Deri and Moshe Gafni would “run circles around” him. Eisenkot subsequently countered, accusing Bennett and Lieberman of engaging in “old politics” and damaging the opposition’s electoral prospects by refusing to agree that the largest party in the alliance should lead the next government.

Lieberman, just weeks before the election, branded Eisenkot “Gantz 2.0” – referring to former defence minister Benny Gantz, who joined Netanyahu’s government in 2020 despite campaigning against him – accusing Eisenkot of secretly pursuing a deal with Netanyahu and acting out of personal ambition. Golan, meanwhile, told Lieberman several days after the election that, if he was to continue to insist on a government that avoids conscripting ultra-Orthodox men, he was “welcome to form one with Netanyahu”.

What did change bloc leaders say about Netanyahu before entering the opposition?

Their previous assessments of Netanyahu have not always been so harsh.

In 2020, Bennett told reporters that, despite their personal differences, he respected Netanyahu “very much”, adding that Israel had “won a victory” by having him in office for so long and that he had “done great things” for the country.

Lieberman, meanwhile, told The Jerusalem Post in 2019 that he wished Netanyahu “only really good results” and hoped that he would be acquitted on the corruption charges that he has since cited, on numerous occasions, as evidence that the prime minister is unfit for office.

Source: Al Jazeera | Published: 2026-11-21 05:46 UTC

Original link: https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/21/can-israels-opposition-bloc-stay-united-against-netanyahu?traffic_source=rss

item.title: Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Zelensky says Putin is a 'killer' after Trump calls Russian leader a friend

- Published

Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has labelled Vladimir Putin as a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" in China this week.

Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".

On the sidelines of a historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin on Thursday, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".

At least nine people were killed in Russian attacks targeting bridges in Kyiv and railway stations on Friday, days after Ukraine badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.

Zelensky called the attack the "biggest this year" and said the country suffered civilian deaths and injuries after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.

Hours after the strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".

"They (Zelensky and Putin) both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.

Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.

However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".

"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he said.

Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he is a "friend" means "he doesn't feel enough pressure".

The war of words came as neighbouring Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace in the southeast of the country early on Friday.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.

Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response.

Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during Friday's massive attack on Ukraine.

Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said one missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

The missile hit about 100km (62 miles) from where European troops - from 11 of the 36 member nations of the Coalition of the Winning - were completing a training exercise, Polish authorities said. Another missile and a jet-powered drone were suspected to have hit two other locations, they added.

- Published17 hours ago

- Published1 day ago

- Published1 day ago

Source: BBC World | Published: 2026-11-21 05:15 UTC

Original link: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cxnv4zvmdy0jo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss

item.title: ‘So what if there’s a hole? It hasn’t collapsed’: Kyiv residents unbothered by Russian attacks on city’s bridges
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Mykola expects to drive his battered beige passenger minibus 20 to 24 times a day past the holes in the road on Kyiv’s damaged Northern Bridge that were caused by a Russian ballistic missile attack on Tuesday.

Buses are now the only motor transport allowed across the normally busy multi-lane crossing, though on their way into the city centre they have to skirt the tears in the tarmac, using the only functioning lane to get by.

“So what if there’s a hole? The bridge hasn’t collapsed. You need to know a bit about bridge construction,” says Mykola, 65, at the wheel of a half -full afternoon bus as it clatters on its way west.

Mykola operates a marshrutka, a single deck private bus, whose drivers are famed in Kyiv mythology for being able to multi-task: chatting, smoking and collecting fares, while driving as fast as possible to take passengers from rivals.

Passengers pay 25 hryvnia (42p) in cash and typically one passenger gets the unofficial job of taking money and handing back change on behalf of the driver. It turns out this has become the Guardian’s task, in order to conduct an interview.

“It would be very difficult to destroy the bridge. It would take a huge number of missiles, and if one or two hit it, it wouldn’t be the end of the world,” Mykola continues, with behind-the-wheel speculation that is so far accurate. By lunchtime the holes have been covered up, perhaps to avoid unsettling passengers eyeing the Dnipro River below.

Alongside its attacks on the capital’s electricity, heating and water systems, Russia has been attacking Kyiv’s bridges since early October, trying to cut off the city centre in the west from the newer, largely residential east, home to about a third of its population.

Moscow struck the bridges twice again this week, first on Tuesday – overshadowed by Ukraine’s partial destruction of the Kerch road bridge to Crimea. Then again during a noisy Thursday night, hours after Vladimir Putin promised there would be a “far more painful” response to the demolition of his pet project.

As of Friday, in an already traffic-snarled city, Kyiv’s other main road bridge, the Southern Bridge, was allowing motor traffic only from east to west. The new Podilskyi Bridge, damaged early on Friday, was similarly restricted, and the city’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, told people to avoid car travel after a night in which six were killed.

The Northern Bridge remains open for public transport – plus any cyclists, scooter riders and walkers willing to brave the damp late autumn weather and ignore missile and drone alerts. But below, earthworks have begun to prepare for a floating pontoon bridge, one of eight planned, in case of the worst.

Dmytro Bespalov, a transport planning expert with Kyiv’s National University of Construction and Architecture, said it was difficult to destroy a suspension bridge like the Northern. They have “a strong construction, with a lot of repairability”, meaning damage can usually be fixed. Though there are holes in the roadway, its supporting structures were so far unscathed, he added.

Russia is thought to have been aiming ballistic missiles at the supporting pylon, requiring a precise and difficult to execute attack, though that is what Ukraine did at the culmination of its complex attack on the Kerch road bridge, which was brought down after a Flamingo cruise missile struck its supporting arch.

Yet, Bespalov cautioned that Kyiv was strategically vulnerable if Russia targets the bridges with “dozens or hundreds” of missiles, because the city did not have enough bridges from before the war. “In 2021, Kyiv was in third place in Europe for congestion on the TomTom traffic index,” he said, behind Istanbul and Moscow.

Particular concern is reserved for the pontoon bridge alternative. They can bear less traffic: “It would take 20 pontoon bridges to have half the current capacity,” Bespalov said – and they are far more vulnerable to missile and drone attack. “I don’t think it would be possible to use pontoons during a red [missile] or yellow [drone] alarm” – not least because vehicles could end up in the water.

At the first busy bus stop on the eastern left bank, Nataliya, 40, and Iryna, 39, are happy to make the crossing over the Northern Bridge. They say they have long got used to the difficulties of war: “The main thing is to get through the first 24 hours at home after the initial discomfort, and then we’ll adapt,” said Nataliya, a customer service specialist.

Iryna added: “If we start to despair, that’s exactly what they want. A bridge can be built. The main thing is that when the attack comes, there are no civilians or military personnel around. It’s just concrete, that’s all. They’ll either repair it or come up with something new.”

It is a core attitude of Kyiv’s remaining residents, who are already contending with hours of electricity shortages and a lack of heating, with the full chill of winter yet to arrive. People want to deal with problems as they arise rather than worrying excessively about what may come – though it is not always easy amid the daily attacks, including a daytime raid on Thursday in which a drone exploded near the Dutch embassy.

Oleksandr, 42, a construction worker, was waiting to get across the bridge. “If the bridges are destroyed we’ll have to leave,” he conceded. If that happened, he and his wife would move to her parents’ house across the river. “I bought them a generator there; they have their own water well. We’d already dug the well during the war. They used to have gas heating, but we’ve converted it to wood-burning. We’re preparing,” he said.

Additional reporting by Galya Rudyk

Source: The Guardian World | Published: 2026-11-21 05:00 UTC

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/21/kyiv-russian-attacks-bridges

item.title: Beating Ebola takes more than medicine – I saw what worked in west Africa a decade ago | Kayode Akintola
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Ebola is terrifying: I know, because I lived through the world’s worst outbreak of the disease. That was in west Africa between 2013 and 2016, when anyone infected by the virus had a nearly 40% chance of dying.

There were 28,600 cases and 11,300 deaths then. Now a rare strain of Ebola is spreading in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, much more quickly than a decade ago in Sierra Leone, Liberia and neighbouring countries. It is the 17th outbreak in DR Congo and already its worst, with more than 5,000 deaths. The UN is warning that the spread of the disease is outstripping the response, and it is widely expected to become the worst Ebola outbreak in history. There is no proven vaccine or treatment yet for the Bundibugyo variant; almost 50% of those infected have died.

The crisis in DR Congo is following a familiar pattern, beginning with the delay in recognising the appearance of the disease, partly because it is in an area scarred by conflict, which in turn accelerates its spread and heightens suspicion, even violence, towards those trying to intervene.

In west Africa 13 years ago, nobody knew how to handle a disease they had never seen before. Touching the body of a victim, even after death, risks infection, so burial without proper protection endangers all those present. But the arrival of anonymous burial teams, swathed in protective gear that made them look like space aliens or evil spirits, and taking away the dead to be buried no one knew where – often in unmarked graves in the early stages – was equally disastrous.

Instead of seeking treatment for victims, families kept them at home and buried them secretly when they died, making it impossible to contain the spread of the disease. It was clear that age-old burial customs had to change, but people weren’t listening to directives from remote officialdom. It took members of their own communities, whom they knew and trusted, to change minds.

Those people were local faith leaders – priests, imams and traditional healers. As the then country director in Sierra Leone and Liberia for Cafod, the Catholic charity, I observed priests finding verses in the Bible and imams doing the same in the Qur’an to persuade people to change their habits in the face of this devastating disease. They succeeded where others had failed to gain a hearing, and played a crucial role in getting the outbreak under control.

Living in Sierra Leone at the time with my wife and two daughters, we all suffered the wider effects of Ebola. Part of my work was to go into the field to manage burial teams, train volunteers, and provide equipment for protection and decontamination. I feared for my own life. When I got home, I would have to tell the girls not to come near me until I had bathed and changed all my clothing. At one point I feared I had caught the disease. It was four days of terror, during which I had to tell my family to keep away from me.

I know what those tackling the outbreak in eastern DR Congo are facing. There have been attacks on clinics and burial teams, and those suffering this violence often find that they are feared and shunned by their own relatives and neighbours.

But the main reason for the virulence of this surge in Ebola is the drastic cut in aid between the last decade and this one.

Not only is the response to the outbreak falling behind, the funding gap is widening. Medical institutions and charities are racing to build, staff and equip treatment and isolation centres, but the UN warns that it could take up to 12 months to bring this latest surge in Ebola to an end – if the money is there.

The lesson of west Africa, however, is that faith-based organisations have a role to play. Tackling Ebola is not just a medical problem.

Source: The Guardian Science | Published: 2026-11-21 06:00 UTC

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/global-development/2026/nov/21/ebola-outbreak-congo-worst-ever

item.title: SpaceX launches classified mission for US Space Force from California
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

SpaceX launches classified mission for US Space Force from California

SpaceX launched a classified mission for the U.S. Space Force tonight (Nov. 20), sending a mystery payload to orbit from California's central coast.

A Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Vandenberg Space Force Base tonight at 11:20 p.m. EST (8:20 p.m. local California time; 0420 GMT on Nov. 21), on a Space Force mission called USSF-317.

The Falcon 9's first stage came back to Earth about 8.5 minutes later, touching down in the Pacific Ocean atop the SpaceX drone ship "Of Course I Still Love You." It was the 11th launch and landing for this booster, which is designated B1100.

SpaceX ended its launch webcast just after that touchdown, so we didn't get to see the Falcon 9's upper stage power its way to orbit.

USSF-317 is a classified mission, so we don't know what the upper stage is carrying or where exactly it's headed. However, some experts think that USSF-317 may be hauling a batch of SpaceX's Starshield satellites to low Earth orbit (LEO) for the Space Force's Space Based Sensing and Targeting portfolio, which helps the military keep tabs on potential targets around the world.

USSF-317 was the 121st Falcon 9 launch of 2026 and the third mission that SpaceX has launched for the Space Force so far in November.

The vast majority of this year's Falcon 9 missions — about 70% of them — have been devoted to building out SpaceX's Starlink LEO internet constellation, which currently consists of more than 11,000 satellites.

The Falcon 9 has been putting up incredible numbers lately — it flew a whopping 165 times in 2025, for example — but the workhorse rocket is on its way out. SpaceX plans to retire both it and the Falcon Heavy in favor of its fully reusable Starship megarocket, which deployed 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites on its most recent two test flights.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

item.title: Math Puzzle: The longest shuffle
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

If you repeatedly shuffle a deck of 10 playing cards using exactly the same method, what is the largest number of shuffles you could need before the deck returns to its original order?

For example, a silly shuffle might simply involve swapping the top and bottom cards, while leaving the rest untouched. After only two applications of this shuffle, the deck is restored. What about for more complicated shuffles? Note: shuffles are based only on the cards’ positions, not the specific card. For example, you can say, “Always move the top card down four positions,” but you cannot say, “Always move the queen of spades down four positions.”

It will take a maximum of 30 shuffles before the deck returns to its original order.

Every shuffle, no matter how complicated, ultimately maps each position in the deck to another position, i.e., a shuffle is some permutation of the deck. Permutations can always be decomposed into discrete cycles. To understand this, consider the example shuffle given below, where the top card ends up in the sixth position, the second card moves to the top, etcetera.

Follow the card that starts on top. The first shuffle moves it to position six, the second moves it from position six to position nine, the third to position two and the fourth back to position one. So it travels around a cycle of four positions: one → six → nine → two → one. Notice that the cards that begin in positions two, six and nine also travel along this same cycle before returning to their original positions. Following the other cards, you’ll find that this shuffle can be decomposed into cycles of lengths four, three, two and one. Every card belongs to some cycle, and no card belongs to two different cycles. (Every position points to one other position and is pointed to from one other position. To take part in two cycles, a position would have to point to two different places or be pointed to from two different places.)

Every shuffle can be decomposed in this way. The length of a cycle represents the number of cards in that cycle, so the lengths always sum to 10. For example, the shuffle that simply takes the top card and puts it on the bottom would create one big cycle of length 10. The vacuous “shuffle” that declines to move any cards decomposes into 10 “cycles” each of length one.

A card in a cycle of length three returns to its starting position after three shuffles and then again after six, nine, 12, and so on. So the whole deck is back in order the first time that every cycle has completed a whole number of trips around. That’s the least common multiple of the cycle lengths. To make the deck take as long as possible to return, we want to split 10 into cycle lengths with the largest possible least common multiple.

Cycles whose lengths share a common factor waste cards. Cycles of four and six, for example, are both back in place after 12 shuffles, but cycles of four and three are as well, and they leave you three additional cards to play with. So the best options use lengths with no common factors. The winner is 5 + 3 + 2 = 10, which takes 5 × 3 × 2 = 30 shuffles.

Fun fact: for a full deck of 52 cards, the longest shuffle uses cycles of length four, five, seven, nine, 11 and 13, plus three cards that stay in their original positions, and it takes 180,180 shuffles to restore the deck.

item.title: What makes rock deep beneath continents break away and sink?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

What makes rock deep beneath continents break away and sink?

Gaby Clark

Scientific Editor

Robert Egan

Senior Editor

We usually picture mountain building as rock being pushed upward. But deep beneath some mountain belts and volcanic arcs, the opposite can happen: dense rock at the base of the crust can become unstable, break away and sink hundreds of kilometers into the mantle, dragging part of the rigid outer shell of the Earth (the lithosphere) with it. Seismic images suggest that this process, known as lithospheric dripping, has occurred beneath the central Andes and California's Sierra Nevada.

What decides whether the rock stays put, sinks as a small drip or pulls a much larger part of the lithosphere down with it? A study led by researchers at Istanbul Technical University (ITU) and published in Terra Nova addresses this question with computer simulations and identifies three distinct outcomes.

"Dense rock beneath continents does not sink the same way everywhere. Our models show that its size and density, together with the density of the layers around it, help determine whether it stays in place, produces a small drip or becomes part of much larger lithospheric removal," said Dr. Açelya Ballı, lead author of the study.

A heavy root beneath a buoyant plate

When continents collide, the crust can thicken to 60–80 kilometers (37–50 miles), and its lowest 20–30 kilometers (12–19 miles) can turn into eclogite, a rock denser than the mantle beneath it. Beneath volcanic arcs, similar dense rock is left behind when magma is extracted. Rock samples suggest, however, that the deep part of old continental plates is chemically depleted and slightly buoyant, so it may not sink on its own.

The team therefore made this layer lighter than the hotter mantle below and asked whether an eclogite root could still pull it down. Eclogite-driven removal has been widely proposed from geological and geophysical evidence, but what controls its style and size has remained unclear.

Three outcomes: stay, small drip or large drip

The team ran 18 simulations with two eclogite shapes, a thick, compact body (25 km (16 miles) thick, 100 km (62 miles) wide) and a thin, broad one (10 km (6 miles) thick, 250 km (155 miles) wide), sized after fast seismic anomalies beneath the Andes, Sierra Nevada and Tibet, and combined them with a range of density contrasts.

In some runs, the eclogite punched through the lithosphere and sank, taking roughly its own volume of lithosphere with it (a small drip). In others, a section of lithosphere about four times larger sank with the eclogite inside it (a large drip). In the rest, nothing moved.

Shape mattered first: only the thick, compact body produced drips, while the thin, broad body stayed in place under every condition tested. Density mattered next. When the eclogite was at most 70 kg/m³ (about 2%) denser than the lithosphere beneath it, nothing sank; the thick body dripped only at 130 kg/m³ (about 4%) and above. Large drips formed only when the lithosphere was just slightly lighter than the mantle below it; otherwise, drips stayed small. These are model results, not universal thresholds, but they set physical limits that can be tested against observations.

Sinking in pulses

In the models, the eclogite did not sink as a single piece. It split and sank in stages, triggering repeated drips. Volcanic records in some arcs show activity in pulses roughly 10–30 million years apart, which has been interpreted as repeated lithospheric removal; in the Altiplano–Puna plateau of the central Andes, two magmatic stages over the past 20 million years have been linked to it. Multistage drips have also been proposed beneath central Tibet and beneath the Konya basin in Central Anatolia, the latter in work co-authored by ITU researchers.

The new results offer a physical explanation: dense roots may be removed in separate pulses rather than all at once. Because the models are two-dimensional and do not simulate melting, the link to volcanism remains a hypothesis to test against field data.

The findings bear on the central Andes, southern Sierra Nevada and Tibet, where lithospheric removal has been proposed, and on passive continental margins such as offshore Norway and the Barents Sea, where eclogite appears to have stayed in place.

"Processes far beneath the surface shape how mountain belts and volcanic regions evolve over millions of years. By identifying what decides whether dense rock stays in place or sinks, and how much material goes with it, we can better read the hidden processes shaping continents from below," said Dr. Oğuz Hakan Göğüş of the Eurasia Institute of Earth Sciences at ITU.

More information

A. Ballı et al., Eclogite Induced Lithospheric Drips: Implications for the Removal of the Lithosphere at Magmatic Arcs and Orogens, Terra Nova (2025). DOI: 10.1111/ter.70008

item.title: Device that measures strawberry skin's strength will aid breeders
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Device that measures strawberry skin's strength will aid breeders

Lisa Lock

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

Resilient strawberry varieties will be more easily identifiable thanks to a tool developed by University of Queensland engineering students. The prototype measures the strength of strawberry skin, a key breeding consideration for the Australian Strawberry Breeding Program at Queensland's Department of Primary Industries.

Queensland Alliance for Agriculture and Food Innovation chemical engineer and food scientist Dr. Jaqueline Moura Nadolny said the industry needed a more objective system for measuring commercial strawberries' susceptibility to abrasion.

"Limiting bruising helps reduce food waste and ensures strawberries meet growing, harvesting and transportation demands," Moura Nadolny said. "Before strawberry varieties are chosen to breed and sell at a commercial level, multiple traits of the crop are tested.

"Strawberry skin resilience is currently measured by a field officer rubbing a finger along a berry once the strawberries are ripe. Although the scale runs from 1 to 9, most strawberries are rated at the higher end of the scale from 7 to 9, which means breeders have very little differentiation between strawberry varieties.

"Being able to broaden this differentiation more would be beneficial to the breeding program."

Moura Nadolny said QAAFI Center for Nutrition and Food Sciences master's student Yen‑An Chen initially assessed abrasion characteristics.

"These included skin toughness, susceptibility to abrasion, resistance to bruising, firmness, surface discoloration and shelf life," Moura Nadolny said. "These characteristics were systematically tested from simple physical manipulation to controlled mechanical tests to see what impact they had on strawberries. This included measuring the force required to damage or break the fruit surface and assessing the degree of tissue damage after impact or compression."

Final-year students at UQ's School of Mechanical and Mining Engineering then used these abrasion parameters to design the measurement tool.

Mechanical engineering lecturer Dr. Tristan Vanyai said the tool measured how a strawberry was impacted by abrasion. "It works by spinning a rubber wheel against the strawberry's skin, measuring force and torque, which is how much pressure they can take," Vanyai said.

DPI senior plant breeder Dr. Katie O'Connor said the tool was promising. "It allows us to identify potential commercial strawberry varieties for our breeding program," O'Connor said. "These varieties could be better suited to new tabletop growing systems or harvesting systems, like robotic harvesting.

"The new device takes a bit longer than the manual way of testing but is so much better and simple to use. It's still a prototype but once we iron out some wrinkles, we have a device we can use."

Vanyai said the tool was proof of the importance of cross-industry partnerships. "Working with external clients gives students a perspective on how their work can really help," Vanyai said.

Provided by University of Queensland

item.title: Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Microplastics may be more dangerous than we thought. Scientists just discovered why

- Date:

- November 20, 2026

- Source:

- Columbia University

- Summary:

- Microplastics may be doing something far more dangerous than simply accumulating in our bodies. Scientists have discovered that tiny plastic particles can interact with water to generate highly reactive molecules capable of damaging cells and tissues. This unexpected chemical activity could help explain growing evidence linking microplastic exposure to serious health problems, including heart attacks, strokes, and neurological disorders.

- Share:

Plastic is used in everything from food packaging and water bottles to children's toys, largely because it is considered chemically stable and unlikely to react with its surroundings. However, new research suggests that this assumption may not hold when plastic breaks down into extremely small particles.

As larger plastic objects fragment into microplastics and even smaller nanoplastics, the amount of exposed surface area increases dramatically. Scientists have now discovered that these newly exposed surfaces can interact with water in unexpected ways, producing reactive molecules that may harm living cells.

Researchers at Columbia University and the University of California, Berkeley identified the chemical processes behind this phenomenon in a new study published in Nature. Their findings challenge the longstanding idea that microplastics are simply passive fragments of material.

"As plastic fragments into smaller and smaller particles, its surface area increases enormously. Then microplastics change the water that surrounds them, generating high-energy, reactive radicals (reactive oxygen species, ROS) that very likely contribute to biological damage that we see in animals and potentially in humans as a result of microplastic exposure," said Wei Min, a Columbia professor of Chemistry and Biomedical Engineering.

Why Microplastics Could Be Dangerous Inside the Human Body

The discovery raises important questions about what happens when microplastics enter the human body. Blood and cells contain large amounts of water, creating conditions in which these tiny particles could continue participating in chemical reactions.

Rather than remaining inactive after exposure, microplastics may generate reactive oxygen species, often called ROS. These highly reactive molecules can damage biological structures, including components of cells and tissues. The findings offer a possible explanation for some of the harmful effects associated with microplastic exposure, although they do not establish that this process causes specific diseases in humans.

The research builds on earlier work by Min's laboratory that helped reveal just how widespread microscopic plastic contamination has become.

In a widely reported 2024 study, the Columbia researchers developed a laser-based microscopy technique capable of detecting extremely small plastic particles. Using this technology, they found an average of approximately 240,000 detectable plastic fragments in a single liter of bottled water (mostly nanometer-sized plastic, nanoplastics). That was 10 to 100 times more particles than previous estimates had suggested.

The discovery helped draw greater attention to the presence of microplastics and nanoplastics throughout the food system.

Growing Concerns About Microplastics and Human Health

Since that earlier research attracted widespread attention, the potential health consequences of microplastic exposure have become an increasingly important public health issue.

In 2026, the federal government launched a $144 million initiative focused on addressing toxic microplastics in the human body. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency also added microplastics to a federal list of contaminants that may be of concern in drinking water, marking their first appearance on the list.

Meanwhile, studies published in major scientific journals, including the New England Journal of Medicine, Nature Medicine, and Nature Health, have reported associations between exposure to microplastics and nanoplastics and serious conditions such as heart attacks, strokes, dementia, and brain tumors.

However, an important question has remained unanswered. If plastic is generally considered chemically inert, how might these microscopic fragments contribute to biological damage?

The new findings identify a previously overlooked chemical pathway that could help researchers understand these potential health risks.

"Our research found that when microplastics interact with water, as they do when they're in bottled water, or when they're absorbed into our bloodstream, they spontaneously generate what we call reactive oxygen species (ROS)," said Naixin Qian, a postdoctoral researcher in Wei Min's lab who helped lead the research. "ROS are textbook examples of the kinds of molecules that can damage animal and human tissue."

How Water Triggers Harmful Chemical Reactions

One of the most surprising aspects of the discovery is that water plays an active role in the reaction.

Many plastics are hydrophobic, meaning their surfaces repel water. When water encounters these surfaces, the molecules and electrically charged particles near the boundary can behave differently than they do in ordinary water.

The researchers found that these interactions can encourage electrons to move between chemical species, allowing highly reactive radicals to form. As plastic fragments become smaller, their greater surface area provides more locations where these reactions can occur.

"Water is a key active player here, rather than just a spectator. It's integral to making these microplastics reactive. Water molecules become chemically active when they come into contact with plastic, which is hydrophobic. Contact between the water and plastic creates an environment that facilitates electron transfer, and the formation of reactive radicals. When plastics fragment into smaller particles, their increasing surface-to-volume ratio creates more of these chemically active areas," Min said.

To investigate the process, the Columbia researchers performed chemical and biological experiments. Their collaborators in Professor Teresa Head-Gordon's laboratory at UC Berkeley used theoretical calculations and computer simulations to examine the interactions between plastic surfaces and water at the molecular level.

The Berkeley team developed a theoretical explanation showing how hydroxide ions, which are negatively charged particles, can become concentrated in the layers of water immediately surrounding a water-repelling plastic surface. In this environment, the ions can more readily lose electrons and form hydroxyl radicals.

Hydroxyl radicals are particularly reactive chemical species capable of damaging biological molecules. Their formation provides a possible link between the physical breakdown of plastics and the biological effects researchers have observed.

Could the Discovery Lead to Safer Plastics?

Understanding the chemistry involved could eventually help scientists develop plastics that are less likely to generate harmful reactive molecules when exposed to water.

"Our fundamental work that the most hydrophobic microplastics interacting with water can drive chemical reactivity could ultimately lead to new engineering solutions by redesigning the chemistry of these commodity plastics to reduce the toxic outcomes on health and the environment," said Head-Gordon.

The implications also extend beyond human health. Microplastics can enter rivers, lakes, and other waterways through industrial waste, wastewater, and everyday activities. The newly identified chemical reactions could influence aquatic organisms and ecosystems exposed to these particles.…

item.title: Upskilling health professionals to deliver emotional well-being support for people with diabetes
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Upskilling health professionals to deliver emotional well-being support for people with diabetes

Sadie Harley

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

For more than 1.5 million Australians living with diabetes, managing their condition is a relentless, 24-hour responsibility. Day after day, people are required to make decisions about medications, glucose monitoring, food, physical activity and other aspects of their care—largely outside the health care system.

This substantial and often unseen work is fundamental to living well with diabetes and reducing the risk of complications. Yet the emotional burden it places on people is too often overlooked.

As health psychology researcher Dr. Edith Holloway, Deakin Institute for Health Transformation (DIHT) senior research fellow at The Australian Center for Behavioral Research in Diabetes (ACBRD), explains, "Up to one in two people with diabetes experience mental health and emotional challenges, such as diabetes distress, which affects their ability to self-manage their condition.

"When people are struggling emotionally, it can become much harder to manage medications, glucose levels, eating, physical activity and engagement with health professionals—this impacts their diabetes health outcomes and can increase the risk of complications."

Inadequate emotional support undermines diabetes self-management

Currently, diabetes costs the Australian health system AU$14.2 billion. Projections indicate the number of Australians living with diabetes will double to 3 million by 2030, increasing the pressure on diabetes services and the broader Australian health system.

Without emotional support to ease diabetes distress and encourage self-management, people with diabetes face increased risk of emergency admissions, hospitalizations and long-term complications. This includes people with limited access to face-to-face diabetes care, such as people living in remote and rural Australia.

"From our needs assessments, we know people with diabetes want to talk to their diabetes health professionals about the emotional side of living with diabetes. We know emotional challenges can be supported during routine diabetes care before they escalate to mental health conditions, which are more costly to the health system and require specialist care."

Upskilling more diabetes health professionals to deliver LISTEN

Because diabetes educators, nurses and dietitians understand the complexities of living with diabetes, they are well positioned as trusted health care professionals to provide timely emotional support to people with diabetes before problems escalate.

The proven early intervention LISTEN (Low-Intensity Support To ENhance emotional well-being in diabetes care) reduces diabetes distress, increases emotional well-being and improves diabetes self-management.

To develop a larger workforce to provide emotional support to more people with diabetes, health professionals can now upskill in LISTEN via a two-stage structured training and accreditation pathway.

The first stage is a self-paced LISTEN e-learning course that provides a foundation for understanding diabetes distress and low-intensity emotional support. This course helps participants develop practical interpersonal skills, including empathy, reflective listening, validating emotions and person-centered communication that can be applied immediately to routine care.

Holloway and fellow researchers at the ACBRD, Deakin University and DIHT co-developed the self-paced course in partnership with Diabetes Victoria. Moving this foundational component from in-person workshops to e-learning makes the training more accessible and gives busy health professionals greater flexibility to complete it around their clinical commitments.

Health professionals seeking to become accredited LISTEN facilitators undertake a second stage of further training, including supervised practice, where they demonstrate they can competently deliver the intervention in accordance with the LISTEN framework.

Aspiring to support all Australians living with diabetes

Importantly, the Australian Diabetes Educators Association (ADEA), the nation's peak body for diabetes education, management and care, has endorsed the online course.

Holloway said scaling and translating the program into routine care is a key piece of the commercialization strategy: "We can't provide LISTEN to all Australians with diabetes if we don't have the health workforce trained and upskilled in how to deliver it."

Workforce upskilling reaches more people with diabetes

While the LISTEN e-learning course is still in its early post-launch marketing phase, ADEA's endorsement and promotion to its more than 3,000 health professional members, including around 2,000 diabetes educators, strengthens LISTEN's impact.

"People with diabetes have been asking for emotional support for a long time. And health professionals want to support their patients and clients, but currently don't have the skills, resources and tools to do that. LISTEN addresses this gap in diabetes care. We have the capability now, with this training, to support around 750,000 Australians who are experiencing emotional challenges," said Holloway.

Better coping for healthier outcomes

In a recent trial, people with type 1 and type 2 diabetes who accessed up to four LISTEN sessions via a trained LISTEN facilitator had significant reductions in diabetes distress, as well as significant improvements in emotional well-being and coping skills, compared to a matched group receiving routine diabetes care.

"The LISTEN program helped people with diabetes be more engaged with their health professionals—exercising more, eating healthier food, monitoring glucose levels more regularly and taking their medication when required. The impact of enhancing all these self-management behaviors is critical for improving physical and clinical outcomes, as well as potential cost savings."

Holloway recently shared her team's research on mental health in diabetes care with government policymakers to help them understand the program's health sector and societal cost benefits. Economic modeling showed that scaling LISTEN nationally could generate AU$2.1 billion in net savings by preventing crisis care, cutting avoidable health system costs and boosting productivity.

Ideally, making LISTEN sessions available for Australians through diabetes services and the Medicare-supported Chronic Condition Management Plan would expand emotional support for people with diabetes and broaden the program's impact. "It's a big undertaking to lobby the government. We've had conversations around the policy implications, and it's something we're working toward."

item.title: Major data gap for gut disorders leaves Aotearoa in the dark
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Major data gap for gut disorders leaves Aotearoa in the dark

Lisa Lock

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

A lack of up-to-date New Zealand research into common gut disorders means the country is effectively flying blind on conditions that may affect about 1 in 3 adults, University of Otago research suggests.

Dr. Simone Bayer and research colleagues from the University of Otago have reviewed all available evidence in Aotearoa on disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBI)—a group of chronic conditions including irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) and functional dyspepsia. Their findings, published in the New Zealand Medical Journal, reveal a striking lack of contemporary data on how common these conditions are, who is affected and what costs they incur to our health system.

Only four New Zealand studies reporting the prevalence of DGBI were identified, with the most recent published in 2002. The studies were limited to Wellington and Dunedin, and none provided prevalence data for Māori or Pacific peoples.

"People living with these conditions can experience significant and ongoing symptoms, yet we don't have any strong contemporary evidence telling us how many New Zealanders are affected," Bayer says. "That means we are also unable to properly comprehend the scale of demand on our health system, or whether different groups of New Zealanders are experiencing these conditions and accessing care in different ways."

DGBI, formerly known as functional gastrointestinal disorders, affect the way the gut functions without an identifiable structural or organic disease being found. Symptoms can include abdominal pain, changes in bowel habits and indigestion.

Internationally, the conditions are common. Research from the United Kingdom and Australia (which both have comparable publicly funded health systems) using contemporary diagnostic criteria found that approximately 37% of adults meet the criteria for at least one DGBI.

Using U.K. estimates of direct health care costs for IBS as a conservative proxy, the researchers estimate that if one-third of New Zealand's adult population has a DGBI, direct health care costs could be about NZ$1.6 billion a year.

Bayer stresses that this is a modeled estimate, rather than a direct measurement of New Zealand's current costs. "However, even this conservative estimate points to a substantial burden. The important message is that we simply do not have the New Zealand data needed to understand the problem properly," she explains.

The researchers found the evidence gap is particularly concerning for Māori, with no study identified measuring DGBI prevalence in Māori. They say future research should be designed from the outset to produce Māori-specific estimates and be undertaken in partnership with Māori health researchers and communities.

The paper also highlights the potential economic consequences of DGBI, which can involve repeated primary care visits, specialist referrals, investigations and medication, as well as lost productivity through absenteeism, reduced productivity at work and leaving the workforce early.

Bayer says the findings demonstrate the need for dedicated research investment. "We need to know how common these conditions really are in Aotearoa, how they affect different communities and what they are costing patients and the health system," she says. "A national prevalence study, alongside a formal analysis of health care costs using New Zealand health data, would give us the evidence needed to improve diagnosis, treatment and planning."

Publication details

Simone Bayer et al., Disorders of gut–brain interaction in Aotearoa New Zealand: a long-standing evidence gap with unmeasured health and economic consequences, New Zealand Medical Journal (2026). DOI: 10.26635/6965.7608

Journal information: New Zealand Medical Journal

item.title: 'Pan-RAS molecular glue' is a safe and effective treatment for lung and pancreatic cancers
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

'Pan-RAS molecular glue' is a safe and effective treatment for lung and pancreatic cancers

Sadie Harley

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

Results from the AURORAS-1 Phase I clinical trial of an anticancer drug called ERAS-0015 have shown that it is safe and has caused tumors to shrink in hard-to-treat diseases such as lung and pancreatic cancer.

Presented at the 38th EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics in Barcelona, Spain, the findings from 148 patients are significant because ERAS-0015 targets tumors whose growth is driven by mutations in the RAS gene. Until recently, it was not thought possible to design drugs that could target these mutations successfully.

Dr. Judy Wang, a medical oncologist at Florida Cancer Specialists and Research Institute, Sarasota, U.S., told the symposium, "AURORAS-1 has enrolled patients who have tried a number of other treatments for their cancer. In this context, ERAS-0015 treatment caused a 44% response rate in patients with RAS-mutant pancreatic cancer and a 60% response rate in patients with RAS-mutant lung cancer.

"A 'response' means the patients experienced considerable tumor shrinkage, and these response rates are important as they show clinically meaningful activity from ERAS-0015 treatment in patient groups that have few if any therapeutic options to address their cancer.

"In addition to this, ERAS-0015 was well tolerated with few severe side effects."

ERAS-0015 is a "pan-RAS molecular glue," which means that it brings proteins together at the molecular level in a way that blocks tumor growth signals from several different cancer-driving RAS mutations. Certain RAS mutations work like a switch that is locked in the "on" position, continuously conveying signals that lead to and sustain cancer. ERAS-0015 is designed to bind to the RAS "switch" while it is in the 'on' state and thereby blocks those signals.

"The overall goal of precision oncology is to match a patient's mutation, or the 'Achilles heel' of a specific individual's cancer, to a drug that directly targets that mutation. This is what we are attempting to do by studying the effectiveness of ERAS-0015 in patients with RAS alterations," said Wang.

The AURORAS-1 trial started in June 2025 and is evaluating ERAS-0015 on its own and in combination with other anticancer therapies in people living with several types of RAS-mutant solid tumors. Enrolled patients have non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) that has started to spread beyond the site of the primary tumor (locally advanced or metastatic), pancreatic cancer, colorectal (bowel) cancer and other solid tumors.

The results presented were for 83 patients with pancreatic cancer and 37 with NSCLC; the trial is continuing to enroll patients.

Doses of ERAS-0015 started at 2 mg and increased up to 40 mg. During an average (median) follow-up period of just over four months, there was no sign that the maximum tolerated dose had been reached.

Tumors shrank in 11 of 25 patients (44%) with pancreatic cancer who received 32 mg of ERAS-0015 and who had been previously treated with chemotherapy. Tumors shrank in three of five patients (60%) with lung cancer who received 32 mg and who had been treated previously with an immune checkpoint inhibitor or platinum-based chemotherapy.

The most common adverse side effects at doses of 16–32 mg in 10% or more of patients were rash, diarrhea, nausea and inflammation of the lining of the mouth. Twelve patients (9.8%) reported severe (grade 3 or higher) treatment-related side effects. No side effects limited the drug doses.

"We are encouraged by the preliminary clinical activity and tolerability of ERAS-0015 in patients who have tried a number of other treatments for RAS-driven lung and pancreatic cancer," said Wang.

"Our goal is to give clinicians new, better options for treating their patients with RAS-driven cancers. Early results suggest ERAS-0015 has the potential to be one of these options."

Limitations of the study are those associated with Phase I trials that always include only a limited number of patients. Further study in greater numbers of patients and in Phase II and III clinical trials is needed to confirm the safety and efficacy of ERAS-0015.

"If these early results are confirmed, ERAS-0015 could offer patients with RAS-driven cancers a new option. Clinical development of ERAS-0015 would be impossible without the patients, caregivers, investigators and participating trial centers that put their trust in us to take part in our study. We are deeply grateful for their contribution to AURORAS-1," she concluded.

Elena Garralda, chair of the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium and co-director of the Vall d'Hebron Institute of Oncology's clinical research program, was not involved with the study.

She commented, "This is the first presentation of these preliminary results from the AURORAS-1 clinical trial and they have been eagerly awaited. They show that the RAS inhibitor, ERAS-0015, has encouraging antitumor activity in cancers that are hard to treat successfully and for which there are few treatment options available. We look forward to further results from larger clinical trials, which are investigating whether ERAS-0015 can help a broader group of patients.

"This is one of several studies being presented at the EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium that are beginning to show it is possible to design drugs that target cancers driven by RAS mutations, which was not thought possible until recently."

More information

Preliminary safety, pharmacokinetics, and efficacy of ERAS-0015: Results from the AURORAS-1 first-in-human trial, 38th EORTC-NCI-AACR Symposium on Molecular Targets and Cancer Therapeutics, Barcelona, Spain, 18–20 November 2026.

Source: Medical Xpress | Published: 2026-11-21 02:40 UTC

item.title: Mental health diagnoses rise with medical complexity, chronicity in children
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Mental health diagnoses rise with medical complexity, chronicity in children

Sadie Harley

Scientific Editor

Andrew Zinin

Chief Editor

The prevalence of mental health (MH) diagnoses increases with increasing medical complexity and chronicity in Medicaid-enrolled children, according to a study published in Pediatrics.

Maria Newmaster, M.D., from Children's Mercy Kansas City in Missouri, and colleagues compared the prevalence of MH diagnoses across categories of complex and chronic conditions in a retrospective cross-sectional study of 2.9 million children aged 5 to 17 years from the Marketscan Medicaid Database in 2022.

The presence of a mood or anxiety MH diagnosis (anxiety, depression, bipolar, obsessive-compulsive disorders, trauma-related disorders and suicide/self-injury) coded at one inpatient/emergency department or two outpatient encounters was examined as the outcome.

The researchers observed an increase in the prevalence of MH diagnoses with increasing medical complexity and chronicity: 7.6%, 16.0% and 20.0% in noncomplex/nonchronic conditions, noncomplex chronic conditions (NCCCs) and complex chronic conditions (CCCs), respectively.

Among children with a CCC, the cardiac, neurologic and renal categories had the greatest odds of MH diagnoses (odds ratios, 1.49, 1.18 and 1.13, respectively). Compared with non-Hispanic white children, Black and Hispanic children had lower odds of MH diagnoses among youth with NCCCs or CCCs.

"These results carry profound implications given the associated increased risk of health care utilization, economic burden, disease exacerbation and poor quality of life," the authors write.

"Understanding specific NCCC and CCC categories and sociodemographic characteristics of patients at greatest odds of having comorbid MH conditions may enable clinicians to improve screening and intervention efforts and promote health equity among medically vulnerable populations."

Publication details

Maria Newmaster et al., Mental Health Diagnoses Among Children With and Without Complex and Chronic Conditions, Pediatrics (2026). DOI: 10.1542/peds.2026-076830

Journal information: Pediatrics
