item.title: NI doctors' strike due to end, with separate walkout planned for Monday
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

NI doctors' strike due to end, with separate walkout planned for Monday

- Published

A 24-hour strike by resident doctors in Northern Ireland is due to end at 07:00 GMT on Saturday.

But consultants and specialist doctors will begin a separate 24-hour strike on Monday, as part of the same pay dispute.

The British Medical Association (BMA) rejected a recommended 3.5% pay rise and wants to restore the value of doctors' pay to 2008 levels.

Health Minister, Robbie Butler, said he had accepted the recommended rise but could not implement it without sufficient funding for his department.

Friday's strike action by resident doctors affected non-emergency services, resulting in the cancellation of many planned outpatient appointments.

Urgent surgery and most GP services continued as normal because senior doctors remained on duty.

How will patients be affected on Monday?

Monday's walkout will involve consultants and specialty, associate specialist and specialist grade (SAS) doctors and will also take place over 24 hours from 07:00 on Monday.

Routine hospital and elective services are expected to be cancelled during the second strike.

But emergency care will continue under Christmas Day cover - which means full emergency cover will remain in place.

The Western and South Eastern health trusts have asked patients with appointments on Monday to attend as planned, unless their trust tells them otherwise.

The South Eastern Trust said the urgent care centre at Lagan Valley Hospital would be closed on Monday and that postponed appointments and procedures would be rescheduled as soon as possible.

Butler said more than 2,200 appointments were cancelled during similar strikes in June and warned the latest action would have "real consequences for patients, waiting lists and service delivery".

Why are doctors striking?

The BMA says years of below-inflation pay rises have made it harder for Northern Ireland's health service to recruit and retain doctors.

Dr Seamus Crumley, an anaesthetics registrar who works in intensive care at the Ulster Hospital, joined Friday's picket line in Belfast.

He told BBC News NI he had taken a pay cut when he moved from Scotland last year, despite securing a more senior role.

"The medical workforce here is very, very vulnerable to losing doctors to literally anywhere else in the UK, but also to the Republic of Ireland," he said.

Dr Steven Montgomery, who chairs the BMA's Northern Ireland Resident Doctors Committee, said his colleagues were facing burnout and emotional distress because of pressure at work.

He said the union was "not looking for this all to be paid in one lump sum" and wanted the minister to set out a plan to restore pay over time.

Dr OisÃn Fearon, a resident doctor in Belfast, told BBC News NI he had considered moving to Australia, but family and local ties had kept him in Northern Ireland.

He said he had begun the process of registering to train in the Republic of Ireland and was keeping that option open.

What has the health minister said?

Butler said he had met the BMA to explain the financial pressures facing his department, external and intended to implement the recommended award as soon as possible.

He said cumulative pay rises over the previous three years averaged 30% for resident doctors, 25% for SAS doctors and 24% for consultants.

Butler said the recommended rise was higher than that for other healthcare staff and warned that going beyond 3.5% would have "significant repercussions for nurses, teachers, police officers and indeed the entire public sector workforce".

Separately, the Northern Ireland Public Service Alliance (Nipsa) released the results of a recent ballot of its health and social care members.

It said 94% of its health and social care members backed strike action, while 97% backed action short of a strike, over growing pressures on the health and social care sector.

The union said it would consider its next steps and warned that coordinated industrial action could spread across the health service in the coming weeks.

item.title: Sales of baby sleeping bag halted by Next after new mum raises alarm
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Sales of baby sleeping bag halted by Next after new mum raises alarm

- Published

Sales of a baby sleeping bag have been halted in the UK by fashion retail chain Next, after a new mum raised the alarm over its safety.

Emma Hunter, 29 from Norwich, contacted BBC Your Voice to say she realised the neck hole was far too big - meaning her daughter Rosie could potentially wriggle down, burying her face and risking suffocation.

Emma recalls: "I woke up my husband and we both agreed there was no way we could put Rosie in it."

Next says its own-brand, 2.5 tog pink floral sleep bag with removable sleeves that comes in three sizes, has been removed from the website and stores and a product recall is under way.

Next will contact and advise customers who purchased the item from them.

A spokesperson for Next said: "We can confirm the item has been removed from our website and all stores. A product recall is in place, and we are contacting all customers who purchased the item directly to advise them of the appropriate next steps."

Emma says she started doing her own research that same night she realised the sleeping bag was unsuitable for Rosie.

Although the product had a label stating that it met British standards, Emma discovered that the maximum neck circumference for that size of bag should be 32cm. When she measured the bag, the neck hole was 36cm.

According to the British Retail Consortium (BRC), a significant hazard arises if a child slips through the neck opening of a sleep bag and the material covers the child's nose and mouth.

They state that "suffocation can occur and may lead to the brain becoming starved of oxygen, which may result in asphyxia and potential brain damage or fatality."

To limit this hazard, the EN 16781 standard specifies a maximum and minimum size for the neck opening circumference in relation to the child's height.

For example, a sleep bag designed for a child 50 cm to 65 cm tall should have a minimum neck circumference of 28 cm and a maximum of 32 cm.

Rosie, who is now three and a half months old, measured 59cm at the time the bag was bought.

After flagging these issues to the company, Emma says she was surprised by their initial reaction.

"They seemed quite laissez faire about it and just offered me a refund, but I said 'it's dangerous, surely you shouldn't be selling it any more and there should be a product recall?'"

Emma was told by Next that they were looking into it and that their product team was examining the bag and would feed back.

Check the gap around the neck

Emma's older brother died of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) as a baby so the risk to babies from suffocation is something close to her heart.

She told the BBC: "I am more aware of this because of what happened to my brother and my family, but it shouldn't take an infant mortality to see change.

"They didn't have any sense of urgency about it at all and I expected a big high street store like that to have a certain standard. You put your trust into these retailers.

"How can a product have a label on it saying it met the British standard, when it clearly didn't?"

Ruth Watts, who is a qualified health visitor in England, says that babies will differ in terms of size and height, despite their age.

But if a sleeping bag covers the chin or face in any way it should not be used.

"The best thing to do is check the gap around the neck. If you can fit one to two fingers around the neck then that's safe. If it's any tighter or looser than that, then you shouldn't use it," she recommends.

The Lullaby Trust is a UK charity that works to prevent sudden, unexpected infant deaths, including SIDS.

CEO Jenny Ward told BBC News that the charity could not comment on the safety of specific products, since it does not carry out independent product safety testing.

But she encourages families to check that any product they use has passed the necessary safety checks and meets British Safety Standards.

She said: "Remember to follow the manufacturer's instructions and if a family is worried about any product we would say to stop using it and contact the manufacturer.

"We support the Office for Product Safety and Standards' recent warning on certain baby sleep bags and would urge families to ensure a sleep bag fits well before they use it."

People can check if any products have been recalled by visiting the OPSS website, external.

Source: BBC Health | Published: 2026-11-21 00:02 UTC

item.title: How to Build an MVP App: Core Features vs Full Build
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

When figuring out how to build an MVP app, the most important step is defining the smallest version of your product that you can launch to solve a real user problem. Founders and developers often face the temptation to pack every possible feature into the initial release. Building an application triggers the urge to pile on user management, complex dashboards, and multi-layered permissions before writing a production line of code. The lean startup methodology counters this by forcing a strict definition of actual utility.

Understanding the minimum viable product approach

An MVP focuses strictly on the core problem your users face daily while cutting out secondary features like dark mode or deep analytics for version one. This approach reduces initial infrastructure and maintenance costs significantly while speeding up the time it takes to get real user feedback in production.

- Focuses strictly on the core problem your users face daily.

- Cuts out secondary features like dark mode or deep analytics for version one.

- Reduces initial infrastructure and maintenance costs significantly.

- Speeds up the time it takes to get real user feedback in production.

Identifying the core value feature

Finding the single feature that drives user value requires looking past what people say they want and watching what they actually do. When software projects stall, it is often because engineers spend weeks optimizing components that do not move user metrics. Technical efficiency matters, but writing clean code for the wrong feature wastes months of development time.

In your MVP, identify that single bottleneck or core workflow and build only around it. If your app connects service providers to customers, the core feature is the direct booking action, not the profile customization screen or the in-app chat. Prioritizing this singular path allows small engineering teams to ship faster and validate market assumptions without burning through capital on unproven ideas.

Managing technical debt and infrastructure costs

Every shortcut taken during early development introduces technical debt, but an MVP requires deliberate shortcuts to survive. The key is separating dangerous architectural debt from acceptable implementation shortcuts. Hardcoding configuration variables for a week is fine, but building a database schema that cannot handle basic relational queries will break your app by month two.

When scaling up a product later, systematic code restructuring becomes necessary to handle modern demands. Founders managing early infrastructure should keep cloud bills low by using managed serverless functions or simple Postgres instances rather than over-provisioning Kubernetes clusters. Monitoring resource usage early prevents unexpected cloud provider bills from cutting your runway short.

FAQ

What is mvp in mobile app development?

An MVP is the earliest functional version of a mobile application that includes only the core features needed to solve a specific user problem and gather feedback.

How long does it take to build an app?

Most focused MVP mobile applications take between six to twelve weeks to design, build, and launch when the feature set is kept strictly minimal.

How do I choose which features to cut?

Ask whether the app fails to solve the primary user problem if the feature is removed. If the answer is no, cut it from the first release.

Sources

Originally published at sundarprakash.in/blog/how-to-build-an-mvp-app by Sundar Prakash P.

item.title: When you replace a library, you also take over everything it did
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

DPOLens is an open-source MCP server that gives AI assistants the text of privacy law. Its search runs on the CPU, so it needs no GPU.

The usual way to run an embedding model in Python is sentence-transformers. DPOLens doesn't use it: with PyTorch's CPU build it installs about 1 GB, against about 200 MB for ONNX Runtime, the tokenizers library and NumPy. So DPOLens calls the model through ONNX Runtime directly, and does the tokenising and pooling itself, in about forty lines.

Those forty lines did their job. What they didn't do was what the library does without being asked. When a new instance starts for the first time, it embeds every clause of the law it carries, and while load-testing the community version, I found that this was the heaviest thing DPOLens ever did. In a container limited to 1.5 CPUs, about what a small server offers, it took nearly 23 minutes and peaked at 3.4 GB.

Two fixes made it 5.1× faster with 65% less memory, and the vectors came out the same. If you've swapped sentence-transformers for raw ONNX Runtime to slim an image, you probably have both problems too.

The setup

DPOLens's meaning search uses multilingual-e5-small. A new instance embeds GDPR, the UAE's data protection law and a sample company policy: 1,350 clauses, from 19 to 512 tokens long, 63 in the middle. The vectors go into Postgres with pgvector, so this happens once, before the instance answers anything.

Every run below embedded those 1,350 clauses inside the published DPOLens 0.1.0 image, the release before the fixes, from a fresh copy of the same database, with 4 GB of memory and a Docker CPU limit: 1.5 CPUs, 2.5 (what the community version gives this step), or none, which on my laptop is 10 cores.

What the library was doing: sorting by length

A model reads a batch as one rectangle. Every string is padded to the longest in its batch, and the padding costs as much work as the text.

sentence-transformers sorts its inputs by length before it batches them, so each batch holds strings of about one length. My forty lines didn't. They embedded 64 clauses at a time in the order they're stored, so a 20-token paragraph next to a 512-token article was read as 512 tokens. I counted: the clauses hold 110,000 real tokens, and the model read 304,000. Almost two thirds of its work was padding.

Padding costs memory too, and more than its share: the memory for attention grows with the number of strings in a batch times the square of the longest. A batch of 64 strings at 512 tokens was the heaviest shape 0.1.0 could make, and in stored order, every batch with one long article had that shape. Sorting alone doesn't prevent it, since the library still batches by count, so the fix also caps each batch by that measure, in the spirit of --max-batch-tokens in Hugging Face's Text Embeddings Inference:

# How much one batch may hold, as its clauses times the square of the longest,

# which is how the memory for attention grows: 64 clauses of 64 tokens, 16 of

# 128, or one of 512.

BATCH_BUDGET = 64 * 64 * 64

def batches(tokens: Sequence[int]) -> list[list[int]]:

found: list[list[int]] = []

batch: list[int] = []

for at in sorted(range(len(tokens)), key=lambda position: tokens[position]):

# Sorted, so this string is the longest the batch would hold.

if batch and (len(batch) + 1) * tokens[at] ** 2 > BATCH_BUDGET:

found.append(batch)

batch = []

batch.append(at)

if batch:

found.append(batch)

return found

Sorted and capped, the model reads 114,000 tokens instead of 304,000, and the longest clauses go one at a time. Budgets from half this one to eight times it were no better.

What nobody was doing: reading the CPU limit

The second problem isn't the library's.

Inside a container limited to 2.5 CPUs on a 10-core machine, Python's os.cpu_count() says 10, and ONNX Runtime, left to choose, starts a thread for each of them. A Docker CPU limit isn't a set of cores but a share of time, so ten threads took turns on two and a half CPUs' worth of it.

dpolens index build now reads the limit from /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max and rounds it up, so 2.5 CPUs get three threads. With no limit, it takes os.process_cpu_count(), which follows CPU affinity but not a time limit. Picking a fixed number doesn't work: three threads were the best with 2.5 CPUs, and with no limit they took 143 seconds, slower than 0.1.0's 129 with all ten.

The results

With 2.5 CPUs, each fix on its own, then both:

The two sorted rows in the middle used a budget four times the one that shipped. Threads changed the time and nothing else. Sorting changed both.

Then 0.2.0, which shipped both, against 0.1.0 at each limit:

The gain is largest where the machine is smallest, which is where a 23-minute first start gets noticed. The peak after, 1,213 MiB at every limit, is exactly what loading the model takes before embedding anything: embedding the whole law now adds nothing measurable to it.

Same vectors, same search

Padding is masked, so in theory it changes nothing. I checked anyway. 885 of the 1,350 vectors were bit-identical to 0.1.0's, and the rest differed by at most 0.00000011 in any component, the rounding of a batch with a different shape. Every published evaluation set scored the same recall@5, recall@10 and MRR, and a test now checks that each clause's stored vector is the one it gets embedded alone.

One more: memory that wasn't given back

Measuring the first start also caught DPOLens's worker, which embeds an organisation's policies, loading its own copy of the model for jobs with nothing left to embed, and keeping it. Closing the model wasn't enough either: glibc keeps freed memory for the process, so a process that held 875 MiB with the model loaded still held 440 after closing it, and 93 after malloc_trim(0). The worker now loads the model only when there's work, and gives the memory back after. It doesn't change what an instance needs, but it frees about 900 MB between jobs.

What I took from it

- A library is more than its API. Forty lines replaced sentence-transformers and kept the image about 800 MB smaller, and they also dropped the sorting the library does without saying so.

- Sort before you batch, then cap by shape. A batch's memory grows with its strings times the square of the longest, so that's what to limit.

-

A container's CPU limit isn't its core count. os.cpu_count() and ONNX Runtime both see the whole machine. Read /sys/fs/cgroup/cpu.max, and don't hard-code a number instead.

- Check the vectors, not only the clock. The same search results are the only reason the change could ship.

Everything here was measured on one laptop, with one model, over clauses whose lengths vary a lot: text of one length would gain little from sorting, and your seconds will differ. The batching is in index.py, the thread count in encode.py, and every measurement, including the options I didn't take, in #68. Both fixes shipped in DPOLens 0.2.0. To run an instance yourself, start with Get started. DPOLens is open source, under the Apache License 2.0.

First published on dpolens.com. DPOLens is an open-source MCP server that gives AI assistants privacy law and an organisation's own policies, clause by clause: github.com/alkhatibdev/dpolens.

item.title: Startup sues Apple in India over tap-to-share contacts feature
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Apple is being sued in India by a U.S.-based startup that alleges the iPhone maker’s NameDrop feature, which lets users share contact information by bringing devices close together, infringes its patented technology.

GG Technologies, the startup behind StayTouch, an app that lets users exchange contact details by bringing their phones close together, is seeking ₹15 billion (about $161.86 million) in damages and an injunction against Apple, per court documents reviewed by TechCrunch.

Santa Monica-headquartered GG Technologies filed the lawsuit in India in October after mediation proceedings initiated in April failed in September, the startup told TechCrunch. Pre-institution mediation is generally required before filing commercial lawsuits in India. The company also sued Apple in the U.S. in April over related patent infringement claims.

In its 781-page court filing in the Bombay High Court, GG Technologies alleged that Apple’s NameDrop infringes its Indian patent on technology that helps phones exchange contact details with nearby devices without requiring manual pairing. The company launched StayTouch in 2019, the same year it first sought patent protection for the technology in the U.S. It filed its Indian patent application in 2021 and received the patent in July 2024.

Apple introduced NameDrop as part of iOS 17 in June 2023. The feature debuted on iPhones later that year, with support for compatible Apple Watches arriving in October through watchOS 10.1.

“We are seeking an injunction to restrict the usage of the NameDrop feature which is native to iOS,” GG Technologies told TechCrunch. GG Technologies urged the court in its filing to restrict Apple from selling or importing iPhones and Apple Watches preloaded with NameDrop in India. The case has yet to be listed for a hearing.

In the U.S., the International Trade Commission opened an investigation into Apple’s alleged patent infringement in August, following a complaint from GG Technologies. The startup is seeking an order that could block imports of infringing Apple devices into the country, along with restrictions on their sale.

Founded in 2018 by Gaurav Goel, a graduate of the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Delhi and a former Goldman Sachs investment banker, GG Technologies developed StayTouch as an alternative to exchanging business cards. The app is available on iOS and Android.

Apple did not respond to a request for comment.

India has become increasingly important to Apple, both as a fast-growing consumer market and a major manufacturing hub outside China. The Cupertino company has expanded its retail presence in the South Asian nation, where iPhones still account for less than 10% of smartphone shipments, giving considerable room for growth.

Source: TechCrunch | Published: 2026-11-21 04:00 UTC

Original link: https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/20/startup-sues-apple-in-india-over-tap-to-share-contacts-feature/

item.title: Senate passes first-ever prediction market bill as Democrats turn up heat on upstart industry
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Prediction markets are facing new limits on Capitol Hill. The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would bar platforms from offering contracts tied to terrorism, assassination, an individual’s death, war, or U.S. military operations—the first legislation targeting the burgeoning industry to clear either chamber of Congress.

Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and John Curtis (R-Utah) introduced the bill, formally called the DEATH BETS Act, to prevent exchanges and clearinghouses overseen by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission from offering or processing those contracts. It would also ban contracts whose outcomes are reasonably expected to depend mainly on someone’s death, even if the wording does not mention death.

The bill passed the Senate by a voice vote and must still pass the House before heading to the president’s desk.

“They are offered with no regard for national security and in far too many cases, even basic morality,” Schiff said on the Senate floor. “These markets are operating in a Wild West, desperately in need of regulation and guardrails.”

As platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket have grown in prominence over the past two years, they have offered contracts on seemingly anything, drawing scrutiny over bets tied to war, violence, or human suffering. They have also raised concerns about insider trading, as users can trade without publicly revealing their identities, making it harder for outsiders to spot potential conflicts of interest.

Several cases have drawn politicians’ attention to these issues. One involved a Polymarket trader who made more than $400,000 betting on Nicolás Maduro’s removal from power before U.S. forces captured the Venezuelan leader in January. Kalshi also drew scrutiny over a market on whether Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei would leave office, which sparked a dispute after his killing when Kalshi declined to pay traders who had bet he would leave office, citing a rule that excluded death as a qualifying outcome.

In his speech, Schiff pointed to a Polymarket bet on whether NASA’s Artemis II mission would explode, raising concerns about wagers on astronauts’ lives. He also cited a bet on whether Russian forces would capture the Ukrainian city of Myrnohrad.

The companies’ leaders have previously pushed back on these criticisms. “We don’t list markets directly tied to death,” Kalshi CEO Tarek Mansour wrote on X in February. Speaking at a conference in March, Polymarket CEO Shayne Coplan called conflict-related markets a “complicated question” but defended their value as a source of useful information.

“Kalshi has never listed death markets,” a spokesperson for Kalshi told Fortune.

Polymarket declined to comment.

Other platforms, such as Novig, avoid these contracts altogether, limiting their offerings to sports markets and restricting trading to users 21 and older.

Pressure builds in Washington

The bill’s passage comes amid growing political scrutiny of prediction markets, particularly after Democrats won control of both chambers of Congress in this month’s midterm elections. Over the past week, several Democratic lawmakers have criticized the platforms on social media.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) pointed Wednesday to Kalshi’s decision to pause trading on contracts tied to President Donald Trump’s public remarks, which have drawn concerns about insider trading. “The CFTC needs to do more to stop insiders from cashing in,” she wrote on X.

Rep. Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) focused on younger users, calling Wednesday for an investigation and a ban on sports prediction markets. He criticized Kalshi for allowing 18-year-olds to bet on sports and said users under 21 had wagered $3.9 billion on the platform. “They call it a ‘prediction market.’ It’s gambling,” he wrote.

Though Democrats have been the most vocal, the scrutiny has crossed party lines. Besides cosponsoring the bill that passed Thursday, Curtis joined Warren last month in questioning Kalshi and Polymarket about potentially improper election-related trading. The Utah Republican has also backed separate legislation to ban sports and casino-style prediction contracts, citing concerns about young users’ exposure to gambling.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) also announced plans to introduce legislation that would bar prediction market platforms from offering sports contracts without state or tribal approval, according to Bloomberg Law.

Update, Nov. 20, 2026: This article has been updated with a comment from Kalshi and Polymarket.

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-20 16:53 UTC

Original link: https://fortune.com/2026/11/20/senate-passes-first-ever-prediction-market-bill-as-democrats-turn-up-heat-on-upstart-industry/

Anthropic’s stock has come within a hair of falling below its initial public offering price on Friday, erasing the gains made one day earlier during the AI company’s blockbuster Wall Street debut.

Shares in the buzzy AI lab traded as low as $83.05 on Friday, down more than 14% on their second day of trading, before recovering some ground and climbing to roughly $87 in midday trading. The shares are down more than 25% from the intraday high of $115.10 they achieved on Thursday, the first day the stock traded.

At its lowest point on Friday, Anthropic’s stock traded just a nickel above its IPO price of $83, at which Anthropic was valued at approximately $1.5 trillion.

The retreat in the stock comes amid broader weakness in technology shares, as investors reassess valuations across the board. Problems at AI giant Nvidia and the results of the midterm elections have also worried the markets in recent weeks.

Anthropic’s decline marks a sharp reversal from Thursday’s opening session, when Anthropic shares opened at $111.50, 34% above the IPO price, and then surged even higher, briefly pushing the company’s market capitalization above $2 trillion. The stock quickly pared back those gains though to close at $97.17, still 17% above its offering price and an impressive first day.

Anthropic’s IPO was one of the largest in history, with the company raising approximately $91 billion through the share sale (including a 147 million-share over-allotment sold by the deal’s underwriters on Friday), plus an additional $26 billion private placement. All told, Anthropic raised more than $115 billion in the offering—capital that will be vital to its efforts to stay ahead in the AI race, regardless of how the stock trades in the coming days and weeks.

item.title: How exactly did Trump get so rich on crypto? We explain
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

How exactly did Trump get so rich on crypto? We explain

Trump's crypto profits raise alarms for transparency advocates

For the last year, Will Ragland and a team of researchers at the Center for American Progress — a left-leaning think tank in Washington, D.C. — have dedicated themselves to counting how much money President Trump and his family have made in his second term.

So far, they put the total at nearly $3 billion. More than 2 billion dollars of the earnings come from cryptocurrency ventures.

"You could probably combine all of the past presidents' income made during their time in office," Ragland says. "And it wouldn't come close to what we're seeing here."

This unprecedented profit could soon become a major political problem for the president.

After campaigning heavily on an anti-corruption message that resonated with voters, Democrats are promising to make holding Trump and his administration accountable a critical plank of their oversight agenda when they take over both the Senate and the House next year.

From Sen. Elizabeth Warren from Massachusetts to Rep. Robert Garcia from California, prominent Democrats are vowing to hold oversight hearings and hold President Trump and his administration accountable.

"Americans should be secure in the knowledge that their government is focused on their best interests—not on making the President's family richer," Rep. Garcia warned in a letter after the midterms this month warning Trump, his family and his administration to preserve records.

Here's a guide to how Trump made his crypto wealth.

Trump's meme coin

Shortly before his inauguration in early 2025, Trump and now-First Lady Melania Trump each launched their own meme coins — or cryptocurrencies based on Internet memes, cartoon characters, or even jokes.

Trump made over $600 million from the meme coin called $TRUMP, according to the president's own disclosures.

In an effort to drum up demand for the coin, Trump also held two galas for the top holders of $TRUMP. The president promised the closest access to himself to those who invested the most in the coin.

A third gala is scheduled for Sunday at his golf course in Virginia.

Many of the guests for the first event last year were likely to have been foreign, according to media reports. The second dinner, held this year, attracted considerably less interest, though participants also described a significant presence of people from abroad.

For Ragland and other anti-corruption activists, the dinners raise significant concerns about potential conflicts of interest.

"This is a way for foreign investors, foreign countries in some instances, to try and get as much influence as they can and use that as leverage for deals that they want to make that are helpful to them," Ragland says.

Already, top Democrats including Rep. Jamie Raskin from Maryland have launched investigations — and the galas are likely to become an aspect of their oversight into Trump's crypto ventures next year.

A White House spokesperson warned Democrats against pursuing "sham investigations" when contacted by NPR about the Democrats' oversight plans.

"As the President has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," Lauren Bis said in an emailed statement. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."

A crypto deal with a U.A.E. firm

But the biggest source of Trump's wealth over his second term comes from a crypto venture called World Liberty Financial, which the president's family helped launch even before Trump won the 2024 presidential election.

Working with Steve Witkoff — whom Trump would later appoint as U.S. envoy for the Middle East — as well as Witkoff's son Zack Witkoff, the Trump family started World Liberty Financial late in 2024.

The venture revolves around a type of cryptocurrency called stablecoin (here's an NPR explainer). Zach Witkoff now serves as the CEO of World Liberty Financial.

Just days before Trump's inauguration, World Liberty received a $500 million investment in exchange for 49% of the company.

The buyer? A firm linked to Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a member of the United Arab Emirates royal family who serves as the kingdom's national security adviser. The news was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.

The investment was an extraordinary show of faith in a young company that was striving to get a foothold in the crypto sector.

Months later, the U.A.E. earned a substantial concession: The U.S. eased export restrictions, allowing the shipment of about 500,000 of the most advanced American AI chips to the kingdom. The shipment was critical in the U.A.E's ambition to build big AI data clusters and become an AI power.

Democrats have seized on the timing, although President Trump has denied any quid pro quo. In a recent interview with CBS' 60 Minutes, the president said he does not keep track of how much money he makes from his business ventures.

"I devote almost no time to my net worth. I don't care. I make – I have a lotta money, and far more than I ever thought I'd have. And I guess it's gone up. I don't even know," Trump told 60 Minutes correspondent Ross Douthat.

But Will Ragland and his team have tallied up the earnings linked to World Liberty Financial and its stablecoin business: The total, they say, is over $1.7 billion.

World Liberty Financial declined to comment.

Another major deal for Trump's crypto venture

Another key deal with World Liberty Financial helped boost the profile of the company's cryptocurrency — and the Trump family's profits.

Using $2 billion of World Liberty Financial's stablecoin, a separate firm — also led by Sheikh Tahnoon — bought a small stake in a top crypto exchange called Binance last year.

The deal instantly elevated World Liberty Financial's stablecoin into one of the biggest in the market.

Months later, Changpeng Zhao — the convicted founder of Binance who no longer runs the crypto exchange — was pardoned by President Trump. CZ, as he's widely known, still has the biggest stake in Binance and weighs in publicly, including when the exchange got hacked earlier this month.

Meanwhile, the relationship between Binance and World Liberty deepened. Binance actively promoted World Liberty Financial's stablecoin to its customers, further elevating the market valuation of the cryptocurrency to $5 billion, according to The New York Times.

While the relationship has come under scrutiny, Binance has strongly defended the acceptance of World Liberty's cryptocurrency as having been done on its own merits.

"Any suggestion that Binance did anything to support World Liberty Financial or USD1 to gain political favour or influence a legal outcome is false," a spokesperson told NPR in an email, referring to World Liberty's stablecoin. A representative for CZ declined to comment.

But transparency advocates are suspicious — and so are top Democrats. In a widely quoted social message, Rep. Robert Garcia posted a social media message for the Trump family and his administration: "Lawyer up."

Source: NPR Business | Published: 2026-11-20 10:00 UTC

Original link: https://www.npr.org/2026/11/20/nx-s1-6038969/trump-crypto-profits-corruption-meme-coin-world-liberty-explainer

item.title: What impact has Brexit had on the UK and EU economies?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

The UK and EU will hold the second summit since Brexit on Friday against a volatile economic backdrop.

Taking place in Brussels as the war in the Middle East hits the global economy, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, will meet the head of the European Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, and the president of the European Council, António Costa.

Burnham has said that Brexit “has not worked”, citing damage to the UK economy from leaving the bloc. However, there are also economic challenges facing the EU. Here we spell out the economic context behind the talks.

How has the UK fared since Brexit?

After the 2016 Brexit vote, years of political turmoil and economic uncertainty damaged business investment. Trade has also been hit by new barriers and red tape for exporters under the Brexit deal agreed by Boris Johnson.

Analysis by the economist Nick Bloom shows that UK GDP per head is between 6% and 8% lower than it would have been without Brexit. The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates a 4% hit over a 15-year period.

UK services trade has fared better. UK goods exports to the EU in 2025 were 14% below 2019 in real terms. Exports outside the EU were 8% lower. Services exports were 28% higher to the EU and 26% higher elsewhere, fuelled by Britain’s dominant financial services sector, as well as travel, accountancy, law, professional services, telecommunications and IT.

Britain has conducted trade policy independently of Brussels since Brexit. This has helped and hindered the UK in different ways. The government has been able to cut tariffs on certain products to help households with rising living costs – including gherkins in last month’s budget. The UK also struck a tariff deal with Donald Trump on better terms than managed by the EU. However, critics say the UK lacks the clout it had as part of the EU to sign international deals, and that sharply diverging from EU policies is undesirable. This is because divergence could undermine trading relations with the UK’s single largest trade partner.

The UK has taken a greater lead in AI adoption than EU nations, ranking third in the Global AI Index. France is the highest-ranked EU nation, in sixth. This is in part – but not entirely – down to the UK taking a lighter-touch approach to regulation than Brussels.

So far this year the UK has grown at the second-fastest pace in the G7, as AI bolsters growth despite headwinds from the war in the Middle East.

How is the EU economy doing?

Brexit also had consequences for the EU, although as a larger market the changes have not been as profound. Barriers to trade have made Britain harder to access for EU exporters and migration has fallen.

Brexit gave a boost to populist political movements in EU countries. A wave of copycat exits did not materialise, with Britain’s political turmoil and economic uncertainty serving as a deterrent. But support for populist Eurosceptic parties remains, and battles over immigration, sovereignty and democratic accountability have not gone away.

The EU economy has faced similar global challenges to the UK – including from the 2022 Russian energy price shock and war in the Middle East. Trump has also aggressively targeted the EU in his tariff war.

Germany in particular has struggled from surging energy costs and Chinese competition hitting its industrial base. France has faced mounting political uncertainty, driving up borrowing costs and hitting growth.

Some EU economies have boomed – including former eastern bloc countries such as Poland, which has benefited from EU membership. Southern European economies at the heart of the 2010s eurozone debt crisis have also staged a marked turnaround.

The latest forecasts from the European Commission show that, as in Britain, the EU economy has proven more resilient than feared to the Middle East war. Germany has raised investment spending, particularly on defence, in response to Trump ripping up the western security consensus. AI-related investment has also bolstered activity.

What challenges lie ahead?

For the UK there will be infighting over the extent of ambition for the future EU relationship. This could fuel uncertainty for businesses and take up political and civil service bandwidth that could have been deployed elsewhere.

Rejoining the EU would not mean a return to 2016. Some UK involvement in EU supply chains may have gone permanently. Investors may remain nervous about British commitments to EU relations – particularly as the next general election draws near.

However, most experts are clear that there would be economic benefits from closer relations. Analysts at Goldman Sachs estimate that rejoining the single market could grow the UK economy by 2-5%, equivalent to £61bn to £152bn by the start of the next decade.

The focus at this UK-EU summit will be on a youth mobility scheme, a food and drink trade deal that could add up to £5.1bn a year to the UK economy, and an emissions linking agreement that could add £3.8bn a year.

The EU will face a series of critical elections next year, including in France, Poland and Italy. Populism is on the rise and Marine Le Pen is leading opinion polls to become the next French president. Germany does not have elections until 2029 but the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party is gaining support.

Early next year there also will be a test for the EU with the appointment of a new president of the European Central Bank to replace Christine Lagarde. That will come against a backdrop of rising inflationary pressures, slowing economic growth and pressures on government borrowing costs. The Spanish economist Pablo Hernández de Cos is considered the frontrunner.

Britain is also expected to face a tougher year in 2027 due to the impact of high inflation from the war in the Middle East, with the squeeze on households also expected to weigh on growth.

Source: The Guardian Business | Published: 2026-11-20 07:00 UTC

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/20/what-impact-brexit-uk-eu-economies

item.title: Extreme rainfalls flood Sri Lanka’s coastal city as wetlands, drains vanish
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

- Several areas of Colombo, Sri Lanka’s commercial capital, were inundated following a high intensity downpour on Nov. 6, opening discussions on the city’s vulnerability to flash flooding.

- Sri Lanka is constrained by the lack of technology such as an operational Doppler weather radar system and hence cannot release accurate forecasts in time, according to weather officials.

- Despite being a RAMSAR-accredited wetland city, the water retention capacity of most wetlands in Colombo have declined due to urbanization, poor waste disposal and spread of invasive species.

- Economists suggest creating a dedicated financial reserve akin to an adaptation and resilience fund to enable local authorities to build resilient infrastructure.

COLOMBO — On Nov. 6, a 129-millimeter (5-inch) downpour flooded parts of Sri Lanka’s commercial capital within minutes, stranding commuters and submerging a large number of vehicles.

Siva Sivasagunthan, a three-wheeler driver working at a local ride-hailing app, told Mongabay that the water levels quickly increased and his vehicle was partially submerged in water. It took him around two hours to reach a location that would have usually taken 30 minutes to reach on a normal day. The downpour left many Colombo residents panicking.

According to Ajith Wijemanna, director of Sri Lanka’s Department of Meteorology, there have been a few instances over the decades when Colombo has experienced rainfall exceeding 400 mm (15.7 in). In June 1992, the city experienced a rainfall of 493.7 mm (19.4 in). In November 2010, a 440.2 mm (17.3 in) rainfall was recorded in 24 hours.

Wijemanna told Mongabay that the intensity of the rainfall — the speed of rainfall received in an hour — is extremely important. According to meteorological department readings, the rainfall intensity on Nov. 6 was more than 120 mm (4.7 in) per hour. The rain gauge reading at another location in Colombo indicated more than 135 mm (5.3 in) of rainfall per hour. “We believe that the main cause of flooding was the high intensity during a short period of time, such as an hour, which was similar to a gushing downpour,” Wijemanna said.

He noted that Sri Lanka currently lacked technology such as a Doppler radar system to support better forecasts with good lead time. Once the system is made fully operational, the agency will have the capacity to issue forecasts and predict rainfall with a lead time.

Pressure on an ancient drainage system

The flash flood occurred soon after Sri Lanka’s prime minister Harini Amarasuriya instructed officials in local authorities, including the department of irrigation and divisional secretariats, to clean canals and drainage systems in Colombo to ensure proper flow of rainwater. Following the flash flood, several authorities deployed workers to clean drains and canals and identified 60 key locations with blocked drains and waterways obstructing the flow of flood water.

According to Deepika Wijethilake, deputy director engineering of drainage design at the Colombo Municipal Council (CMC), the sewer and storm water systems in Colombo are about a century old and have been designed to function separately. She told Mongabay that the storm water system has been designed to withhold a capacity of 30 mm (1.18 in) of rainfall per hour.

“But on Nov. 6, there was a rainfall exceeding 100 mm [3.9 in] per hour. Since it rained heavily, there was extensive pressure on the system and it took some time for the water to recede,” she said, adding that the construction of more pavements also means less ability for rainwater absorption.

Real estate boom impacting wetlands

Besides grey infrastructure, Colombo’s wetlands also play a role in flood retention and mitigation. However, due to various development projects, Colombo’s wetlands are now under threat.

A 2025 study by the Colombo-based nonprofit Centre for a Smart Future (CSF) looked at the emerging environmental pressures from the booming real estate development in Colombo’s suburbs, particularly around the Thalangama environment protection area, a picturesque Colombo suburb. According to the study, wetlands, rice fields and peri-urban landscapes are being positioned as exclusive residential enclaves and marketed as ‘green living.’

The study showed that the desirable features of the wetlands were being highlighted by property developers to increase demand. Interestingly, it also referred to areas such as Kaduwela, Malabe and Thalawathugoda — areas considered residential and all situated around wetlands — having witnessed an annual spike in property prices by about 30-40%.

According to CSF co-founder and director Anushka Wijesinha, these property developers are doing very little to ensure what they market. “This is a very sensitive wetland complex. They are able to leverage on the wetland to create demand and price premia, but hardly ensure that their projects are nature-positive, which is problematic. The ecological value of the wetland is not reflected in the prices that are being charged or the fees paid to local councils or environmental authorities,” he told Mongabay.

Wijesinha said that most people see this green space idea narrowly and only from an aesthetic point of view. “But beyond that, it is a fundamental element of the city that makes the city resilient to various climate impacts. Over 45% of the country’s GDP is generated by the Western Province, of which Colombo is a major part. Then there’s a huge amount of logistics and international connectivity. There are supply chain risks when the city floods. Rather than concentrating on just the aesthetics, we need to look at it from a point of resilience, where these issues are a risk to the economic competitiveness of the city,” he said.

He highlighted the importance of assessing the economic worth of a wetland. Citing a 2003 study of the Muthurajawela wetland, a coastal peat bog near Colombo, Wijesinha said how this wetland complex provides certain ecosystem services such as flood control. “Without these services, the country would have to spend billions to put up [human]-made solutions,” he said.

Improving wetland connectivity

Colombo lies in a low-lying area downstream of the Kelani river basin and is a RAMSAR-accredited wetland city.

Chethika Gunasiri, an environmental scientist who focuses on urban wetlands and sustainability, noted that colonial cities are located in coastal or flood plain areas where floods are a natural phenomenon. “To mitigate these disasters, flood plain areas have natural infrastructure called wetlands. Their main function is to absorb rainwater, temporarily hold it and slowly release this water to the drainage system. Part of this water also goes through the soil and recharges the groundwater table,” she said.

The Colombo Wetland Complex (CWC) comprises several urban and municipal council areas and not only the Colombo Municipal Council area. According to Gunasiri, 37% of rainwater that comes into Colombo is retained by this wetland complex.

“But we now see how these wetlands are being filled and developed. The drainage system is not sufficient to manage high volumes of rainfall. There is no natural vegetation to retain or temporarily hold the water coming into the city,” she said.

According to her, around 20 square kilometers (7.7 square miles) of wetlands in the wetland complex remain, making it important to connect these wetlands to the Colombo flood management plan. “Most wetlands in Colombo are there as green patches, but their water retention capacity has decreased. Many wetlands have been invaded by pond apple [Annona glabra], [which has converted] them to terrestrial land where that water absorption capacity gets swiftly reduced. So we have to restore wetlands,” she said.

Sustainable solutions…

Source: Mongabay | Published: 2026-11-21 03:14 UTC

Original link: https://news.mongabay.com/2026/11/extreme-rainfalls-flood-sri-lankas-coastal-city-as-wetlands-drains-vanish/

item.title: It’s time to put Africa’s forest communities on the map (commentary)
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

- The new standard world map adopted at the recent U.N. General Assembly more accurately depicts the size of Africa, which is in reality much larger than formerly standard Mercator projection maps.

- A new op-ed argues that there is now an urgent need for large-scale participatory mapping of community lands and resources in places like the Congo Basin — as well as accompanying legal and policy reforms to formally recognize these areas — as technologies and regional expertise now exist to put thousands of forest communities on the map.

- “A radically different and fairer vision of the Congo Basin is within grasp, and it starts with putting communities on the map,” the writers argue.

- This article is a commentary. The views expressed are those of the authors, not necessarily of Mongabay.

The U.N. General Assembly’s recent adoption of a new standard world map, more accurately reflecting the true size of Africa than depicted in the Eurocentric 16th-century Mercator projection, is great news and a welcome reminder that multilateralism isn’t dead yet.

It also doesn’t tell the whole story.

We’re not talking about how the continent was carved up between the former colonial powers through such events as the Berlin conference of 1884-1885, though the social, economic and political impacts of the often straight and artificial lines drawn on those maps are still felt today.

No, we’re talking about how maps of Central African states are still used by foreign interests and political elites as tools to perpetuate power — with control of natural resources and the benefits they generate tending to flow outwards and upwards — rather than to the people living in these areas.

Today, much of the Congo Basin, the world’s second largest rainforest, resembles a patchwork of extractive industry concessions, strictly protected areas and an ever-increasing array of carbon offset projects which our organization has documented. These have largely failed to stem deforestation and biodiversity loss, while delivering few or no benefits to local populations, and in many cases, causing severe impacts on human rights and food security.

What maps typically don’t show are the systems of longstanding customary rights and usage by Indigenous and local communities (IPLCs) that extend across the vast region, and which have been little documented, let alone formally recognized.

By our estimates, only around 5% of the forest is currently under formal community tenure or management rights, significantly less than the estimated 35% under Indigenous title in the Amazon despite a much higher population density. Most of these come in the form of community forests in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), while other countries in the region either have very ill-adapted legal frameworks for community tenure (Gabon or Cameroon) or no enforceable legislation at all (Central African Republic and Republic of Congo).

The continued absence of forest community tenure from maps is not only deeply socially unjust, but it also goes against the evidence that the best and fairest way to protect forests is to place them under the formal control of the people who live there. Lack of tenure clarity and security is also one of the biggest impediments to self-determination and responsible investment in the region, including a new wave of payment for environmental service schemes planned in the region.

So, what needs to happen? First, governments and donors in the region need to accelerate and implement legal and policy reforms related to community land tenure.

Encouragingly, several important steps have recently been taken in this direction. Last November at the climate COP in Belem, Brazil, the DRC government committed to placing more than 50 million hectares (over 123 million acres) under the control of IPLCs, a tenfold increase on the current area, alongside other reforms it is advancing on Indigenous rights and land-use planning. Other positive examples include draft legislation on community forests in the Central African Republic and on community managed protected areas in Gabon and Cameroon.

These are all promising developments, but laws are only powerful insofar as they are enforceable. To turn these commitments into tangible and enforceable tenure rights for forest-dwelling communities, there is an urgent need to scale up demarcation and recognition of these areas.

That is why the second key need is to greatly expand provision for participatory mapping tools and support, so that communities themselves can demonstrate their presence in the forest and for policy makers and the private sector to take account of and recognize this presence.

Our MappingForRights program has supported hundreds of communities in the Congo Basin to produce highly accurate and detailed maps of their resources and territories, but this covers only a fraction of what is needed.

Thankfully, advances in mapping technologies are breaking down cost barriers and making it easier for communities to generate, control and manage their data and to integrate this into government cadasters. There is also a large pool of untapped civil society capacity in the region to facilitate participatory mapping processes.

The challenge now is to bring all this altogether and make these resources widely available to forest peoples and grassroots organizations across the region, to enable the vital mapping of thousands of ‘invisible’ communities and to turn promising laws and policies into enforceable rights.

A radically different and fairer vision of the Congo Basin is within grasp, and it starts with putting communities on the map.

Georges Thierry Handja is senior manager of the Land and Livelihoods program for Rainforest Foundation UK, where Joe Eisen is executive director.

Banner image: New technologies paired with regional expertise can help put thousands of forest communities on the map of Africa. Image courtesy of Cargill.

item.title: Where family foundations can help marine conservation
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

- Research and reporting from across the Americas show that marine conservation outcomes depend heavily on how well protected areas are managed, fishing regulations are enforced, and local communities are involved in decision-making.

- Some of the most promising opportunities for smaller family foundations lie in improving the management of existing marine protected areas, strengthening community fishing rights, and addressing shortcomings in illegal fishing enforcement.

- The evidence for habitat restoration is more mixed, while research on migratory marine species points to opportunities to improve fisheries management beyond the boundaries of protected areas.

- Drawing on academic literature and Mongabay’s reporting in English, Spanish, and Portuguese, Founder Founder and CEO Rhett Ayers Butler examines where relatively modest philanthropic investments could help address persistent gaps in marine conservation.

COP17 ended in Armenia amid disappointment over the lack of concrete measures to reduce biodiversity loss by 2030. Finance was a sore point. Philanthropy is only a small part of that picture, but foundations can take risks that public agencies often cannot. I think there are some particularly good opportunities for smaller foundations in marine conservation.

My intended audience is family foundations that give away perhaps $2 million to $15 million a year and have a handful of staff.

Over the summer I went through the academic literature and Mongabay’s coverage in English, Spanish, and Portuguese to see what the evidence actually shows about marine conservation outcomes in the Americas. A first summary of that assessment – “From paper parks to lasting protection, here’s what works in marine conservation” – appeared last month. In some cases Mongabay’s reporting helped me understand why the results of a study were so disappointing. Our reporters had spoken to the people responsible for managing these areas, as well as people who lived or fished in them.

In reading about some of these places, I was struck by how long the laws protecting them had been on the books. Some of the agencies responsible for enforcing those laws lack adequate funding. Elsewhere, the designation of a protected area was done with little regard for the people who fished there.

Making existing protected areas work

I suspect it’s easier to raise money to establish a marine protected area (MPA) than to pay the salaries of the people who will patrol it. The same applies to restoration: there is often more interest in planting mangroves than in what happens to those mangroves three or four years later.

No-take reserves and other highly protected areas have a strong ecological track record. But even some of the better-known MPAs in the Americas have problems with illegal fishing. At Revillagigedo, the Mexican archipelago in the Pacific, Mongabay found that some complaints of illegal fishing had been archived or remained unresolved.

Some MPAs have been in existence for years without the ecological monitoring needed to determine whether they’re working. There are others where I think money would be better spent on enforcing fishing restrictions or working with local fishers.

If the agency responsible for an MPA lacks the legal authority to enforce its rules, better-equipped patrols may accomplish very little. And if a grant is going to pay for patrols, who will pay for them once the grant runs out?

Fishing rights and local governance

Some of the more interesting opportunities involve relatively small fishing communities. These communities don’t necessarily need an MPA to manage the waters they fish. Chile’s territorial use rights for fisheries (TURFs) and fisher-created refuges show how area-based rights and local organization can support stewardship. Costa Rica’s marine areas for responsible fishing may do more for conservation than standard protected-area figures suggest.

Getting legal recognition for an area that fishers already manage could be a good use of a foundation’s money. So could helping a fisher organization keep better records of what its members are catching.

I’d want to know who actually makes decisions about the fishery. Women and poorer fishers may have little say, even in places heralded for community-led conservation. And sometimes it’s an outside organization that has most of the authority.

Enforcing fishing regulations

Illegal fishing is much easier to detect than it used to be, but seeing a boat on a screen is a long way from boarding it or levying fines on its owner.

At Revillagigedo, patrolling a vast marine reserve more than 500 kilometers off Mexico’s Baja California is difficult and costly. Before funding more surveillance at Revillagigedo, I’d want to know why some of the cases mentioned in our reporting didn’t go anywhere. Was it a problem with the evidence or with what the authorities did with it?

It may be considerably cheaper to catch a vessel breaking the law when it comes into port than when it’s hundreds of kilometers out at sea.

I’d be particularly mindful of the risks of asking local people to document illegal fishing in areas where the boats belong to powerful commercial or political interests.

Restoring coastal habitats

I was less convinced by some of what I read about restoration. Restoration projects appeal to funders partly because planting is easy to count. But the number of seedlings or coral fragments says little about whether a damaged habitat will recover. In mangrove restoration, for example, reestablishing tidal flow may be more important than planting trees. On reefs, the conditions that contributed to the loss of corals, including pollution and overfishing, may need to be addressed before much is spent on outplanting.

In Florianópolis, in southern Brazil, one of the arguments for restoring mangroves is the protection they afford coastal communities as the climate changes. Some of the money for this work could potentially come from climate funders.

Beyond protected areas

I spent some time looking at conservation efforts in the Eastern Tropical Pacific, particularly in the waters around Galápagos, Cocos, Coiba, Malpelo and Gorgona (CMAR). These islands are important for some of the same populations of migratory marine animals.

Much has been made of the marine corridors in this part of the Pacific. Research on shark movements helped make the case for the creation of Ecuador’s Hermandad Marine Reserve in 2022. But a study published this year found that silky sharks tagged in Galápagos spent about half their time outside protected areas. Could seasonal fishing restrictions or changes in fishing gear reduce shark mortality there? That seems worth exploring.

Even where MPAs have benefited from decades of investment, fisheries management can remain a problem. Conservation groups have worked on the Mesoamerican Reef for decades, and Belize has long-term monitoring and ways of financing its MPAs. Overfishing is still widespread, and most commercial stocks still lack catch controls.

Sharks, rays, turtles, seabirds and forage fish die in fisheries operating well beyond the boundaries of protected areas. Studies of illuminated gillnets in Peru have shown that bycatch can be reduced while maintaining target catch and market value.

On the demand side, Mongabay has reported on government purchases of shark meat in Brazil and the mislabeling of shark meat in Ecuador. I wouldn’t know where to begin as a small funder interested in addressing either problem without the help of someone who knows the industry well.

One question I had while reading some of the studies was what happened after the researchers left. Was there still money to manage the protected area or maintain the restoration site five years later?

There may be some good opportunities to provide a few years of funding to MPAs that are in the process of securing government funding or setting up a trust fund.…

Source: Mongabay | Published: 2026-11-20 17:48 UTC

Original link: https://news.mongabay.com/2026/11/where-family-foundations-can-help-marine-conservation/

item.title: Ecuador copper mine advancing despite opposition from Indigenous communities
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

- The Warintza copper mine in southeastern Ecuador could force Indigenous Shuar communities to relocate, while clearing primary forest and altering natural waterways.

- The mine would operate within the Indigenous territory, overlapping with a stretch of the Andes mountains known as the Cordillera del Cóndor.

- Critics of the project say the government granted exploration rights without consulting the communities.

- Now, the government is conducting another consultation. However, many residents say they no longer trust the process and believe the project will move forward regardless of their objections.

A proposed copper mine on Indigenous land in southeastern Ecuador is getting closer to opening despite opposition from some Shuar communities, who say they reject the project altogether and don’t want to participate in talks with the government.

The Warintza mine received environmental authorization this year, and officials will now begin meeting with Indigenous communities about how the project, if constructed, would impact their way of life. But some community members don’t want to be consulted at all, and say they’re worried about relocation from the territory.

“We want absolutely nothing to do with mining,” one community member, who asked to remain anonymous due to fear for his personal safety, told Mongabay. “And we don’t even want to be consulted.”

If the project moves forward, Lowell Mineral Exploration Ecuador S.A., a subsidiary of Solaris Resources, would extract copper for around 22 years from approximately 8,660 hectares (21,399 acres) across six concessions. It would also extract molybdenum concentrates and some gold and silver.

Construction would clear more than 2,025 hectares (5,003 acres) of primary forest and divert the Warints and Piuntz rivers, critical to Indigenous communities’ way of life, according to the environmental impact assessment, which received technical approval in April.

It could irreversibly change the landscape in some places even after the mine is closed, the assessment said. Surface water and groundwater quality also face high risk, threatening aquatic flora and fauna.

The area sits in the Cordillera del Cóndor, a stretch of the Andes that extends into Peru. The mine site provides habitat for 552 plant species, 20 of them endemic, according to the assessment. It also has 154 bird species, 69 amphibians and reptiles, and 31 mammal species, including the Andean bear (Tremarctos ornatus).

One activist, who wished to remain anonymous due to fear for his personal safety, told Mongabay the assessment left out other threatened and endangered species, and disregarded some pollution risks.

“There are serious errors regarding the types of chemicals that will be emitted, the heavy metals and the radioactive metals that will come out of the mine,” he said.

Solaris Resources didn’t respond to a request for comment from Mongabay in time for publication.

The mine would also overlap with homes in the Shuar communities of Warints and Yawi, the assessment said. The open pit would be around 3.4 kilometers (2.1 miles) long and 1.2 kilometers (0.75 miles) wide, and a tailings facility would cover around 860 hectares (2,125 acres).

The operations are so close to the villages that it would be unsafe for them to stay, the assessment said. It recommended total relocation of residents, approximately 512 Warints people and 210 Yawi. It rejected “scattered individual relocation” and moving into nearby mestizo communities as options.

“The impact cannot be avoided or minimized through design adjustments, so relocation is unavoidable, and planned relocation is an enabling condition for eliminating exposure and serious risk,” the assessment said.

Relocation is first subject to Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC), a process in which communities are given the nature, size, pace, reversibility and scope of the project and how it could impact their lives.

In 2021, a complaint with the International Labour Organization (ILO), a U.N. agency, argued that Ecuador should have begun that process before granting the company exploration rights in the area. In 2024, the ILO upheld that position and also said the mine shouldn’t move forward without consulting the Shuar communities of Maikiuants, Warints, Yawi and Tinkimints.

In a September statement, Solaris Resources said it’s working toward finalizing water permits, mining concession administrative processes, infrastructure-related clearances and other legal requirements.

It also said the Warints and Yawi communities had finalized “life plans,” defined as community-led, long-term development frameworks that identify each community’s priorities and aspirations and provide a roadmap for future decision-making.

Company agreements with communities don’t qualify as consultation, the 2024 ILO ruling noted.

The Ministry of Energy and Mines didn’t respond to Mongabay’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Some residents say they’ve lost confidence in the consultation process after the exploration rights were granted without consultation in 2021. They said they’re worried the government will authorize the project regardless of what the communities decide.

“The government violates [our] constitutional rights and the international rights reinforcing them. Nevertheless, after all of that, they want to hold a prior and well-informed consultation,” the same community member told Mongabay.

If the communities ultimately reject the process, the project can still legally move forward. Ministry of Energy and Mines regulations say consultation results are non-binding, and the state can proceed without consent if it makes efforts to minimize impact and fairly compensate residents.

“It’s no longer a consultation process,” the activist said, “but instead becomes a process of negotiation and harm.”

Banner image: The outside of a traditional Shaur kitchen. Image by Brandi Morin/Survival International.
