item.title: Could a short tail mean a new monkey species in Laos? Some scientists think so
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

- A new-to-science species of monkey has recently been proposed in the Vietnamese Journal of Primatology: the short-tailed langur, or Trachypithecus brevicaudus.

- The description is based on analysis of photographs of monkeys in the Annamite Mountains of Laos with unusually short tales.

- Although other new-to-science primate species have initially been described on the basis of photographs, an independent expert interviewed by Mongabay says he doesn’t believe the data yet support the declaration of a distinct langur species.

- The next stage for the researchers is to collect droppings to use in genetic analysis, and to search for remains in nearby villages.

There is no body. No genetic evidence — yet. There are just photos, but some scientists say those photos show a distinct enough primate to declare it a new species: the short-tailed langur, or Trachypithecus brevicaudus. The proposed species was described in the Vietnamese Journal of Primatology and lives in the Annamite Mountains of Laos.

“A photograph of a langur, published by the Saola Foundation, caught my attention because the animal’s tail is noticeably shorter than that of any other species within this group of limestone langurs,” said Tilo Nadler, lead author of the paper and a wildlife consultant for the Vietnamese government and various NGOs.

This photo led Nadler and colleagues to investigate. They traveled to the area, a remote set of limestone karsts in Bolikhamxai province in central Laos, and took their own photos.

“The first time I observed a group of these langurs, it was immediately clear to me that they were different from all the other limestone langurs I had previously encountered and knew well,” Nadler told Mongabay in an email interview. “It was a very exciting experience.”

But not all scientists agree that these photos prove a new-to-science species.

“It could well be a new species, but I think the data that have been presented do not give sufficient support for this,” said primate expert Vincent Nijman, director of EcoVerde Global Consulting, who wasn’t involved with the paper.

But Nadler said the encounter, and photos, proved his hunch: this wasn’t a one-off case of an animal that lost part of its tail, but a whole population of langurs with shorter, thicker tails. To the untrained eye, the tail of the short-tailed langur still looks quite long, but it’s noticeably shorter than other related species, according to Nadler. (Hence the proposed name: brevicaudus means “short tail.”)

“These animals possess a shorter and thicker tail compared to closely related species of limestone langurs from the southern group — such as the Lao langur (Trachypithecus laotum) and the Hatinh langur (T. hatinhensis),” Nadler wrote.

He added he tried to scour local villages for any specimens that may have been hunted, to take back for genetic testing, but was unable to find any remains.

A future expedition plans to search for remains more thoroughly in local villages and collect the monkey’s droppings to use in genetic analysis.

Nadler said he’s not the first scientist to describe a new primates based only on photos: the highland mangabey (Rungwecebus kipunji) from Tanzania in 2003, and the Arunachal macaque (Macaca munzala) in 2005, and white-cheeked macaque (Macaca leucogenys) in 2015, both from the Himalayas, were all first described from just photos, with DNA to come later.

Nijman agreed that a species can be described using just photos and based on a single characteristic — in this case the tail. But he said he’s not convinced by the paper’s findings, arguing that the tail measurements as currently done still show some potential overlap with other species.

“The Hatinh langurs (male and female) with the shortest tails have as short a tail as the new species with the longest tail,” Nijman said via email. As for thickness, “they were not able to quantify this,” Nijman wrote.

Whether a new species or not, it was first photographed by Rob Timmins, the technical director of the Saola Foundation, in 2024. The Saola Foundation is currently searching for the saola (Pseudoryx nghetinhensis), a species of bovid often called the Asian unicorn, in the Annamite Mountains.

Lorraine Scotson, CEO of the Saola Foundation for the Conservation of the Annamite Mountains, said in an email interview that the group wasn’t involved with Nadler’s research, but that “a new primate is significant news, and we’d love to see this species get the wide attention it deserves.”

The Annamite Mountains are a biodiversity hotspot, housing dozens of species found nowhere else, including the giant muntjac (Muntiacus vuquangensis), the Annamite striped rabbit (Nesolagus timminsi), two species of gibbon, and the Laotian rock rat, or kha-nyou (Laonastes aenigmamus). Three percent of the world’s land-based vertebrates are found in the Annamite Mountains, which likely hosts many undescribed species.

Not long ago, the karst-dwelling monkey was the victim of heavy hunting, Nadler said.

“In the past, these langurs were hunted extensively, particularly in connection with the cultivation of hidden poppy fields used for opium production,” he said. “However, poppy cultivation has ceased due to legislation and strict enforcement, and with it, the hunting has also come to an end.”

Still, many mysteries remain. Chief among them: how many short-tailed langurs are there? Nadler said their range is “unclear,” with only two populations currently known. But he added, “there are other, extremely inaccessible limestone massifs where further populations might exist.”

Next year, the Saola Foundation plans to launch a new program with this proposed new species as its flagship animal to conserve these unique limestone karsts.

“Having been geographically isolated for millions of years, this karst complex habitat is likely to host many other endemic species of the Annamites Bioregion,” Scotson said, “and quite possibly some of them still undescribed to science.”

Banner image: A group of short-tailed langurs consisting of five adults (three in the photo) and two juveniles, approximately 1.5 to 2 years old. Image by Tilo Nadler.

Greater Mekong proves an ark of biodiversity, with 380 new species in a year

item.title: Quechua community in Peru builds up Andean bear camera trap project on their own reserve
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

- An Indigenous-led conservation project on the Pumataki private community reserve in Peru, gathers data on the presence and numbers of Andean bears — compiling some of the first local records of the species on the reserve.

- The project was developed by Maribel Pacco, a local from the Pillco Grande community, who uses the camera traps to inform a Quechua-language environmental education program for youth, though limited funding has forced the project to scale back some of its future plans.

- Pumataki is recognized by a legal framework which allows landowners, in this case the community of Pillco Grande, to convert their holdings into a nature reserve called a Private Conservation Areas (ACP).

- The Andean bear (Tremarctos ornatus) is listed as vulnerable to extinction on the IUCN Red List; in Peru, it is threatened by habitat loss, poaching and the impacts of climate change.

Maribel Pacco grins as she recalls the first time she saw an Andean bear close-up in the wild. At the forest edge, a mother and her cubs browsed on bromeliads while the volunteer ranger watched for hours in awe.

“I’m not a biologist, but at that moment, I decided to become a conservationist,” she says.

Today, Pacco leads a camera-trap project to estimate bear numbers and movements in Pumataki, a private community-owned reserve in the buffer zone of Manu National Park, in southeastern Peru. With the help of her Indigenous Quechua community of Pillco Grande, the project has generated some of the first local records of Andean bears (Tremarctos ornatus) in Pumataki. So far, they have identified 10 individual Andean bears, distinguishable by the unique pattern of facial markings.

Though modest and only 3 years old, information gathered from the camera traps helps inform a Quechua-language environmental education program for youth and is shared at community meetings to highlight the area’s biodiversity.

“In the last few years, I’ve seen a lot more involvement of women in Andean bear conservation which is fantastic to see,” said Rebecca Zug, a professor of biology at the Universidad San Francisco de Quito, who is not involved in the project. “There is also so much more power in Indigenous communities building conservation from within and learning about their own biodiversity from someone like Maribel than in having an outside voice come in.”

For now, limited funding has forced the project to scale back some of its future plans. However, environmental education and camera trap monitoring continue, with community members taking turns in groups of five to visit the reserve and to maintain the cameras.

The team Pacco has gathered is analyzing the behavior and activity patterns of different species to compile a biodiversity inventory. They hope the information gathered on the number of Andean bears and their territories will be used by universities in future research.

The Andean bear, also known as the spectacled bear, roams from Venezuela and Colombia in the north to northern Argentina in the south while facing an array of threats along the way. Despite being classified as vulnerable on the International Union for the Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Red List, Andean bear populations face pressures from habitat loss and fragmentation, poaching, retaliatory killings due to crop raiding and the effects of climate change.

Peru, particularly in southeastern Peru where Pumataki is located, is one of the species’ strongholds. An estimated 5,000 bears are believed to roam cloud forests, dry forests, and the páramo and puna grasslands across the country.

“Peru has some of the biggest blocks of habitat left for the species across its range, but this is a forest-dependent species, so habitat loss and habitat fragmentation are major threats,” says Russ Van Horn of the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance and co-chair of the IUCN Andean Bear Expert Team.

Important refuges remain where extensive protected forests continue to support Andean bear populations. Pumataki — a private cloud forest reserve — is one such refuge in the Cusco region.

Bridging different communities

Though small in size, this reserve is recognized by a legal framework which allows landowners to convert their holdings into a nature reserve called a Private Conservation Areas (ACP). Recognition can be granted for a minimum of 10 years, with the possibility of renewal, or made in perpetuity.

Pumataki lies on the eastern slopes of the Andes, bordering the vast Manu National Park. Often shrouded in mist, the forest teems with wildlife. It is a home to the Indigenous Quechua community of Pillco Grande, whose members own and manage the reserve.

For local people, this rugged landscape traditionally holds deep spiritual significance. It is the abode of Apu Kañaqway, a sacred mountain revered in the Quechua worldview as a protective spirit.

For Pacco, who grew up among these forests, conservation is entwined with a spiritual connection to the land.

“In my childhood, I would hear stories about the Apu, which is very important in our culture, and my father would take me to visit the reserve where he worked as a volunteer guard,” she says.

Pacco’s early connection to the landscape eventually drew her into conservation work. During college, she became a volunteer ranger in Manu National Park, where she encountered one of its most elusive residents: The Andean bear. She quickly developed a fascination with the species, she tells Mongabay.

“I fell in love with bears, their behavior, everything about them, and the role they play in the forest ecosystem. The other rangers taught me how to track their footprints and use camera traps, and I learned a lot,” she says.

Those experiences laid the foundation for her own conservation project. In 2023, Pacco received a Conservamos por Naturaleza (We Conserve for Nature) grant from the Peruvian Society for Environmental Law (SPDA) to launch a community-led initiative to monitor Andean bears in Pumataki and conduct environmental education.

According to the SPDA, Pacco’s ability to bridge different communities was a strength.

“Maribel can connect with different people. She speaks Quechua and can communicate with local communities, but she also speaks Spanish and English and can communicate with people from abroad,” says Carolina Butrich, a manager at the SPDA.

A community effort

Tracking one of the cloud forest’s most elusive large mammals is no easy feat. With camera traps, a GPS device and training from the San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance, Pacco began surveying the forest and reaching out to her community to document the presence of bears.

One of the principal hurdles, however, was getting more local people to participate.

“The biggest challenges were getting more people in the community involved, because most of us are just looking for ways to work and support our families,” says Justa Peña Condori, an early recruit to the team.

Gradually, through persistence and group meetings, Pacco was able to convince more community members to accompany her on camera-trapping excursions in the forest. She also began conducting environmental education in Quechua at the local school, teaching children about Andean bear ecology using images and video footage captured by the camera traps.

Individual bears can be distinguished by their own “fingerprint”: A unique pattern of facial markings around the eyes, often resembling spectacles. These markings allow the team to identify individual bears caught on camera. The process has also been a way to engage schoolchildren, who can give each bear a name and learn about conservation in a more personal way.

The camera traps have so far identified 10 individual Andean bears, providing the first records of the species in the area. The traps have also caught images of other cloud forest species such as the clouded oncilla (Leopardus pardinoides), dwarf brocket deer (Subulo chunyi), puma (Puma concolor), opossums and coatis helping to shift local attitudes toward wildlife.…

item.title: Jackson Boxer’s vegan recipe for almond sorbet with grape granita
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Ice-cream holds an irresistible allure for me. That combination of richness, lightness, and the pure, sensual pleasure of it melting gently across the palate maintains an unbreakable hold over my imagination. In fact, other than fruit, it’s the only sweet food with which I have a genuine emotional relationship: I can remember many ice-creams I’ve eaten incredibly vividly, and in a way I just don’t with almost all other desserts and pastries. Today’s ice is a case in point, having been developed from a memory of an almond gelato eaten in Sicily just after the annual harvest.

Almond sorbet with grape granita

The amaretto and tonka beans help round out the flavour in a way that old blanched almonds off the shelf might not.

Prep 10 min

Cook 15 min

Chill/freeze 2 hr+

Serves 4

For the sorbet syrup

250g sugar

160g glucose powder

10g xanthan gum

For the sorbet

400g blanched almonds

700

ml almond milk – Plenish is by far the best

100ml amaretto

4 tonka beans (about 5g)

4g flaky sea salt

(about 1 tsp)

500ml sorbet syrup (see above and method)

For the granita

1kg black seedless grapes

125ml light red wine – a vegan beaujolais is ideal

Fresh lemon juice, to taste

First make the syrup. Put everything in a bowl or jug with 120ml water, stir until the sugar and glucose dissolve and the xanthan gum has hydrated, then put in the fridge to chill.

Put all the sorbet ingredients bar the syrup in a blender and blitz on full speed for 10 minutes. Add the sorbet syrup and blend again, this time on low speed, for another minute. Put in the fridge until cold, then transfer to an ice-cream machine and churn (if you don’t have a machine, decant into a suitable container, freeze for 30 minutes, then scrape and beat vigorously with a fork. Return to the freezer, and repeat at half-hourly intervals until you have a smooth ice).

Now for the granita. Pick the grapes off their vines, removing and discarding all stems, then blend on low speed until totally pulped. Pass the grape pulp through a fine sieve, so you’re left with just the juice, then discard the grape solids. Stir in the wine, then add lemon juice to taste – you want to brighten up the flavour and balance the sweetness, so the amount will depend on how sweet the grapes are and on personal taste: I like quite a lot of acidity to temper the sweetness of the fruit.

Transfer the granita mix to a container, cover and put in the freezer. After 20 minutes, remove, use a metal whisk to break up any ice formations and return to the freezer. Repeat every 20 minutes for about two hours, until you have a nice, even, cloud-like snow of granita.

Using an ice-cream scoop or a warm spoon, put two scoops of the sorbet in four very well-chilled bowls (put them in the freezer first), then spread out a little. Top with two spoonfuls of granita, then spread that out evenly, too. Top with another scoop of sorbet and serve at once.

- Jackson Boxer is chef/owner of Brunswick House, Vesper and Dove, all in London, and culinary director of Cowley Manor near Cheltenham and the Henrietta in London

item.title: Butter Mochi Cake With Maple-Miso Pecans
item.description:

For Shuai Wang, chef of King BBQ in North Charleston, South Carolina, mochi brings back memories of holidays with family. His other dessert love? Classic Southern pecan pie. This Hawaiian-style butter mochi cake draws on both, pairing a rich, chewy cake with a generous layer of maple-miso pecans.

The batter gets its signature bounce from mochiko, a distinct style of rice flour that gives butter mochi its chewy texture—not the fluffy crumb of a conventional cake. Coconut milk and melted butter add richness, while the pecans provide crunch. Let the cake cool completely before slicing so the texture has time to set.

The secret to the pecan topping is a little white or yellow miso, which brings savory depth to the maple syrup, much like the salt in salted caramel. The nuts need only a brief head start in the oven; they’ll continue to toast as the cake bakes.

Can I use regular rice flour instead of mochiko?

No. Mochiko, also called sweet or glutinous rice flour, has a different starch composition from regular rice flour. It’s responsible for butter mochi’s characteristic springy, slightly sticky chew. Regular rice flour or all-purpose flour won’t produce the same texture.

What kind of miso is best for baking?

White and yellow miso are both good choices for this cake. White miso tends to be milder and slightly sweeter, while yellow miso has a somewhat more pronounced savory flavor. Either adds complexity to the maple-coated pecans without overwhelming their buttery, nutty flavor. Learn more about the different types of miso and how to use them.

Is butter mochi cake gluten-free?

Mochiko is naturally gluten-free, despite the sometimes confusing name glutinous rice flour. This recipe can be gluten-free, but check your miso: Some varieties contain barley or wheat. If you’re baking for someone who needs to avoid gluten, choose a miso labeled gluten-free and check your other packaged ingredients.

What you’ll need

- Sweet Rice Flour $2.99 At Weee!

- 9" Round Cake Pan $21 $16 At Amazon

- Wire Cooling Rack $18 At Amazon

- Rimmed Baking Sheet $35 At Amazon

- French Wire Whisk $18 At Amazon

- Rubber Spatula $13 At Amazon

Recipe information

- Total Time 1 hour 30 minutes, plus cooling

- Yield 10–12 servings

Ingredients

Pecans

2

2

8

1

Cake and Assembly

6

2

1¼

1

1

2

1⅔

1

Need to make a substitution?

Preparation

- Pecans Step 1 Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lightly oil a rimmed baking sheet with vegetable oil. Whisk 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 tsp. white or yellow miso (gluten-free if needed) in a medium bowl until smooth. Add 8 oz. raw pecans, coarsely chopped (about 2 cups) and 1 Tbsp. sugar and toss until evenly coated. Spread out on prepared baking sheet; bake until fragrant and matte looking, 6–8 minutes (nuts won’t be fully toasted). Let cool.

- Cake and Assembly Step 2 Lightly grease a 9"-diameter cake pan with unsalted butter and line bottom with a parchment paper round. Vigorously whisk 2 large eggs, 1¼ cups (250 g) sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth. Add one 13.5-oz. can unsweetened coconut milk, well shaken, heated slightly if fat is solid, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, and whisk well. Add 1⅔ cups (254 g) mochiko and 1 tsp. baking powder; whisk vigorously until combined and batter is smooth and thick. Scrape batter into prepared pan. Step 3 Toss pecans to break up any clumps and scatter evenly over batter, going all the way to the edges (it may seem like a lot). Bake cake until sides start to pull away from pan, top is golden brown, and a tester inserted into the center comes out clean (some pecans will sink), 50–55 minutes. If pecans begin to brown too quickly, loosely tent pan with foil. Transfer to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 15 minutes. Turn cake out onto rack; peel away parchment and discard. Carefully turn cake right side up and let cool completely (at least 1 hour). Step 4 To serve, slice cake and top with scoops of vanilla ice cream. Do Ahead: Cake can be made 1 day ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature. Editor’s note: This recipe was first published in our August 2023 issue and has been updated with additional guidance. item.title: Dirty Spaghetti
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Dirty Spaghetti

Dirty rice has met its noodle match with our Louisiana-style dirty spaghetti.

Let the good times roll with this Louisiana-inspired dirty spaghetti dish! It’s a riff on Cajun-Creole dirty rice that transforms the original into an easy one-pot pasta.

The key it its flavor is Cajun seasoning, a blend cayenne pepper, garlic powder, black pepper, paprika and thyme. And herein lies an important cooking tip: When using store-bought seasoning blends like this one, give them a little taste first before adding anything to the pot. Different brands rely on different ratios of ingredients, and a tablespoon of one product could be much milder (or pack way more heat!) than a tablespoon of another. Your personal preferences matter, too. So whether you are sensitive to spice or like to pack on the heat, make sure you’re adding the proper amount of spice for your taste.

What is dirty spaghetti?

Dirty spaghetti is a riff on dirty rice, a classic Cajun-Creole side dish. Traditional dirty rice is made with chopped organ meats such as chicken livers or gizzards, which, along with the herbs and seasonings, color the white rice and earn it its “dirty” moniker. This dish, however, has a meaty base that’s made with ground beef and diced andouille sausage. Like the original, it also features the “holy trinity” of Cajun and Creole cooking: chopped onion, bell pepper and celery. A healthy dose of Cajun seasoning ensures each bite is packed with bold flavor.

Dirty Spaghetti Ingredients

- Olive oil: A drizzle of olive oil is used to saute the meat and veggies.

- Holy trinity: Chopped yellow onion, green and red bell pepper and celery provide a flavorful base for this dish’s meaty sauce.

- Ground beef: A blend of beef that’s 90% lean retains plenty of flavor and is ideal for this recipe.

- Andouille sausage: This smoked sausage has roots in France, but has become a staple of Louisiana cooking. It has a deeply smoky and spicy flavor, and is traditionally seasoned with Cayenne pepper, garlic, black pepper and thyme.

- Garlic: Use freshly minced garlic for the most robust flavor.

- Tomato paste: Tomato paste adds richness and complexity to the sauce.

- Seasoning: Cajun seasoning is the star of the show here. Be sure to give it a taste before adding it to the recipe to gauge how spicy it is, as different blends can vary widely in terms of heat. After the dish is cooked, season the spaghetti to taste with salt and black pepper.

- Beef broth: Use a low-sodium beef broth to control the salt, because both the Cajun seasoning and sausage add their own saltiness. Of course, store-bought beef broth works perfectly fine here, but homemade beef stock is also a great option.

- Spaghetti: You will need 8 ounces of dry spaghetti for this recipe. (Assume about 2 ounces of spaghetti per person.) To cook the spaghetti without it clumping, break the noodles in half before adding them to the simmering sauce.

Directions

Step 1: Brown the beef

Heat the oil in a large Dutch oven or large high-sided skillet over medium-high heat. Add the ground beef and cook it until it’s browned, four to six minutes, using a wooden spoon or spatula to break it into small crumbles.

Editor’s Tip: If you use a skillet, make sure it has a lid.

Step 2: Add the sausage and veggies

Add the chopped andouille sausage, onion, celery, red pepper and green pepper. Cook them until the vegetables are soft, about three to four minutes. Add the garlic and cook it until it’s fragrant, 30 to 60 seconds. Stir in the tomato paste and Cajun seasoning, and cook for one to two more minutes. Add 3 cups of broth and bring the mixture to a simmer.

Step 3: Add the spaghetti

Add the broken spaghetti to the pot, ensuring that the noodles are submerged in the liquid and separated as much as possible. Add more liquid if needed. Bring the mixture to a boil, then reduce the heat to medium-low. Cover the pot and simmer the pasta for six minutes.

Remove the lid and continue simmering until the spaghetti is al dente, stirring every two to three minutes. Add more broth as needed. Remove the pot from the heat, and season the pasta to taste with salt and pepper.

Dirty Spaghetti Variations

- Lower the heat: For a less-spicy dirty spaghetti, use just a teaspoon of Cajun seasoning. You can also substitute Italian hot sausage, chicken sausage or a mild smoked sausage like kielbasa for the andouille sausage.

- Add a green garnish: Top the spaghetti with sliced green onions or fresh chopped parsley.

How to Store Dirty Spaghetti

Leftover dirty spaghetti can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to four days.

What is the best way to reheat dirty spaghetti?

The best way to reheat a pasta dish like this one is either in the oven or on the stovetop. To reheat leftover dirty spaghetti in the oven, transfer it to an oven-safe baking dish, cover it tightly with foil, and cook it in an oven preheated to 350 degrees for about 20 minutes or until it’s heated through. To reheat it on the stovetop, heat a saucepan over medium heat and add a drizzle of olive oil. Add the leftover pasta and sauce and saute them for about two to three minutes or until they’re hot.

Can you freeze dirty spaghetti?

Yes, you can freeze dirty spaghetti. After allowing it to cool completely, transfer leftovers to a freezer-safe container and store them in the freezer for up to three months. Allow the dirty spaghetti to thaw overnight in the fridge before reheating it.

Dirty Spaghetti Tips

What’s the best pan for making one-pan dirty spaghetti?

The best pan for making this one-pot pasta dish is a Dutch oven or a large, high-walled skillet or pot with a tight-fitting lid.

How do I make this dirty spaghetti less spicy?

First, be sure to give your Cajun seasoning a little taste first because seasoning blends like this one can vary widely in spiciness. Depending on how spicy your Cajun seasoning is, add more or less to taste. You could also make a homemade Cajun seasoning blend and customize the amount of cayenne pepper and chili powder to your personal taste. The andouille sausage also adds quite a bit of spice; for less heat, skip it entirely, or swap in sweet Italian sausage, breakfast sausage, chicken sausage or a milder smoked sausage like kielbasa.

What should I serve with dirty spaghetti?

You’ll definitely want to pair this dirty spaghetti with crusty French bread, garlic bread or cornbread to sop up any extra sauce. Southern-inspired side dishes to consider include southern green beans, collard greens or black-eyed pea tomato salad. Or, complement the pasta dish’s spicy flavor with a fresh and crisp green salad.

Source: Taste of Home | Published: 2026-11-20 16:03 UTC

How we tested protein powders

Each protein powder was prepared following pack instructions using cold water and mixed with a small electric milk frother for consistency. We consulted nutritionist Kerry Torrens and tasted every product ourselves, assessing flavour, texture, mixability and overall drinking experience. The aim was to understand how these supplements perform during everyday use, whether you're looking for a whey-based option after training, vegan alternative for smoothies or low-calorie way to increase your protein intake.

To reflect the breadth of products available in the UK, we tested a range of formulations, including whey isolate, clear, plant-based and organic blends, alongside products aimed at women, muscle gain, weight management and recovery. We also considered options that stand out for flavour, nutritional profile and overall value.

The type and source of protein were also taken into account, with ingredients such as pea, hemp, collagen, casein and beef noted where relevant. Dietary suitability was another key factor, including vegan, gluten-free, lactose-free and unflavoured options. We also assessed how well each product aligned with different goals, from maintaining muscle and supporting recovery to weight management and increasing calorie intake.

We assessed the following key areas:

- Taste and texture: was the flavour enjoyable and balanced, or overly sweet and artificial? We compared everything from classic vanilla protein powder, vanilla whey protein powder and chocolate protein powder flavours to fruit-inspired clear protein drinks, assessing whether powders blended smoothly, without a gritty or chalky finish.

- Type of protein: we noted whether each product was whey-based, plant-based, collagen-based, casein-based or derived from ingredients such as pea, hemp or beef. We also recorded whether the protein was supplied as a concentrate, isolate or hydrolysed form, as this can influence protein content and digestibility.

- Nutrient profile: protein content per serving was compared alongside calories, fat, carbohydrate and sugar levels. This allowed us to identify products suited to a variety of goals, including muscle gain, recovery, weight management and healthy ageing.

- Sweeteners: we recorded whether products contained sugar, stevia or artificial sweeteners, as these can have a significant impact on flavour and overall drinking experience.

- Dietary suitability: vegan, vegetarian and gluten- and lactose-free claims were verified to help identify products suitable for different dietary requirements.

- Value for money: cost per serving was weighed against ingredient quality, protein content and pack size to assess overall value and support an informed protein powder comparison.

- Labelling and transparency: we checked ingredient lists, nutritional information and any available third-party testing or quality assurances. We also considered how well brands addressed common consumer questions, including 'is protein powder good for you?' and 'does protein powder expire?', through their labelling, websites and supporting information.

item.title: Sheet-Pan Cider Vinegar Chicken
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Slashing bone-in chicken thighs (carefully, around the bone, of course) allows a punchy maple-Dijon-ACV marinade to permeate the meat deeply in a short amount of time. And that waiting time is well spent: Scatter torn sourdough bread on a baking sheet and bake until crisp, then toss croutons aside to make way for the thighs. Once the chicken is cooked through, toss the croutons in the rendered fat and cook until everything is bronzed and glistening. A few handfuls of arugula make an elegant finish—who needs a side salad?

Recipe information

- Total Time 1 hour 10 minutes

- Yield 4 servings

Ingredients

5

½

8

3

1

2½

1

3

8

3

2

Need to make a substitution?

Preparation

- Step 1 Whisk 5 garlic cloves, finely grated, ½ cup plus 3 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar, 5 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, 3 Tbsp. Dijon mustard, 1 Tbsp. plus 2 tsp. pure maple syrup, 2½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1½ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) in a measuring glass or small bowl to combine. Transfer 2 Tbsp. vinegar mixture to a small bowl; set aside. Step 2 Arrange 3 lb. skin-on, bone-in chicken thighs (6–8), skin side up, on a cutting board. Season lightly with salt. Turn over and season lightly on other side with salt, then carefully use a sharp paring knife to make 3 long slashes, going most of the way through meat (avoid the bone). Transfer to a large bowl and pour vinegar mixture in measuring glass over. Toss chicken to coat, making sure to get liquid into slashes. Let chicken sit at least 30 minutes and up to 1 hour. Step 3 Meanwhile, place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 425°. Place 8 oz. country-style or sourdough bread (about ⅓ loaf), torn into 1" pieces, on a rimmed baking sheet. Drizzle remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil over and sprinkle with a pinch of salt and a pinch of freshly ground black pepper; toss to coat. Arrange bread in a single layer and bake until golden, 12–15 minutes. Transfer croutons to a plate; reserve baking sheet. Step 4 Arrange reserved chicken on reserved baking sheet and nestle 3 large shallots, quartered lengthwise through root ends, around; pour any excess vinegar mixture in bowl over. Bake chicken until golden, cooked through, and an instant-read thermometer inserted into thickest part, avoiding bone, registers at least 165° (it should be well over), 25–30 minutes. Step 5 Scatter croutons over empty areas of baking sheet and toss to soak up juices. Roast until chicken and croutons are deeply browned, 10–12 minutes. Let cool 5 minutes, then top with 2 oz. arugula and drizzle with reserved vinegar mixture in small bowl.

item.title: From You Can See Everything to Take That: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Going out: Cinema

You Can See Everything

Out now

“Masterpiece” – it’s an overused word, but sometimes, it’s the only word. This funny, tragic, gripping, three-hour sensation (and, yes, masterpiece) arrives in the UK after a record-busting run in the States, where Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s portrait of their time immersed in the world of Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes has gripped US audiences.

Josephine

Out now

Winner of the Audience and Grand Jury prizes at Sundance, this drama sees eight-year-old Josephine become witness to a horrific assault on a jogger in San Francisco’s Golden Gate park. Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan star as the girl’s parents.

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother

Out now

Mahershala Ali stars as a former military hitman dealing with multiple crises. These range from orders to assassinate a Muslim porn studio head honcho’s charismatic Christian enemy, to finding fresh breast milk for his baby daughter, whose mother has recently passed, and who can’t digest formula.

Filipiñana

Out now

Seventeen-year-old Isabel (Jorrybell Agoto) works at an elite golf course in the Philippines as a “tee-girl” – setting golf tees in the ground so that wealthy golfers don’t have to suffer the indignity of bending down themselves to do it. An examination of national identity as well as a personal drama, it marks the debut of director Rafael Manuel. Catherine Bray

Going out:Gigs

Jungle

to 28 November; tour starts Leeds

With a Brit win, a Mercury nod and five Top 10 albums, dance-pop trio Jungle have quietly (and, let’s be honest, pretty anonymously) become one of Britain’s biggest bands. Their stealthy rise is cemented via this arena tour in support of August’s Sunshine album. Michael Cragg

Knats

Future Yard, Birkenhead, 21 November; Waiting Room, Stockton-on-Tees 22 November

This jazz, rock and dance trio’s punky “geordie jazz” started making waves in 2025. Their latest release, A Great Day in Newcastle, reveals hard-hitting poetry, humour, and a rebellious energy sure to take them far. John Fordham

Manchester Collective

Lakeside Arts, Nottingham, 25 November; touring to 6 December

The latest programme from this boundary-storming contemporary music ensemble mixes an experimental work by Icelandic soundtrack queen Hildur Guðnadottir with Bach chorales and movements from James Tenney’s 1980s electroacoustic classic Glissade. At its centre lies Black Gold, Luke Mombrea’s powerfully atmospheric audiovisual piece inspired by an oil well fire. Flora Willson

Action All Areas

Roundhouse, London, 26 November

Self Esteem, James Bay and Jade Bird are the musical performers at this one-off night of “intimate and unplugged” music and activism in aid of Greenpeace. It’s hosted by comedian and writer Sophie Duker. MC

Going out: Art

Barbara Hepworth and Greece

Pallant House, Chichester, to 2 May

Arguably Britain’s most important modernist, Barbara Hepworth found inspiration for her elegant, curving sculptural forms everywhere. But a journey through Greece in 1954 changed everything for her, and this exhibition shows us the gorgeous results.

Nan Goldin

Hayward Gallery, London, 24 November to 14 March

Get ready to feel a lot of feelings. American photographer Nan Goldin has spent her career documenting queer subcultures, personal relationships and addiction, often to devastating effect.

Ragnar Kjartansson

Goodwood Art Foundation, Chichester, 26 November to 12 April

This playfully melancholic Icelandic conceptualist was last on these shores with a hugely popular Barbican show 10 years ago, and now he’s bringing his signature blend of humour and discomfort to Chichester.

Peggy Guggenheim in London

Royal Academy of Art, London, to 14 March

Peggy Guggenheim became one of the biggest and most important art collectors of the 20th century, and it all started on Cork Street in London. This exhibition looks at Guggenheim’s first gallery venture in 1938, and the way it shocked conservative British tastes. Eddy Frankel

Going out: Stage

Birmingham Royal Ballet: The Nutcracker

Birmingham Hippodrome, to 12 December

One of the best Nutcrackers you’ll see in the UK, Birmingham Royal Ballet’s production was presented as a gift to the company by former director Peter Wright back in 1990 and has been a hit ever since. It ticks all the Christmas boxes: giant tree, falling (and dancing) snowflakes, and a full orchestra playing Tchaikovsky’s magical music. Lyndsey Winship

Eurotrash

Young Vic, London, to 9 January

A stellar double act – Ben Whishaw and Kathryn Hunter – lead this stage adaptation of Christian Kracht’s darkly comic novel. It’s about a formidable mother and son who embark on a road trip across the Swiss mountains, intent on giving away the (slightly dodgy) family money, stashed in a plastic bag. Miriam Gillinson

My Fair Lady

Pitlochry Festival theatre, to 31 December

Alan Cumming stars alongside Verity Power in a chamber production of My Fair Lady, the final show of Cumming’s opening season as artistic director. It’s directed by Maria Friedman, whose work always has such grace and wit. MG

Sam Campbell

Touring to 1 December

Four years after winning Edinburgh’s best show prize, the Aussie eccentric has infiltrated the comedy mainstream; first as a contestant on Last One Laughing: UK, then via his surreal Channel 4 series Make That Movie. His new standup show Kid Giblet promises plenty more absurd flights of fancy. Rachel Aroesti

Staying in:Streaming

Sweetpea

NOW & Sky Atlantic, 26 November, 9pm

Fallout’s Ella Purnell is back as the wispily fringed Rhiannon, a meek outsider who finds her niche in vigilante serial killing in this smart and gruesome drama that reflects wryly on female empowerment and the concept of embracing your flaws. Will she continue to get away with murder in series two?

The Witch Farm

iPlayer & BBC One, 22 November, 9pm

King of the contemporary ghost story Danny Robins has adapted his Radio 4 drama about a couple who (unintentionally) move to a haunted farm in south Wales in the late 1980s into a goosebump-inducing TV thriller. Black Doves’ Gabrielle Creevy and This Is England’s Michael Socha co-star.

Oobah: Scams For A Better Tomorrow

HBO Max, 22 November

Fraudsters, grifters, conmen: to be alive today is to be besieged by bad actors – and Oobah Butler wants a piece of their pie. That’s the droll setup of his new series, which will really see the prankster documentarian highlight swindles in areas including wine, wellness and dating.

Blade Runner 2099

Prime Video, 25 November

This sequel to the 1982 and 2017 films picks up the action a half-century later, when lab-grown humanoids rule over LA’s actual human inhabitants. Our protagonists are replicant Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) and human-pretending-to-be-a-replicant Cora (Hunter Schafer) who team up to track down a bunch of their awol peers. RA

Staying in: Games

Appulse

PC, out 26 November

An ingenious combination of pinball machine and top-down shooter, Appulse has you blasting enemy spaceships while rebounding between flippers and bumpers earning special upgrades. Surely, a veteran gamer’s dream.

Am I Nima?

PC, out 27 November

Locked in a basement and suffering from amnesia, you must convince your mum that you are in fact her daughter. Created by Vancouver studio Ho! Games, this is a psychological horror game with a truly interesting and unnerving premise. Keith Stuart

Staying in: Albums

Lambchop – Demoed

Out now

In August Kurt Wagner shared his 17th album as Lambchop, a folk freakout titled Punching The Clown. This followup EP finds guest artists singing over a handful of that album’s demos. Vocalists include MJ Lenderman, Lauren Auder and Flock of Dimes.

Take That – Dreamers

Out now…

item.title: In a Sydney gallery, Philippe Parreno’s art is powered by a desert 17,000km away
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

I’m standing in a massive white-cube space, staring at a perplexing assortment of objects. There are several expensive looking lamps; a massive industrial fan; a couple of speakers; marquee-style lights; a glowing assemblage of power adapters. At the back of the gallery, a silvery light slides up and down a pole. The bulbs are flickering erratically, and there’s a low hum of machine noise, overlaid with bird song and distant barking.

As an installation, taken by itself, it’s deceptively underwhelming – a spectacle without a story.

This will be visitors’ first encounter with the Museum of Contemporary Art’s summer blockbuster exhibition, Philippe Parreno: 5 Moons, named for the five lunar cycles of the show’s duration. It’s the first major Australian exhibition by the acclaimed French contemporary artist, renowned for taking over museums and galleries – including Tate Modern’s Turbine Hall and the Palais de Tokyo in Paris – with discombobulating and delightful kinetic arrangements of objects, screen works, sound and lighting.

Parreno’s medium of choice is the exhibition itself; he creates holistic, unpredictable environments for the visitor to navigate.

At the MCA, Parreno has created a series of connected environments across the museum’s three levels, featuring works made over his four-decade career.

Upstairs, there’s an orange-carpeted gallery populated by floating, helium-filled, fish-shaped balloons in citrus tones, in which a grand piano plays an enigmatic score. On another floor, a giant luminescent cuttlefish gazes out impassively from a screen, its fins and arms gently undulating, as ambient electronic noise emanates from large swiveling speaker banks.

These spaces feel like haunted houses; machines operated by ghosts or powered by supernatural energy.

In fact, they’re powered by nature: real-time data – including wind speed, humidity and temperature – captured on sensors on an abandoned almond farm in the Tabernas desert in south-eastern Spain, a region best known internationally as the backdrop to spaghetti westerns such as The Good, the Bad and the Ugly and Once Upon a Time in the West.

Data from the farm has been reconfigured into an algorithm that influences the sound, air flow and lighting 17,000km away in Sydney. The land is improvising a score, and the museum is playing it.

In a darkened gallery on the museum’s third floor, a massive screen is showing an 11-hour film composed of footage shot on the abandoned almond farm. Visitors can, if they choose, sit and watch a night pass under the Spanish moon.

Live sound from this terrain is also played in the gallery, making for an uncanny mix: during my visit, nocturnal insect noises from Spain are punctuated by the toot of an ocean liner docked outside in Sydney Harbour.

“What I normally try to do for exhibition is to try to create sort of a milieu, or an ecosystem, where things are responding to each other,” says Parreno, whose family migrated from the same region of Spain hundreds of years ago, to Algeria, where he was born.

Backstory is important for Parreno’s art: without it, his ecosystems risk seeming frustratingly opaque or worse, inane.

Some parts of the MCA exhibition stand alone, without narrative, thanks to their aesthetic or mise en scene. Some are more tenuous: a white-walled area in which a layer of helium filled speech-bubble balloons covers the ceiling, while a series of coloured lights flash. When you learn the lighting pattern is a morse code translation of a mystical adventure by French writer René Daumal, it suddenly feels more substantial.

Parreno’s most famous artwork, his 2016 takeover of the Tate’s Turbine Hall, delighted some and frustrated others. But his backstory, involving a jar of yeast in a hidden lab whose biodata was influencing the whole thing, was almost irresistibly intriguing.

“Lots of the things I do require people to endorse a fiction,” Parreno commented at the time.

His interest in fiction is more than a gimmick, it’s deeply philosophical, and 5 Moons is underpinned by ideas of how our perceptions of a thing change it; how the way we imagine land, by knock on effect, influences and transforms it.

When Parreno showed an earlier iteration of the 5 Moons film at Munich’s Haus der Kunst in 2024, he said the work was designed to feel as if the land was “speaking to you”. “With the ways climate change is changing the world, how do we address the landscape? Are we going to keep transforming it? Or is it maybe the other way around – that the land is looking at us.”

When he started out making exhibitions in the late 80s and 90s, Parreno had revolutionary ideals. “You want to change the world. You want to produce a new reality,” he tells me.

And now? “I want to create that thing that you don’t see much [these days],” he says. “In the system we live in, you are always obliged to respond to a signal. Here you are not. You just float with your own attention, and you spend the time you want.”

- Philippe Parreno: 5 Moons is on at the Museum of Contemporary Art, Sydney, until 26 April 2027

Source: The Guardian Art and Design | Published: 2026-11-21 01:00 UTC

item.title: Is GTA VI the Art Miami Deserves?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Is GTA VI the Art Miami Deserves?

Miami-based artists Leo Castañeda and misael soto join Hyperallergic in a conversation about the tensions of a game that portrays a changing city locked in time.

“Driving at rush hour. SIGNIFICANTLY less cars on the road.” The text was from Miami-based artist, educator, and organizer misael soto, sent yesterday, November 19, a few hours after the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. We’d come full circle: The bumper-to-bumper traffic that Miami, the city I once called home, is now notorious for — in no small part due to overdevelopment, climate change, and strained infrastructure — was being alleviated by a video game that keeps people at home, inside a simulation of the same city locked in time.

The premise of GTA VI is simple on the surface. The game follows Lucía Caminos and Jason Duval in the criminal underworld of Leonida, a fictionalized state based on South Florida: Miami becomes Vice City, the Everglades are the Grassrivers. But its portrayal of real-life hardships, socioeconomic inequality, and even Lucía and Jason’s love story, among other elements, has elicited deeper reflections and responses across our increasingly blurred online and physical worlds.

To help make sense of these tensions, I got on a phone call with soto and Leo Castañeda, two Miami-based artists whose work I admire. Castañeda is an artist and video game designer exploring Latin American Surrealism in the digital age, and soto co-leads Artists for Artists: Miami, which is leading a boycott of Art Basel next month, and works in the overlapping arenas of labor rights, public infrastructure, and conceptual and social practice.

Our conversation was edited and condensed for clarity. I hope you enjoy it.

Hyperallergic: Before we even get into GTA, I was hoping each of you could tell me a little bit about your relationship to Miami — how long you've been there? How do you feel about living there now?

Leo Castañeda: I moved to Miami first when I was 11. My parents first moved to New York [from Colombia], and then they thought it was too cold, so they moved to Miami. I went to middle school and high school here, then I moved to New York for college, and I moved back in 2015. When I first moved back after college, it was mostly because of the cost of living in New York. And then, within the 10 years that I've been here, it became the same cost of living as New York, except with Florida salaries.

I do feel grateful, though, to be part of the Bakehouse Art Complex, where I have an affordable studio. I live in the North Beach area, and I was able to find a sustainable rent. Miami has a lot of arts nonprofits that help over time. I do feel that, as complicated as the Miami arts ecosystem is, it is pretty supportive — but at the same time, it is tied to all the different layers of money that have come in and dominate the arts, which are very present here.

misael soto: I moved here right after undergrad. I grew up in South Florida, originally from Puerto Rico, and Miami was always la locura, down south. We would visit my cousins and whatnot from time to time. As I became more and more interested in starting my own practice, I moved down here and have continually been sucked back in. I try to leave, and it pulls me back for whatever reason. Since COVID, everything's changed. Miami became the second most expensive city in the country. The influx was palpable: All of a sudden, there were Texas and California and New York license plates, Teslas zipping around town, and rent just started skyrocketing. There's more flooding. But at the same time, it's gorgeous, and it's special. I live in Mid-Beach. I can go to the water, I can breathe in some sea air, I can hear 10 different languages at once.

It's a really complex relationship with Miami. Especially, I think, both of us make complicated art — we both make art that is unconventional and perhaps even, you could say, difficult to collect. I don't know if you describe yourself that way, Leo, but I definitely do. And making this kind of work in a hyper market-driven neoliberal city like Miami, on the one hand, it gives me a lot of fodder, a lot of material, a lot of things to talk about, as we're doing right now. But at the same time, it can be really frustrating and alienating and lonesome, ultimately.

H: I moved from Argentina to Miami when I was little because my mom got a job there. We lived in the Doral neighborhood, where most people I knew were also from Latin America, until I left for Chicago for college at 18. I've lived in New York for over a decade now, but I still feel a strong pull to Miami, I feel seen, surrounded by people whose identities are a bit fractured the way I feel mine is.

And on the note of nostalgia, GTA is a game that was made over the last 13 years, so it chronicles a Miami that’s partly gone. For example, users say Lucía's home is based on a cute salmon-pink, 13-unit condo in Edgewater that was demolished in 2022 to build a 55-story tower, yet it lives on in the game. What does it mean for a video game to preserve a place that no longer exists?

LC: Well, a few thoughts. During that 13-year development, I would assume the map design was one of the first things they did. But there are also aspects of the chronicling of Miami, or Miami becoming this satire through the game, that have evolved in a shorter time period. For example, this morning I woke up, and there was a Miami Instagram influencer saying that in the fictional version of the Cuban coffee shop Versailles, which is called Antoinette, the bakery has a sign posted outside that says something like, “any politician must pay for all the food when they leave.” That's a reference from a few years ago, when Trump reportedly went to Versailles, ordered food for everyone, and then didn't pay and just walked out.

So it does seem like a video game takes a long time to make, and this one is probably the most ambitious one ever made — 4,500 people working really, really hard, to the point of even having the union situations that they have in the UK branch of the company. But at the same time, I feel like they studied Miami extremely well, and the integration with some local businesses and local artists in particular — I've seen a few street artists like Ahol Sniffs Glue, Soak, Tatiana Suarez, Typoe, as well as musician Nick León. One restaurant is based on Juvia on Lincoln Road, which doesn't exist anymore — they got priced out, and now there's a record of it. The game takes so long to make, but it lives in an ever-present, because it doesn't matter if you made an asset 13 years in the past, like Lucía's apartment, or now; they feel like the present. It's an interesting amalgamation. I would have to spend more time with it to really know: Does this feel like Miami in 2014 or Miami in 2026, or a hybrid?

H: To get into the politics of the conversation around GTA, I have a lot of icky feelings about one narrative that's taking hold online, which is that the game is “Woke 3.0,” and that the incels and Trump supporters are pissed about it. I only played for a few hours last night, and I went into a gun shop and bought a shotgun. That, to me, panders much more to the NRA hawks and the pro-gun community than to anything that could be considered woke, you know?…

Source: Hyperallergic | Published: 2026-11-20 23:51 UTC

Original link: https://hyperallergic.com/is-gta-vi-the-art-miami-deserves/

item.title: The Beauty of the Game: Artist Paul Pfeiffer and Collectors Larry and Allison Berg on the Evolving Crossover Between Art and Sports
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

The convergence of art and sports has become too prevalent to ignore. During Art Week NYC, a citywide festival organized by ARTnews, Artforum, and Art in America, ARTnews convened a panel of people who brought different perspectives to this new development: Larry Berg, co-managing owner of the Los Angeles Football Club and the incoming commissioner of Major League Soccer; his wife Allison Berg, an art collector who, with Larry, founded the A&L Berg Foundation to support early-career arts professionals and artists whose work explores social practice (the Bergs helped the Los Angeles County Museum of Art acquire Fútballet, a sculpture by Lyndon J. Barrois, Sr. that brings soccer and art together); artist Paul Pfeiffer, who has long used video, photography and sculpture to transform familiar images from the world of sports and entertainment, making us reexamine fame, crowds, and the power of spectacle, and who was recently appointed the first artist-in-residence at Barclays Center in Brooklyn. My colleague at PMC, Scott Soshnick, editor-in-chief of Sportico, co-moderated.

At our talk on Friday, November 13, at the PMC Studio in Midtown Manhattan, which you can watch in the video above, we discussed how sports is bringing a new audience to art; the connections between team ownership and art collecting; how art can function in a stadium setting; and the beauty of the game.

item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

The Real Miami Museums and Artists Behind GTA VI’s Vice City

From The Bass in Miami Beach to the murals of Wynwood, the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto VI is heavily inspired by the local arts scene.

After 13 agonizing years of waiting for Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6), gamers worldwide wasted no time tearing up the streets of the game's fictional state of Leonida after it was released yesterday, November 19. The South Florida-inspired game environment is heavily influenced by the culture, environment, and architecture of Miami — from its Art Deco resorts, white-sand beaches, Cuban quarter, and strip clubs, right down to its museums and arts venues.

As fans embed themselves in GTA 6's immersive landscape, many have recognized real-life locations across South Florida making unexpected cameos. One such case is the Vice Museum of Art, which Rockstar Games confirmed is modeled after the Bass Museum of Art in Miami Beach.

“It was totally unexpected to see Grand Theft Auto VI reimagine The Bass as the ‘Vice City Museum of Art,’” said Silvia Karman Cubiñá, executive director of the Bass Museum of Art, in an email to Hyperallergic.

“It’s a wonderful reminder of how art and architecture can become part of popular culture,” she continued. “Now, I’m just curious: will the Vice City Museum of Art get more visitors than we do?!”

While not listed as a landmark like the Vice Museum of Art, another building in Downtown Vice City appears to be directly modeled after the Pérez Art Museum Miami (PAMM). Situated near the Vice City Arts Center, which is heavily based on Miami's Adrienne Arsht Center for Performing Arts, the PAMM-inspired building sits right on the water's edge just as the museum does in real life.

“We were as delighted as anyone else to find PAMM in what feels like the biggest video game of all time,” said Alexa Ferra, PAMM's senior director of marketing and communications, in an email to Hyperallergic.

Ferra attached a photo someone sent her from the game showing the PAMM dupe and some gummy bear-inspired sculptures installed in the shallow water.

“It's a testament to our stunning Herzog & de Meuron building, and goes to show if you stick around long enough, you'll pop up in the unlikeliest — but inevitable — of places.” Ferra added.

Other references to Miami's arts and culture scene include Leonida's Stockyard neighborhood, which directly channels the street murals and warehouse-lined roads of the Wynwood Arts District. It was reported earlier this summer that Rockstar Games had hired over 50 real street artists to design the in-game murals across Stockyard. Users shared they've spotted the works of street artist Ahol Sniffs Glue (David Anasagasti), among others.

Miami-raised contemporary photographer Josh Aronson also took notice of GTA 6's inclusion of his installation at the Catalina Hotel & Beach Club in Miami Beach during Miami Art Week 2024, which Rockstar Games incorporated in Vice City's own Catalina Hotel. From Aronson's Florida Boys (2020–) photo series, the photo “Spring” (2024) was made into an enormous sublimated fabric print that hung from the second-story window of the hotel.

The same printed photo, which features a group of cheerful young men photographed from above while floating in water, is shown at Vice City's Catalina Hotel.

“Florida Boys is my own imagined version of Florida, so I love that it gets to live on in another imagined Florida,” Aronson told Hyperallergic. “The installation at the Catalina was temporary, but in Vice City, someone might stumble upon it years from now. It’s a reminder of the wild ways we encounter art today, and how a work can find new life long after it comes down.”

GTA6's pre-holiday release comes just before Miami Art Week begins early next month. Those dropping in can find some of Aronson's installations on view beyond Vice City at the Vizcaya Museum and Gardens and the Museum of Contemporary Art, North Miami, and also pay homage to the cultural venues and districts that inspired Leonida.

Source: Hyperallergic | Published: 2026-11-20 19:42 UTC

Original link: https://hyperallergic.com/the-real-miami-museums-and-artists-behind-gta-vis-vice-city/

item.title: Student Wrecks Scottish Exhibit in Attempt to Sit on Stone of Destiny
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

A French student who smashed a vitrine protecting the storied Stone of Destiny in Scotland said he did so by right, claiming to having been born in Scotland and thus having been bestowed the privilege of sitting on a relic that had been used to crown Scottish monarchs until the 13th century.

As reported by the BBC, “Arnaud Hercules Harixcalde Logan, 36, pleaded guilty to a charge of maliciously damaging the historic artefact’s glass casing at Perth Museum in July last year. Perth Sheriff Court was shown CCTV footage which showed Logan using a blue and white hammer to strike the reinforced glass cabinet 24 times—causing £9,000 [around $12,000] worth of damage.”

The incident, which forced the closure of the Stone of Destiny exhibit for three months, led to Logan being tackled by a museum visitor and a member of its staff. After an initial court appearance last year, the perpetrator fled to Australia and failed to check in with police for several months, as required by law. To that and the smashing incident, Logan pled guilty, with sentencing to follow on January 6.

About the jarring day at the museum, a public prosecutor said, “Members of the public appeared distressed and panicked. Staff evacuated everyone from the building. He said he was called Logan and that the Logan clan had been betrayed and that the Stone of Destiny had been stolen from him.”

Source: ARTnews | Published: 2026-11-20 19:16 UTC
