item.title: Meet Lanza Atelier, Frida Escobedo's pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Meet Lanza Atelier, Frida Escobedo’s pick for the most influential architect of the next 20 years

They started the year crowned the 2026 Serpentine Pavilion architects and are ending it as trailblazer Frida Escobedo‘s pick for the practitioners who will shape the next two decades.

In this interview for Dezeen’s 20×20 series sponsored by Kohler, Lanza Atelier discuss the bathrooms that brought them together, the yin and yang of their partnership, and their hopes for the future.

The 20×20 series, launched to mark 20 years of Dezeen, is a two-stage affair: first, we rounded up 20 designers and architects who we’ve seen make a major impact over those 20 years, then we asked them to nominate the emerging practitioners that they think will make a big impact on the next 20.

With just 10 years between the start of their practices, Escobedo and Lanza Atelier represent two crests on a new wave of Mexican architecture that has brought regional references to the world stage and made adventurous but sympathetic interventions at home in Mexico City.

Escobedo was one of Lanza Atelier’s Alessandro Arienzo’s teachers at the Universidad Iberoamericana in Mexico City, and he and partner Isabel Abascal cite her as an inspiration whose success with kindred ideas has given them the confidence to pursue their vision.

They are becoming known for distilling complexity down to simple and pure gestures, whether in the appropriately snaking crinkle-crankle walls of their Serpentine Pavilion, inspired by the English countryside, their Cancun house with materials and forms drawn from sea snail shells, their Re-Source exhibition design that visitors could take home, or their hierarchy-challenging Family of 4 chairs, prompted by the arrival of their second son.

For Escobedo’s part, she identifies Arienzo and Abascal’s dedication to concept and process, which involves extensive research and testing, as key to their strength.

“Their work is poetic and intellectually rigorous,” said Escobedo. “They work seamlessly across scales, bringing together material intelligence, generosity, and a sense of play that makes their architecture both thoughtful and joyful.”

The Lanza story began in 2015, with toilets. Arienzo was approached by a client who, nearing the end of their bike path development in Mexico City, realised that they needed public bathroom facilities along the route. Arienzo suggested to Abascal, originally from Madrid, that they work on together on the project.

Their work is poetic and intellectually rigorous. They work seamlessly across scales, bringing together material intelligence, generosity, and a sense of play

Quickly, their collaboration turned one of architecture’s humblest structures into a nexus for meaning and care.

“We were exploring the scarcity of means and materials, but also the boundaries between inside and outside, and how to make something very simple like a toilet become something larger, like a meeting point and a resting space,” said Abascal.

“And also how to plan for the future of public architecture that might not be very taken care of or maintained by combining landscape and construction.”

The finished project features semi-open structures built from concrete blocks and filled with planting, creating a network of shaded resting points along the exposed track.

From the very first project we did together, we needed to arrive at something that was not Alessandro nor me, but Lanza. Our process has been so similar, in a way [ever since]

Bamboo trees loosely divide the male and female toilets, but they share common sinks – a feature that Lanza Atelier pushed for as part of their vision for a space of respectful coexistence between all users.

“It came out really naturally and fun, and simple,” said Arienzo. “That first interaction made Lanza happen because we needed to build a company after that.”

The nature of the collaboration pushed them to establish a distinct language from the get-go, adds Abascal.

“From the very first project we did together, we needed to arrive at something that was not Alessandro nor me, but Lanza,” she said.

“Our process has been so similar, in a way [ever since]. We explored so many different options, and we were so opinionated about how it should be. We very rigorously really gave all the importance to designing a toilet.”

As Escobedo identifies, Lanza Atelier’s work has a remarkable sense of play considering it lacks the colour, ornamentation or usual curlicues that would prompt association with the word.

Their use of materials is almost austere, in the sense that many of their projects have seen them hone in on just one material and push it to its limits, as in the local Sienna bricks of their Serpentine Pavilion.

Arienzo characterises this “extreme” approach as being “maybe a phase” more than a signature of the studio’s work. Instead, the key feature is how they arrive at the choice.

“We pick materials because of where the project is or what we have close to the site,” Arienzo said. “We analyse what’s the best or least aggressive way to build [in that place], because, we always say, building is really violent.”

Using fewer materials also allows them to focus more on questions of space, and makes it easier for their pavilions and installations, often demountable as a matter of principle, to find a second life.

“The main issue is achieving a degree of simplicity, which is very hard to do, because you start with complexity, and then you have to make decisions and to clean and to extract,” said Abascal.

The main issue is achieving a degree of simplicity, which is very hard to do, because you start with complexity, and then you have to make decisions and to clean and to extract

That’s where the playfulness comes in, the designers identify, allowing them to dig into various elements, flip them, manipulate them and be curious about them.

“That, I think, is the playground,” adds Arienzo.

When asked what qualities each of the duo brings to the table that makes their work together so strong, Arienzo is initially flippant.

“I’m the bad cop,” he says with a smile.

But when the duo finally answers seriously, their responses do seem to reveal something about the alchemy going on behind the scenes.

“I used to call Alessandro’s gaze towards the world ‘the laser eye’,” said Abascal. “He is always pointing things out to me – mostly in our everyday lives, it’s things that the city creates and produces informally, but his laser eye applies to every context.”

“And it’s not only something visual but has to do with how things are and are put together and solved.”

For his part, Arienzo describes Abascal as the powerhouse behind Lanza’s ideas and concepts.

“I think she gives a lot of meaning to the projects,” said Arienzo. “I think without this, I would just do soulless stuff. She connects the work with history, with literature, with art.”

Lanza Atelier’s slate currently includes a house in LA to replace one destroyed by the wildfires, several projects in Mexico City and the design for the Expanded Tradition exhibition on contemporary Mexican craft at Qatari museum M7. When we speak, Abascal is on her way to the Canary Islands to conduct research on bird migration and pregnancy. It’s a patchwork that is idiosyncratically Lanza.

Neither Arienzo or Abascal seems to be the type to have a 10-year plan – asked about professional goals, Arienzo replies that they’re more orientated towards taking better care of themselves and their children – but they identify housing, particularly collective housing, as the type of architecture they most want to work on.

They hope to do it within a global industry that demolishes less and values what’s already built more, and that learns from the original “sustainable architecture” of vernacular construction in places like Mexico.…

Source: Dezeen | Published: 2026-11-20 11:15 UTC

Original link: https://www.dezeen.com/2026/11/20/lanza-atelier-interview-frida-escobedo-20x20/

item.title: Unprecedented Design Museum exhibition surveys "the beauty and the depth of Black design"
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Unprecedented Design Museum exhibition surveys “the beauty and the depth of Black design”

Work from 16 of the most exciting Black designers working today has been brought together under one roof for the first time as part of The Nue Black Aesthetic exhibition at London’s Design Museum.

The all-star lineup features work from fashion designers like Bianca Saunders in dialogue with the buildings of architect Tosin Oshinowo and products by Ini Archibong, Samuel Ross, Simone Brewster and Nifemi Marcus-Bello.

It marks the first time the UK has hosted such a show, according to its guest curator Charlene Prempeh.

The writer and founder of design consultancy A Vibe Called Tech originally came up with the idea for the exhibition while researching her monograph on a century of Black design and was confronted with the lack of documentation she could find on the topic.

“It was a really difficult process because it was just impossible to find any literature or any real evidence of the design work,” she told Dezeen.

This led her to investigate whether any museum shows today were doing a better job chronicling the work of contemporary Black designers.

“I was like: ‘Oh, there hasn’t been anything like that in the UK that I’m aware of,'” explained the curator.

With The Nue Black Aesthetic, Prempeh and the Design Museum‘s project curator Tiya Dahyabhai hope to remedy this. The duo has brought together more than 100 works that range from tailored suits to football kits, from minimalist lighting and headphones to a sculptural West African instrument and a trophy for a dominoes league.

Presented together, they act as a rallying cry against the idea that Black design can only look one way, Prempeh says, allowing its textural and conceptual richness to be experienced in person.

“If people stopped thinking of Black design as just bright colours and wax print, that would be incredible,” she joked.

The show opens with a short look back at the last century of Black design, beginning in the 1920s with Ann Lowe – the first African American fashion designer to become a leading couturier.

“It’s not like Black people weren’t making work before, but in terms of people knowing who they were and there being names and there being evidence of how that work filtered out into the mainstream, that was a really good moment to define,” Prempeh explained.

From here, the show zooms past key moments – the Black Aesthetic movement born out of the Civil Rights era, the pop-infused New Black Aesthetic of the 1980s, the ascendancy of African craft led by Diébédo Francis Kéré and Stephen Burks in the 2000s.

The timeline culminates in 2023 with Lesley Lokko’s curation for the Venice Architecture Biennale, which explored Africa as a “powerful place from which to examine the issues that will dominate the next century”.

Against this backdrop, The Nue Black Aesthetic sets out to chronicle the three key topics that seem to be occupying designers across the diaspora today – identity, community and systems.

“I was looking at the shared ideas that existed within Black design, and those were the themes that kept on coming up again and again and again,” Prempeh explained. “It’s not saying that everyone does everything the same way, but it is saying that there are shared concerns.”

The first section features work that explores themes of identity.

Here, a C-shaped bench made from a single sheet of metal by Nigerian designer Tejumola Adenuga reinterprets Yoruba design principles, while an intricately embroidered cap worn by the Kanuri people is shown next to a school designed for the displaced community by Lagos-based Oshinowo Studio.

Garments from London fashion designers Bianca Saunders and Saul Nash explore ideas of gender and heritage through cloth, and British-Nigerian artist Taiba Akhuetie reframes Black hair styling as a craft through furniture pieces made from carefully sculpted braids of synthetic hair.

Next, the exhibition looks at design as a tool for community building. For some, community comes in the form of sport, as seen in designer Mac Collins‘s monumental trophy for the Nottingham dominoes league and a high-fashion version of Foday Dumbuya‘s viral Pan-African away kit for London football club Arsenal.

Phoebe Collings-James, on the other hand, explores community through craft practice. The Jamaican British sculptor contributed a series of experimental pots born from their studio Mudbelly, which offers free ceramics classes by and for Black people through an anti-elitist lens.

Similar themes show up in the work of Ethiopian fashion designer Feben Vemmen, embodied in a luscious, chainmail-style gown she co-designed with bead makers in Accra, and furniture maker Andu Masebo, who contributed a modular, communal table recently used by a rotating cast of 16 musicians during a live eight-hour jam session.

The exhibition’s final section brings together works that aim to challenge the status quo. Some of these challengers come from within; among them Ross, who’s brought his distinctive language to brands like Nike, Zara and Beats by Dre while also running the Black British Artist Grant Association to uplift the next generation of talent.

There’s also Rachel Scott, who is currently weaving her politics into her work for Proenza Schouler, where she became the first Black woman to lead an established American high fashion house when she joined as creative director in 2025.

On the other end of the spectrum are more collectable designs that criticise the system from the outside, courtesy of genre-bending artist Brewster, British-Ghanaian architect Giles Tettey Nartey and Nigerian designer Marcus-Bello.

Standout pieces include a giant contemporary balafon – a predecessor to the xylophone – and a series of aluminium furniture that questions why craftsmen in Nigeria are relegated to working with scraps from the Global North, when the raw materials are mined locally.

The exhibition concludes with a piece created especially for the show by Nigerian-American designer Archibong: a sweeping Murano glass chandelier that hopes to capture the show’s central idea around the whole African diaspora being engaged in one conversation but with very different perspectives and backgrounds.

For Prempeh, the show is also a way to counter the “lack of curiosity around Blackness” – not to mention the open prejudice – which she says has crept back into society since the height of the Black Lives Matter movement.

“I want to present all of the beauty and the depth of Black design as a counter narrative,” she said.

The Nue Black Aesthetic is on show at London’s Design Museum until 8 August 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for more architecture and design events around the world.

Source: Dezeen | Published: 2026-11-20 11:00 UTC

Original link: https://www.dezeen.com/2026/11/20/the-nue-black-aesthetic-exhibition/

item.title: "All over the world, buildings designed to be explored in 3D are subject to restrictions"
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

“All over the world, buildings designed to be explored in 3D are subject to restrictions”

Controversy over visitors having to pay to access the walkable roof at the new Shanghai Grand Opera House brings into focus the need for architects to be realistic about how buildings operate, writes Aaron Betksy.

The beauty of many recent Chinese buildings is that they are also landscapes. You can walk up to them, around them, and through them, but also over them.

Ma Yansong’s buildings are often hills that you are invited to climb: the new Shenzhen Bay Cultural Center is a case in point, as is the Quzhou Sports Center, which actually is five different scalable hills, but his oldest major building, the Harbin Opera House of 2015, also offers a path over the auditorium. The Kowloon High Speed Train Station, designed by Andrew Bromberg of Aedas, is meant to be a continuous curve rising over the waiting hall you can ascend to view over to Hong Kong Island.

And now Snøhetta’s just-completed Shanghai Opera House offers you a cantilevered stair with a view back over the river to the city.

Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks

There’s only one problem: sooner or later, you will hit a barrier, usually makeshift and consisting of moveable fences and lots of yellow and black tape.

Sometimes the restrictions are monetary. Many building owners who have paid a little extra to get that architectural rizz have realized, once they see their building overwhelmed by selfie takers, that they can monetize their outlooks and prospects. The Shanghai Opera House is the latest case: to ascend that-stairway-almost-to-heaven you must pay 50 RMB, or about eight bucks.

That last move has raised the consciousness of the masses to a much higher degree than the inability to climb Mount Ma in various cities. The digisphere is not happy. Apparently, people feel that photographing themselves against an urban view should be a right, even if the institution giving them that opportunity invested (albeit, in this case, mainly through state funds) in making that experience possible.

Nor is this a problem only in China: all over the world, buildings that were designed to be explored in three dimensions are often subject to restrictions. The fluidity of which architects dream drowns in a sea of concerns about safety and security.

In Europe, the restrictions are a bit more akin to the maze airports have put in your way between security and the gates: you can get to the top of MVRDV’s Depot in Rotterdam or Herzog & de Meuron’s Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg for free, but you have to figure out how, and are meant to be tempted to buy at least a drink along the way.

In our experience economy, that seems par for the parcours to me. Space and views are among the most valuable luxuries on offer, so, until the revolution comes, I do not see the big deal.

A both bigger and smaller issue is the barriers themselves. Even those who confront them in Shanghai and don’t mind forking over the yuan find that the kluges stand in the way not only of free access, but also of the views and of the architecture.

You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences

That is because the architects never intended the fences to be there in the first place, so they did not design them into the building. They are the most obtrusive part of the many signs, furnishings, and security devices that festoon buildings especially in China, but all over the world as well.

The architect Theo Deutinger has written a wonderful compendium, Handbook of Tyranny, listing and diagraming many of the devices that control our movements. Many of them we do not notice, but those that are added after construction stick out the most. You can ignore the Eyes in the Sky hidden in the ceiling, but not the fences.

Ironically, part of the reason they are so obvious in China and other Asian countries is because until recently there were so many fewer of them. When the Harbin Opera House opened a little over a decade ago you could clamber all over it, and the same was true of the Kowloon train station.

In recent years, local authorities have become concerned about the same issues that have restricted flows in the Western world. That is largely because of heightened accountability: you can’t easily sue if you trip in China, but local authorities can face consequences from government over mishaps in buildings they oversee – and architects there tell me this is increasingly common.

To be clear, beyond the aesthetic concerns these developments are not entirely negative. Accessibility provisions have often been poor in China, but recently ramps and other devices are opening more spaces to those with mobility issues – including toddlers and older people who might enjoy these urban landscapes the most. Architects design tiered complexity at the risk of eliminating many users, as Steven Holl, for instance, found out in the case of his Brooklyn Library.

The solution should be relatively simple: architects should design both accessibility and risk-avoidance into their vertical landscapes. Ma’s Lucas Museum in Los Angeles and its surrounding park, designed by Mia Lehrer, already do so (pictured left). There is no reason beyond economics and design complexity that people should not be guided and seduced up and over buildings, even if they might have to pay for that privilege.

When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers

That leaves only a deeper issue, which is that of the difficulty of fulfilling the promise of fluid space. When Zaha Hadid started on her folds and later curves, she dreamed of a truly open architecture in which urban life would move without barriers in and out of covered and even conditioned places. Blobitecture or parametricism offered the same prospects, and Wolf Prix has been screaming for an “open architecture of the open eye, the open mind, the open heart” for decades.

Objective reality stands in the way. Buildings are still buildings – both because of the limits of what structures and conditioning systems can do, leading to the hoary problem of where you put a door, or even a toilet, with sufficient headroom in a blob – and because somebody pays for them.

Inside, as Rem Koolhaas once said, “all conditioned space is conditional” and outside we are finding that the same is true. You have to pay to play, or for right of way.

As is so often the case, the mountable building landscapes that have been constructed with increasing frequency and at larger and larger scales in the last few decades are more promissory notes for a future open society than built utopias. You can go with the flow and climb any building or mountain, but sooner or later economic and regulatory reality will bring you back down to earth.

Aaron Betsky is a senior design associate at Carlo Ratti Associati, a visiting professor at Kean University and a visiting lecturer at the University of Pennsylvania. He was previously a professor at Virginia Tech School of Architecture and Design and president of the School of Architecture at Taliesin. He has written more than a dozen books on architecture, design and art, including Landscrapers: Building with the Land, published in 2002.

Dezeen In Depth

If you enjoy reading Dezeen’s interviews, opinions and features, subscribe to Dezeen In Depth. Sent on the last Friday of each month, this newsletter provides a single place to read about the design and architecture stories behind the headlines.

Source: Dezeen | Published: 2026-11-20 10:30 UTC

item.title: The Relief of Rock Bottom: George Orwell and the Secret Springboard of Success
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

The Relief of Rock Bottom: George Orwell and the Secret Springboard of Success

By Maria Popova

It happens to everyone — to kings and paupers, to astronauts and poets. Nothing will protect you from it — not money, not love, not perfect health — for it spares no life that is fully lived, not the sunniest or the most privileged or the best planned.

It begins with the wall — the one you hit over and over and over, not breaking through. And then, after the exhausted collapse, the bottom. The floorboards of despair, cold as granite, absolute as gravity.

But then something extraordinary happens — something George Orwell (June 25, 1903–January 21, 1950) captures perfectly in a passage from Down and out in Paris and London (public library), recounting his experience of abject poverty while trying to become a writer, working in restaurant kitchens in Paris and wandering London as a tramp.

What Orwell observes of material poverty applies equally to the spiritual poverty of hope and meaning we call despair:

When you are approaching poverty, you make one discovery which outweighs some of the others. You discover boredom and mean complications and the beginnings of hunger, but you also discover the great redeeming feature of poverty: the fact that it annihilates the future.

It annihilates, he means, anxiety about the future, for when you have nothing left to lose, there is nothing to worry about losing. That is the relief of rock bottom — a feeling that is “a great consolation” when you are at your lowest, and one that “everyone who has been hard up has experienced”:

It is a feeling of relief, almost of pleasure, at knowing yourself at last genuinely down and out. You have talked so often of going to the dogs — and well, here are the dogs, and you have reached them, and you can stand it. It takes off a lot of anxiety.

Two millennia before him, Marcus Aurelius had anchored his meditation on turning suffering into strength in the same premise:

Be like a headland: the waves beat against it continuously, but it stands fast and around it the boiling water dies down. “It’s my rotten luck that this has happened to me.” On the contrary, “It’s my good luck that, although this has happened to me, I still feel no distress, since I’m unbruised by the present and unconcerned about the future.” What happened could have happened to anyone, but not everyone could have carried on without letting it distress him.

Here, the Stoic perspective converges with the Buddhist, best articulated by Pema Chödrön in her timeless field guide to transformation through trying times:

Only to the extent that we expose ourselves over and over to annihilation can that which is indestructible be found in us.

And that is the thing about rock bottom: Not only does it hold, but it is there you discover the part of you that also holds — the bedrock of your being unassailable by all the loss, all the failure, all the frivolities of chance. Orwell, being neither a Stoic nor a Buddhist, understood the universality of his experience. “It is a fairly trivial story,” he writes at the end of his memoir — trivial because its essence is so common, no matter the guise; trivial because it touches an elemental truth: The relief of rock bottom is not that you have sunk to it but that, having survived it, you can only rise.

The manuscript of Orwell’s memoir was twice rejected, including by T.S. Eliot at Faber & Faber. In a fit of despair, Orwell tossed it into his friend Mabel’s garbage bin. She fished it out and, without his knowledge, took it to a literary agent she knew. We could say that the rest is history, but the selective collective memory we call history is an erasure machine for the myriad failures behind every success, for the rock bottom that is so often — so much oftener than our culture likes to admit — the springboard for the redemption of our suffering.

—

Published November 20, 2026

—

https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/11/20/rock-bottom/

—

item.title: Flash Fridays: K-POP TRADWIFE
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Dear AGENT,

I’m seeking representation for K-POP TRADWIFE, my 80,000-word downmarket novel about an elite and miserable K-pop idol, a character you’ll want to be and also love to hate, a fertile young woman who marries into an American bulgogi-sauce dynasty, where she learns of the dark side of wealth via the cutthroat world of convenience foods, cultural appropriation, and protein-maxxing. For fans of YESTERYEAR and TRADER JOE’S, this book features both obscure and well-loved Korean cultural references, the infectious and ligament-ripping dance sequences of K-POP DEMON HUNTERS, and the WASP obliviousness of STRANGERS by Belle Burden.

K-POP TRADWIFE follows the industrialized rise and fall of #MEYoo, a beautiful, childlike orphan adopted as an idol trainee who, despite her struggles with anxiety and depression, achieves global success as part of the K-pop supergroup 5G (GooGooGahGahGirlz) with the mega-hit, “OPPA Issues.” But after gaining five pounds and neglecting her sponsored 10-step skincare regimen by a single toner pad, she is brutally ousted from this ruthless kingdom by her managers and replaced with her understudy #NOWYoo.

Everyone seems to be abandoning #MEYoo, triggering her to fly to Los Angeles for a Dancing with the Stars audition. In the lobby of the Chateau Marmont, she meets the thrice-divorced Korean American man with dual country-club memberships, Jason Kim, who promises to solve all her problems through a highly publicized lavender marriage, prayer group, and raising a Jesus army—of children, AKA trustees.

With a family on the cusp of developing a protein-infused bulgogi sauce at the intersection of wellness, strength training for menopausal women, and Korean barbecue, #MEYoo, who now goes by the more respectable (and English-friendly) YooMe, cannot resist salvation in the form of a future with an actual shelf life and a Black Card. But after seven kids via IVF, each with varying levels of success and IQs, her mother-in-law begins to wonder who the father of these children, with questionable prospects and in desperate need of eyelid surgery, actually is. Only a genetic test will tell.

Who really is YooMe, and who is she related to that can make or break this family? As they await the results and her next embryo implantation, a manager from her past resurfaces, searching for new idol trainees, and she looks to her children—perfect specimens, just like their mother once was. Is YooMe merely part of a scheme to create more duplicates of herself? Where are all her husband’s ex-wives and his children? And is selling her children her only way out? With a shocking, military-grade twist and the potential for a YESTERYEAR-level media chokehold, this is the novel that affirms: Women are wicked and can’t be trusted at all. More importantly, K-POP TRADWIFE asks: Is America really special? Or is it literally just like every other country that’s stolen stuff? This is gonna tear every single damn group chat and book club apart.

I was born and raised a Korean American. I am also a wife and a mother. In addition, I have published two novels, THE LAST STORY OF MINA LEE and WHAT WE KEPT TO OURSELVES. I have never used AI, even though everything I touch has been hijacked by it without my consent. I spend a lot of time these days going through “security and privacy settings.” But the only things I am sure of are that my fingers are typing these letters one by one, I can still touch my toes, and this is the book that will take readers on a journey away from their fears of “turning into their parents,” being kinda chill with #authoritarianism, and climate collapse. I look forward to discussing K-POP TRADWIFE over painstaking charcuterie boards constructed with the devotion of Michelangelo at the Sistine Chapel, collagen-filled s’mores, nonalcoholic beverages infused with peptides, and “Korean ingredients”—the opposite of dying.

Thank you for your consideration.

Sincerely,

N. Jooyoun Kim

Source: The Rumpus | Published: 2026-11-20 16:34 UTC

item.title: Girl on Girl: Does a Woman’s Sexual Experience Inform Her Identity?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

I totally hear what you’re saying and respect it completely. I think we come at the word whore—and sexuality, perhaps—from two very different upbringings and experiences and I believe there is room for both your reaction and mine (and so many others!) in this conversation.

I will never know what it was like to be raised Mormon or even religious (I grew up with zero dogma as a secular Jew who celebrated Christmas and was very into crystals) but I do know what it was like to be the horny girl. And because my sexuality has always been a way I identify, I disagree that a woman’s sexuality is peripheral to her character. I have fought against the prudishness of our culture since I was old enough to realize how much it informed my own shame as a teenage girl. As an adult, sex still informs my work, character, and identity as much as anything.

Where it starts to make me uncomfortable is when you suggest that a woman should not feel elevated by her sexual power, insinuating that a woman’s sexual experience is neutral. There’s more church than you realize behind those words, flattening sexuality into something that doesn’t matter as much as I believe it does. A woman who feels sexually free is very different than a woman who has never explored that part of herself, who was robbed by shame of her own eroticism.

A woman’s sexuality is deeply personal, primal, and holier than any book, and therefore should be exalted as something for her to explore. A woman who owns her sexuality owns herself and, for many of us, how we understand ourselves sexually is intertwined with our identity as artists. That is why these churches try to shame women away from our bodies, handing them over to men with one hand while covering our mouths with the other. And the fact that female sexuality is so feared—by both men and women—proves my point.

The day you published your last column, my eighteen-year-old daughter—who comes with her own set of feelings and experiences re: the word whore—came home from school and announced that she was going to perform the Shane Gillis SNL cold open as her monologue for senior showcase. Her reaction to that shit was: Look at this fucking loser. How fun, now I get to make fun of him on stage, lol.

I took a very similar approach at her age as a young writer and never really stopped. I believe every woman should be responsible for how she defines her own power and if that means embracing the word whore, or even using it as a term of endearment or pride, more power to her. There is nothing shameful about sex work or empowerment through sexuality and, as long as women are criticized for their “body count” and praised for having limited sexual experience, I will keep pushing against that imbalance.

Also, I want to say I am grateful for the way you reacted to some asshole’s stupidity on a late-night comedy show. You took the rage it inspired, built a blowtorch out of words, then turned that fire toward the Mormon church. And at the risk of sexualizing that, IT TURNED ME WAY THE FUCK ON. Because to me, there is nothing hotter than a woman who knows where to put her anger. There is nothing more galvanizing than a woman who takes back her energy from god-sick fools and reinvests it in her own rebuilding. There is nothing that makes me prouder of a woman than her refusal to back down to the men who believe it’s somehow holy to leer over her. Women who call bullshit on the men who hide behind Jesus in order to justify their twisted worldview that, for women, submission is holier than power.

This SNL bullshit pushed you deeper into your own story. You reacted to some dude’s bad joke with this surge of fearlessness. You started working on the story you aren’t supposed to tell because it goes against everything you were taught not to say.

That is why I feel so hopeful about this moment. I am watching what’s happening in you and me and my daughters: our refusal to diminish, to dim, or to quiet. I am noticing the lack of fear women suddenly have, even those who were raised marinating in it.

Part of me is grateful for the Shanes of the world. They keep us activated. They remind us why we can’t be complicit, why we need more women on stage (and behind the scenes). More women burning down the churches that try to replicate a woman’s life force with the botched teachings of dead men. More women who unabashedly share their experiences and spend their lives unlearning in order to understand themselves and set each other free.

And, yes, I’m talking about you. In all your power, glory, rage, and brilliance, you.

Love,

Rebecca

Source: The Rumpus | Published: 2026-11-20 15:18 UTC

item.title: A Call to Action from Electric Literature
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

news

A Call to Action from Electric Literature

Independence is our greatest asset. Community is our greatest resource.

This article is free to read. So is every article Electric Literature publishes. No limits, no paywalls—now or ever. Support from readers like you makes that possible.

We need to raise $60,000 to start off 2027 strong. Donate now to our end of year fundraiser to help ensure the future of free, accessible literature for all.

—————

Dear Reader,

Last year, Electric Literature decided not to apply for funding from the National Endowment of the Arts. You might remember that our decision resulted from an Executive Order handed down by the Trump Administration and new compliance guidelines drafted by the NEA, both stipulating that applicants must not “promote gender ideology.” It was a blatant attack on trans people, period—and applying would have been a betrayal of the values held so closely by EL and its community. I was part of the decision to forgo funding, and while it was nerve-wracking to walk away from money we relied on, standing up for our beliefs was a no-brainer. We trusted that our community would have our back and fill the gap. And it did.

When I was preparing to take over as Executive Director and Publisher earlier this year, EL had the chance to speak publicly (in an amicus brief attached to a lawsuit targeting the NEA) about how the loss of NEA funding impacted our ability to practice free speech as an independent literary magazine. As I was interviewed by lawyers from the National Coalition Against Censorship, I took a moment to reflect on the prior year. I felt more sure of our decision than ever. Though our funding had been cut, though we had been forced to revise our financial strategy without notice, we stood with the communities whose rights, protection, and humanity we are forever committed to uplifting—trans people and the queer community, people of color, people with disability, immigrants, women. Rather than feeling fearful about what the future might hold, I only felt immense pride.

Over the course of this year, I’ve become acutely aware that independence is our greatest asset—which means community is our greatest resource. Because Electric Lit is completely independent, we retain the freedom to defy a government that sometimes wishes to silence us. That independence also means we rely on our people to keep us going. We need to raise $60,000 by the end of the year to ensure we remain a beacon for the writers and stories we most care about publishing.

Electric Lit is committed to safeguarding the freedom, dignity, and humanity inherent to creative expression, but we are only as powerful as the people standing with us. An anonymous donor has kicked off our campaign this year with a matching gift of $15,000. Helping us match that gift will get us halfway towards our goal. I believe in Electric Lit, but more than that, I believe in the people that power Electric Lit. Join us in this fight by making a gift today.

With warmth and gratitude,

Denne Michele Norris

Executive Director and Publisher

Source: Electric Literature | Published: 2026-11-20 12:00 UTC

What to Watch This Weekend, YA Edition

Netflix has been having a time with adaptations lately. There are so many great ones that are either birthed from YA novels or that reimagine stories with younger protagonists.

The following YA adaptations are available on Netflix. In them, love gets messy, one bullied teen in Brazil gets a summer he’ll never forget, and a sword-toting princess avenges her father.

💌To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before: It feels like this adaptation of the 2014 bestselling release by Jenny Han came at a time when the Netflix adaptation game wasn’t as strong. In fact, I wouldn’t be surprised if the success of this movie encouraged more YA adaptations.

- The 2018 release follows the book fairly closely, though there are also a few differences. High schooler Lara Jean’s world gets rocked when the love letters she wrote to her five crushes get mailed out to them.

☀️ Here the Whole Time: This Brazilian-set coming-of-age film was adapted from a 2017 YA novel of the same name in English, but originally titled Quinze Dias by Vitor Martins, translated by Larissa Helena.

- Interestingly enough, the novel gets compared to To All the Boys I’ve Loved Before, except the main character is a fat gay teenager who finds out his crush is staying with him and his mother for 15 days one summer.

🗡️ Scarlet: This fantastical anime adaptation of Shakespeare’s Hamlet looks gorgeous. It follows a teen princess on a quest to avenge her father.

item.title: Literary Advocacy in the Wake of the Midterms: Book Censorship News, November 20, 2026
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Literary Advocacy in the Wake of the Midterms: Book Censorship News, November 20, 2026

When it came to the candidates who will hold office and represent the people, the midterms were an overwhelming success for the freedom to read.

When it came to state- and local-level policies, referendums, and amendments, the midterms were much less successful.

With the results settling and the reality of 2027 just a little over a month away, literary advocates can continue their efforts to support anti-book ban, pro-public library, pro-public education. There’s a lot on the table across the country, and each step an individual takes builds the kind of momentum that helped ignite change, as we saw at the ballot box this month.

So where to begin?

Support Florida. Don’t Denigrate It or Write It Off.

Florida did not “go blue” the way that Texas did, but races across the state were tremendously close. Several major democratic wins occurred in the very areas that republicans deliberately gerrymandered. Those republicans spent a lot of money on their candidates and their ballot measures, and the fact that several democrats came within just a few points of winning both showcases that Florida isn’t a “lost cause”. It highlights how deeply impacted voters are in the state by voter suppression, gerrymandering, and disenfranchisement. Rather than write off the state, it’s beyond high time for advocates to pay attention to and support those doing tremendous work on the ground to protect access to books, libraries, and public education.

One of the biggest disappointments from the midterms in Florida was the passage of Amendment 3. More than 60% of voters supported tax cuts, which state Republicans sold as a way to ease their financial challenges. What those republicans did not say–and that libraries, firefighters, and other municipal services both within and beyond the state shouted about for over a year before voters saw their ballot–was that this meant local service funding would be decimated. Homeowners may pay less on their properties, but that could mean potentially devastating bills if they need to use services like fire or ambulance services or their public libraries.

Public libraries in Florida are already bracing for impact. Many ran the numbers before the election, noting that they might need to slash their budgets by 60 or 70 percent. That means significant cuts to staff and materials, which trickle down to cuts in hours and online services. With the uncertain future of the Federal Communications Commission’s E-Rate–an affordable way for libraries and schools to provide internet services at their facilities–this could be the kind of mass disenfranchisement not seen in generations.

Understand that libraries across the state have been begging for help for years. They’ve had to do so quietly, for fear of retaliation from the state. This includes the state’s library association. Their lack of posting calls to action isn’t by choice; it’s by force, and it’s abetted by tremendous fear of being targeted by politicians.

Here’s what library advocates can do in the face of what feels like an insurmountable hurdle for libraries in Florida.

- When service changes happen at public libraries, explicitly name why this is. It was Amendment 3, voted for by over 60% of state residents, in the 2026 Midterm elections. Yes, it was widely reported on. Yes, this means you lost your library and its robust services because your tax money pays for those things.

- Then, be a library hyper person. Shared by Marion County Library System, this graphic has some very easy ways to advocate for the library every single day.

- Get involved in your library’s Friends of the Library group or its Foundation. Either/both–they’re different organizations, to be clear–fundraise on behalf of the library. They are independent of the library, and in many cases, they have far greater ability to advocate on behalf of libraries than the libraries themselves. If you’re involved, encourage this kind of advocacy and help spearhead initiatives to raise funds for the library. If your library does NOT have a Friends group, consider starting one. Learn from the library how this might operate, whether there’s been one in the past, and where to get started. United for Libraries offers numerous resources to help launch or revive Friends of the Library groups.

- Follow your local library and take direction from them. Every library operates differently, and each will be surmounting unique hurdles. In some libraries, it will be staffing; in others, hours; in still others, collections. Because of the state of fear that may further silence libraries, go into your local library and ask to talk with them about what you and others like you can do to help them. Here’s a great example from Miami-Dade–as shared by their Friends of the Library–and a great example of communication from Broward County Library’s Foundation. Another great example, as shared by their Friends of the Library group, comes from Ocala. As noted in the previous bullet, Friends and Foundations are going to be crucial communicators on behalf of libraries in addition to their role as fundraisers.

- Understand that what you’re allowed to borrow from your library may change. Whatever that looks like, know that utilizing the library is especially crucial right now and into the future. Borrow all the books you can, attend every program that you can, try out the digital resources from home, and encourage everyone to do the same. Now is the time to get your library card if you don’t have one. Coordinate a library date with friends or family members who also need to get one.

- Call your state-level representatives in support of local libraries and encourage them to fight to protect library services as core services, the way public schools are in the new law. Tell them what is at stake and why they need to push for exceptions and carveouts to Amendment 3. The legislature must pass laws to implement the amendment, so your voice is especially important right now. DeSantis only has so long to do the job before his term expires, and the work would fall to the incoming (republican) governor. Your voice can impact where and how the library piece of this comes into play.

- Follow and engage with advocacy happening both in and beyond the state. EveryLibrary has set up a website and campaign to keep Florida libraries open, and groups like the Florida Freedom to Read Project have been on the ground covering censorship issues in libraries for years.

Of note: a similar tax slashing scheme in Wyoming did not pass, which is good news for municipalities in that state.

At the Federal Level

There hasn’t been much news to report on the slate of book banning bills and the defunding of the Institute of Museum and Library Services since mid-August. That’s because republican leadership decided to put the House on an extended recess until after the midterms to avoid impeachment talk for Pete Hegseth. The House is back in session, as is the Senate, and though it is a lame duck session, republicans will use whatever they can to pass their bad bills with significant consequences to the American people.

That means even now, continue to reach out to your current federal representatives and future ones about the following issues.

- Funding the Institute of Museum and Library Services (IMLS): Earlier this year, Trump zeroed out the Fiscal Year 2027 budget to the only federal agency overseeing public libraries for the sixth time. Right now, the federal government is operating under a Continuing Resolution, which will expire on December 11. That means if they don’t pass a budget before then, the federal government will once again shut down until one passes. The IMLS needs your advocacy to ensure that its minuscule budget gets passed for the coming fiscal year. IMLS was already gutted in the first months of this administration;…

Source: Book Riot | Published: 2026-11-20 11:15 UTC

item.title: Why is Shabana Mahmood tackling ‘two-tier policing’ if she doesn’t believe it exists? | Gaby Hinsliff
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Ten years ago this month, Stephen Port was convicted of the murders of four young gay men lured to their deaths via the dating app Grindr.

But it took another five years for their families to learn through an inquest what some had long suspected: that the Metropolitan police’s failure to link the murders quickly enough may have contributed to the later deaths, raising difficult questions over whether that would have happened if the victims were straight. The year after that, officers at Charing Cross station were caught WhatsApping each other rape jokes and insults like “fuck you bender”, contributing to Louise Casey’s conclusion in a review not long afterwards that the force was both institutionally homophobic and misogynistic.

There have been extremely good reasons for the decision many forces across Britain made to let uniformed police officers march openly at Pride events in recent years, rather than simply stewarding. It seemed a quick, tangible way of signalling that times have changed, that hate crimes will be taken seriously and that gay officers are welcome to serve or join. But in a case brought against Northumbria police last year by a lesbian arguing that gender critical activists had been made to feel unwelcome at Pride, a judge ruled that Pride had become so politically contested that marching breached impartiality rules, warning other forces to take note. This week, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, made clear that she supported that ban. Some forces had drifted “out of the realm of policing and into the world of politics” in trying to engage the public, she told police commissioners, suggesting in future they stick to “tea and biscuits” with residents’ associations rather than hanging out with activists.

That sideswipe came as Mahmood made a speech announcing plans to tackle so-called two-tier policing – the false and inflammatory idea that the police routinely and deliberately go soft on ethnic minority offenders. These plans have been undeniably complicated by the fact that, as Mahmood herself acknowledged, there’s no evidence that the problem actually exists outside Nigel Farage’s imagination. Her solution was to scrap a police statement on anti-racism principles that Reform UK made hay with in the wake of the tragic murder of Henry Nowak, the teenager unforgivably handcuffed by police as he was dying of stab wounds because they mistook him for the assailant rather than the victim.

The statement argues that equality “does not mean treating everyone the same”, an established principle in anti-discrimination law (forcing a pregnant woman to lift the same heavy boxes as everyone else working in your warehouse is technically equal treatment, but that doesn’t make it fair). Though there’s no evidence that it directly affected the officers’ decisions the night of Nowak’s murder, and Mahmood acknowledged she could see what it was trying to achieve, she insisted that the public find it “patently absurd”, and she wasn’t about to argue with them. So there will be a new impartiality code, including rules on avoiding politicised symbols – another Reform gripe is LGBTQ+-friendly rainbow markings on police cars – and on engaging with the public, which is where Pride marches come in.

Police should, she argued, beware “misguided attempts at course corrections” made while scrabbling to keep up with culture wars. Though if the police seem confused, they’ve arguably only been reflecting successive governments, who have done their share of handbrake turns over LGBTQ+ rights.

What Mahmood was trying to do this week was one of the hardest tasks in politics, which is to side with the public on an issue where the public is hopelessly divided. Plenty of Britons now believe two-tier policing exists, according toYouGov research this summer; unfortunately, they disagree on who is in which tier. Over half think black people are singled out for differential treatment, but they’re more likely to say this treatment is extra strict than extra lenient. A third think the police come down harder on people with far-right views, but one in five think they’re harder on people with far-left views. And though 25% think white people get a uniquely raw deal, exactly the same number think they have it easier, with a marked tendency for people to think their own group is especially hard done by. (Though YouGov didn’t poll LGBTQ+ people specifically, Stonewall research suggests one in four of those who had experienced a hate crime and not reported it said it was because they didn’t trust the police.) It’s hard to draw any firm conclusions except that distrust of the police is remarkably widespread; but evidently that’s not the story either Reform or Labour wants to tell.

If Mahmood looks increasingly out of step with a cabinet that has shifted at least rhetorically to the left under Andy Burnham, that’s in part just the nature of being a Labour home secretary. Since Labour never gets the benefit of the doubt over law and order, its home secretaries end up forced into taking the hardest possible line on law and order so that nobody can say they’re soft on it. But there is another difference between Mahmood and her new boss emerging, and it’s about the willingness to make an argument.

If the public fervently believe something that you think is nonsense, is your job to agree with them or to bust the myth? On Brexit, Burnham chose the latter, pointing out politely but firmly that it hasn’t worked out. But Mahmood seems to be choosing the former, cracking down on a “perception” of injustice she freely admits is a chimera. The trouble with boxing shadows is that sooner or later, the wrong person risks getting punched in the face.

- Gaby Hinsliff is a Guardian columnist

Source: The Guardian Opinion | Published: 2026-11-21 06:00 UTC

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/21/shabana-mahmood-two-tier-policing-britain-public-myth

item.title: 5 Famous Books That Were Written Under the Influence of Drugs
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

You might think that taking drugs wouldnât be conducive to writing a good book, but there are actually a few famous novels that defy that idea. There are some books that clearly owe a debt to the authorâs drug habitâThe Doors of Perception (1954) by Aldous Huxley and Naked Lunch (1959) by William S. Burroughs being two of the most famous examplesâbut there are a few other titles that unexpectedly fall into this category. Here are five such books that were surprisingly written (at least partly) by authors who were under the influence of drugsâranging from peyote to cocaine.

Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde (1886) // Robert Louis Stevenson

Robert Louis Stevenson suffered from chronic lung problems for most of his life and itâs thought that the drugs he took to ease his symptomsâhe had trouble breathing and would cough up bloodâmay have actually aided his creative process. In 1885, the Treasure Island (1883) author was taking cocaine and a hallucinogenic called ergotine. He was in a drug-induced stupor one night when his wife, Fanny, woke him up from a nightmare. âWhy did you wake me?â he complained. âI was dreaming a fine bogey tale.â

That âbogey taleâ inspired Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hydeâthe first draft of which Stevenson frantically wrote over the course of just three days. That version ended up being thrown into the fire because the allegory wasnât strong enough, but whether it was Stevenson or Fanny who destroyed the pages remains uncertain. He then spent another three days frenziedly rewriting the now iconic horror novella.

On the Road (1957) // Jack Kerouac

Literary legend has it that Beat Generation writer Jack Kerouac wrote the first draft of his seminal novel On the Road on a 120-foot-long scroll in one feverish burst that lasted three weeksâa feat that was sustained by amphetamines (specifically Benzedrine). But while Kerouacâs use of the stimulant is accurate, the real story of the novelâs creation is a little more complicated.

Kerouac first noted down his idea for the novel in August 1948: âtwo guys hitchhiking to California in search of something they donât really find, and losing themselves on the road, coming all the way back hopeful of something else.â He wrote up a few drafts, but struggled to find the right prose style for the story. Then at the end of 1950, he received a rambling freeform letter from his friend Neal Cassady (who inspired the character Dean Moriarty) and realized it was the exact style he was looking for. Kerouac dubbed it âspontaneous proseâ and, armed with thorough notes and Benzedrine, he then sat down to bash out On the Road on the huge scroll.

Cujo (1981) // Stephen King

Stephen King isnât shy about his former substance abuse problem, telling Rolling Stone in a 2014 interview that he was a heavy cocaine user from around 1978 to 1986 and would often write while high and drunk. This means that a number of his most famous books were written under the influenceâincluding Cujo (1981), Pet Sematary (1983), and IT (1986). âI barely remember writing [Cujo] at all,â he admits in his memoir, On Writing (2000). âI donât say that with pride or shame, only with a vague sense of sorrow and loss.â But although King managed to produce some masterpieces during this drug-fuelled time, he told Rolling Stone that âthe books start to show it after a while.â He cites The Tommyknockersâwhich was the last book he wrote before quitting cokeâas one of his worst books.

One Flew Over the Cuckooâs Nest (1962) // Ken Kesey

In 1959, Ken Keseyâthen a student at Stanford Universityâvolunteered to take part in MK-Ultra, a drug research program being run by the CIA. Participants were given psychoactive drugs, including LSD, psilocybin, and mescaline. While high in the ward, Kesey looked around and began to wonder: âWhatâs the difference between the orderlies and the nurse and the patients?â His wife, Faye Kesey McMurtry, recalls that âhe began to see that they were all damaged in some way or another.â Not only did the experience help to inspire One Flew Over the Cuckooâs Nest (as did actually working on a psychiatric ward), but he also liked LSD so much that he continued taking it. The first three pages of the novelâwhich was adapted into an Oscar-winning 1975 film starring Jack Nicholsonâwere also written while Kesey was high on peyote.

Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? (1968) // Philip K. Dick

Philip K. Dickâs literary career kicked off in the early 1950s, and from the very beginning his writing was fuelled by amphetamines. In a 1975 interview with Rolling Stone, the sci-fi author said that every novel heâd written up until A Scanner Darkly (1977) was done so with the aid of speed. This means that his most famous book, Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?âwhich in 1982 was adapted into a film by Ridley Scott under the title Blade Runnerâwas written while he was on drugs.

âI believed there was a direct connection between the amphetamines and the writing,â Dick explained in the Rolling Stone interview. âI attributed my speed of writing, my high productivity and my pushing myself to the amphetamines.â Throughout the â60s, he also took mescaline, marijuana, LSD, and PCP. His doctor warned him that his liver was at risk of collapse and he eventually kicked the habit (although he had already done permanent damage to his pancreas). Fortunately his creative output didnât suffer in the long run though, and he continued publishing until his death in 1982.

Source: Mental Floss | Published: 2026-11-21 02:00 UTC

item.title: 5 Things You Probably Didn't Know About Artemis, the Greek Goddess of the Hunt
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

More gods from the Greek pantheon are making an appearance in Percy Jackson and the Olympians season 3. Chief among them is Artemis. In the series, her presence is tied to an invitation that she extends to Annabeth Chaseâone that would shift the young demigodâs allegiance to the goddess of the hunt and put her on a path that Percy and Grover cannot walk with her.

In Greek mythology, Artemis holds dominion over the wilderness and wild animals. She is associated with the moon and considered to be both a harmonious and opposing force to her twin brother, Apollo, the god of prophecy and music who is associated with the sun.

Most know Artemis by her hunting bow and quiver of arrows, though sheâs sometimes draped in a deerskin cape complete with a hood or crowned with a diadem. Famously, she is a virgin goddess whose followers pledge chastity and are held to living pure lives under penalty of severe punishment.

But what might you not know about her? Letâs get into some of the long-held and most disputed beliefs behind the goddessâ origins, meaning, and actions, according to ancient Greek stories that have stood the test of time.

Artemis Delivered Her Twin Brother Apollo

The Titaness Leto is the mother of Artemis and Apollo. Her affair with Zeus, which produced a pregnancy, angered the goddess Heraâthe Queen of the Gods and Zeusâ wifeâso violently that she forbade Leto from giving birth on land or in water. To ensure Leto adhered to her order, the giant serpent Python was commanded to pursue Leto throughout her pregnancy. She was given no leave to rest as nowhere was safe.

Fortunately for Leto, she came upon Delos. The floating island allowed her to stay within the bounds of Heraâs words. First, she gave birth to Artemis. Then, according to some versions of the myth, her daughter served as her midwife and delivered her twin into the world. That is why Artemis is a goddess of childbirth along with her many other duties.

The Goddess of the Hunt Loves to Dance

Artemis is primarily thought of as a huntress. Her youth, athleticism, and vigor are typically visible in depictions of her, and she is also often portrayed alongside animals, her trusty silver-and-gold bow and quiver of arrows in hand. But, like Apollo, she also loves music, and that includes dancing to it with the nymphs in her retinue.

Her worshippers often honor her through choral dance, a style of rhythmic movement that is coordinated and done in unison. It includes singing and vocalization, and participants often run and mimic animals in devotion to the goddess.

Artemis Is Both the Protector and Bringer of Death to Girls

In antiquity, Artemis was portrayed as a maiden because she is considered to be the protector of girls up until they marry. While her charge is their safety, that does not mean she always keeps girls from harm.Â

As is true of the rest of the Grecian gods, Artemis can be fickle. She can act in favor of one mortal, healing their wounds and ending their suffering, while bringing ruin through sudden death or disease to another.

She Is Responsible for the Constellation Orion

Though the prevailing belief is that Artemis has never fallen in love, she had a close companion in Orion. The giant huntsman skilled with weaponry had earned her respect so deeply that Apollo grew jealous, and tricked his sister into shooting her friend. Grief-stricken, she laid Orion to rest among the stars.

Some stories suggest Apollo betrayed Artemis to protect her vow of chastity as she was in love with Orion. Others claim that she purposefully shot the giant because heâd attempted to assault her or one of her attendants, and in these stories, there is no mention of her making him a constellation.

Artemis Is Incredibly Vengeful

Blessed with the power to transform herself and anyone she chooses into an animal, Artemis has also been said to use her abilities to punish those who incur her wrath.Â

When her handmaiden Callisto was seduced by Zeus after he took the goddessâs form, Artemis turned her into a bear after learning of Callistoâs pregnancy. She then banished her to the wild.

The hunter Actaeon suffered a worse fate. Artemis transformed him into a stag after she caught him watching her bathe in a spring with her nymphs. She set his hounds on him, and they tore Actaeon apart.

There was also Niobe, queen of Thebes, whose children and husband bore the consequences of her boastfulness. She had compared her 14 children to Letoâs twins, and the slight drew Artemis and Apolloâs ire. They killed all seven of her sons and her seven daughters as well. The pain of the loss resulted in Niobeâs husband also dying, though itâs disputed whether he killed himself or was slain to ensure he didnât try to avenge their children.

Niobe was turned to stone, either in pity by the gods or because her devastation was so great that it literally petrified her. However, the transformation didnât stop her tears, which continued to fall from her eyes.

Source: Mental Floss | Published: 2026-11-21 00:00 UTC
