item.title: If Democrats want to win, blue-collar populists are the key | Dustin Guastella and Jared Abbott
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Democrats had a huge night on 3 November. The party ran an average of about 15 points ahead of Kamala Harris’s 2024 margins, and picked up seats that Trump carried by double digits just two years ago.

Of course, the size and scope of the blue wave make it hard to draw specific lessons, and the results will inevitably serve as a Rorschach test reflecting each commentator’s prior beliefs. Democrats of all stripes won elections in all sorts of unlikely places.

But it would be a big mistake to assume that because all sorts of Democrats won big in 2026 thanks to a backlash against Trump, any Democrat will do in 2028. There is now a decade of experience, 2026 notwithstanding, showing us that “I’m not Trump” is not the slam dunk Democrats want it to be.

That’s to say Democrats still need a program and political pitch for 2028. One way to get a sense of what might be the best way forward is to look at which candidates did best relative to their districts’ political lean, demographic makeup and other Democrats.

And here is the big story of the night: neither the down-the-line professional-class progressives nor the corporate-sponsored centrists did as well as the working-class populists who have a bold economic vision for working people but also know how to talk to workers.

Before we dig into those results, first, some cold water.

Despite Democrats’ big night, the party is still doing badly with working-class voters.

That matters because not only is this group the largest in the electorate (57% of 2026 voters lacked a four-year degree), it is also a swing group. In 2024, voters without a college degree swung seven points toward Trump, from a six-point Republican margin in 2020 to a 13-point one. In 2026, they swung back hard, by 17 points.

Still, Democrats won college graduates by 26 points and voters without degrees by just four points, leaving a 22-point education gap, and they lost white voters without degrees by 19 points.

If Democrats want to win a commanding and durable majority, one capable of implementing their progressive economic plans and finally delivering for working Americans, they will need to do better with these voters.

The question is, what kind of Democrat can do it?

Progressives have long argued that they are the Democrats best suited to winning back the working class, but the results in 2026 don’t bear this out – at least not in a straightforward way.

In general, though they of course performed well overall, the most liberal candidates fared worse compared with their centrist counterparts. Nominees backed by Justice Democrats ran about one point behind our estimate of how a typical Democrat would have done in the same district, given its 2024 presidential vote, demographics and whether an incumbent was running (a statistic known as “wins above replacement”, or War), and Bernie Sanders’s Senate endorsees ran about six and a half points behind.

As a result, centrists have taken to social media to crow about how their brand of politics is more suited to building majorities. But here they might be overstepping, especially when it comes to the question of social class.

Joe Weisenthal of Bloomberg’s Odd Lots podcast tweeted: “The whole theory that to expand the map that Dems had to nominate working classoids who dress in Carhartts just seems totally obliterated.” Is that true? Hardly.

As it happens, blue-collar populists such as Brian Poindexter (a union ironworker in Ohio), Bob Brooks (a firefighter in Pennsylvania), Sam Forstag (a former smokejumper in Montana) and Rebecca Cooke (a waitress in Wisconsin), who were all backed by both Bernie Sanders and the moderate Blue Dog Democrats, as well as Randy Villegas (a community college professor from California’s Central valley), outperformed both professional-class progressives backed by Sanders and progressive Pacs – such as Abdul El-Sayed (a doctor) and Peggy Flanagan (a non-profit executive turned lieutenant governor) – and centrists backed by the New Democrat Coalition, such as Tom Suozzi and Jared Moskowitz.

Compared with our estimate of a typical Democrat’s performance, Poindexter ran almost 11 points ahead, Forstag about five, Cooke about four and Brooks about two, for an average of about +5, compared with about +2 for nominees backed only by the Blue Dogs and about even for those backed only by Sanders. Villegas, whose race is still being counted, ran about 14 points ahead.

El-Sayed and Flanagan ran five and six points behind, and Suozzi and Moskowitz trailed by one and a half and six points, respectively. As a group, the four Blue Collar Brigade nominees (Poindexter, Villegas, Forstag and Brooks), union-backed working-class candidates who ran as a slate, averaged a War of nearly +8, and all four ran ahead of comparable Democrats, by about eight points on average.

No other progressive or centrist group’s nominees averaged better than about +3.

In fact, the sweet spot looks like the vaunted “Bernie-dog” candidate who leans left on wages, jobs and the economy, is good at talking about those issues in plain language, and steers toward the center on issues like immigration and criminal justice.

These are candidates who are justifiably frustrated with trade deals that shipped their communities’ jobs overseas, who value patriotism and tradition while sticking up for the working class against the economic giants that are grinding them into dust.

Plus, it really does matter when populist candidates come from the popular classes. While professional-class progressives, like El-Sayed, soak up a lot of media attention, and moderates like Jon Ossoff clean up with donors, blue-collar candidates remain underappreciated for their ability to break through.

Social class remains a major issue unto itself and blue-collar populists are uniquely able to tap into the frustrations of blue-collar voters.

Just look at Troy Jackson, the soon-to-be senator from Maine. Jackson was subject to a late-campaign attack ad that questioned his competence by virtue of his background. Susan Collins’s now-infamous “cord of wood” ad implied that Jackson was better suited to logging than legislating.

That kind of visceral class condescension makes the Gilded Age economy much more real for voters and could have shifted his margins in a favorable direction. Jackson succeeded in unseating the supposedly untouchable Susan Collins.

It’s not clear what direction the Democratic party will go in the future but one thing is certain: blue-collar populists are still the most underrated current in the party and if the bigwigs want to win back working-class voters, they really ought to start investing in candidates who are used to showering at the end of the day rather than in the morning.

- Dustin Guastella is a research associate at the Center for Working Class Politics and the director of operations for Teamsters Local 623

- Jared Abbott is the director of the Center for Working-Class Politics

Source: The Guardian Opinion | Published: 2026-11-20 15:00 UTC

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/20/democrats-blue-collar-populists

item.title: Is it genuine love – or obsessive passion? Kierkegaard, the father of existentialism, had some thoughts
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Young love, honeymoon love, infatuation – these often feel spectacular. You have a burning need to be in constant contact, and you don’t want to let that person out of your sight.

It’s the start of many happy love stories. But at times, that feeling of obsession never fades – and the relationship never matures, or it even proves harmful. You know the relationship is bad for you, but you can’t end it. The more you try to break free, the more you feel stuck.

As a counselor, I often work with people whose relationships feel like an addiction, and who mistake that emotional roller coaster for love. And as a philosopher, I sometimes turn to 19th-century Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard to reflect on the differences between the two.

Kierkegaard is best known for his writing on religion. Today, he’s considered the father of existentialism, which stresses individual freedom, self-creation and personal responsibility. It is no surprise, then, that love is a central focus of his work. What he called “ethical” love expands freedom, while “aesthetic” love restricts it.

Aesthetic love

In 1843, a young Kierkegaard published “Either/Or,” his first book of philosophy – and one of his most important. The two volumes were published under the pseudonym “Victor Eremita,” one of many that Kierkegaard used throughout his life.

“Either/Or” makes a distinction between “aesthetic” and “ethical” ways of living. The aesthetic life is focused mainly on personal pleasure, while the ethical life expands to an awareness of how actions affect others.

Each way of life has its own form of love. Aesthetic love is one that you “fall” into. It comes over you. It is a powerful, seemingly irresistible force. The aesthetic lover “desires the individual absolutely,” Kierkegaard wrote.

Some lasting love begins that way, too. But aesthetic love lacks the trust and respect needed for stability. The yardstick of good and bad, right and wrong is centered on feelings and desires, not principles.

Feeling connected to and dependent on someone you don’t trust creates the tumult of addictive love. It can destroy the lover and the beloved, but often neither wants to give it up.

A counselee of mine fell instantly and madly in love. The passion was unlike anything he’d ever experienced. Though he doubted that the relationship could last, he told me he’d give up everything just to ride the wave for a year, or even six months. He was in the process of upending his life to be with her when the relationship failed a few months later. He went to a very dark place, doubting himself and the world.

This was a textbook example of Kierkegaard’s “aesthetic” love, which he talked about as an obsession or compulsion. In today’s terms, I’d consider it similar to addiction: a pattern that we feel compelled to continue, despite knowing how much it hurts us and others around us. Psychologists and philosophers debate how to define “addiction,” and whether love can become one, but research indicates there can be similarities in behavior and brain activity between the two.

Obsessive, compulsive love often uses the relationship to escape the lover’s own issues. He or she may seem besotted with their beloved. In reality, though, they see the beloved as an object that can fill their emptiness or resolve their angst, rather than an independent human being with his or her own needs and desires.

At its root, Kierkegaard writes, aesthetic love is “a kind of despair,” rooted in estrangement from oneself, a kind of self-rejection or self-deception.

Obsessing over someone can serve to distract us from our self-rejection and emptiness. Aesthetic love seeks freedom through the other person, rather than freely loving them.

Ethical love

For Kierkegaard, there is an alternative: ethical love, rooted in virtue, choice and a solid sense of self. Kierkegaard discusses this kind of love in the second volume of “Either/Or” and in “Works of Love,” a book he published in 1847 under his own name.

Kierkegaard maintains that ethical love lacks the obsession and compulsion of aesthetic love. It is rooted in self-awareness, conscious choices and freedom, not thoughtless desire.

Ethical love is, in short, an ongoing conscious commitment, independent of the ebb and flow of emotion. This holds for all love, romantic or otherwise. Love is “a matter of conscience,” not impulse or calculation, Kierkegaard wrote in “Works of Love.”

It should be based on respect: treating other people as ends in and of themselves, not means to our own ends. In addition, ethical love is anchored in trust. Without these foundations, only the illusion of intimacy is possible.

Love centered on principles, not feelings, may sound like duty. But for Kierkegaard, it was freeing. No one should accept mistreatment: “Duty alone makes for genuine freedom. Spontaneous love makes a man free and in the next moment dependent,” he wrote.

This paradoxical view results from his idea that we must use our freedom to become ourselves, a concept he develops in his philosophy of existentialism. He maintains that human beings need an anchor in something greater than ourselves to fully utilize our freedom. Ultimately, for Kierkegaard, this was a personal God, but his insights can be illuminating even without reference to God.

Kierkegaard stresses that ethical love liberates not only the lover but the beloved: “The highest that one human being can do for another is to make him free, to help him stand alone.” This kind of love isn’t the joining of two into one – that is the enmeshment of obsessive, compulsive, addictive love. Ethical love is between two individual human beings who have chosen to trust, respect, support and forgive one another.

The distinction between the illusion of love and real love has a long history. Kierkegaard provides insight into how to effectively tell the difference – and how the power of real love lies in mutual liberation.

Source: The Conversation | Published: 2026-11-20 13:44 UTC

item.title: El Niño created a skiers’ paradise in Chile – now it’s Sierra Nevada and Southern Rockies’ turn
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

El Niño has a reputation for being a skier’s dream, bringing lots of snow to California’s Sierra Nevada and the southern Rockies. Tahoe-area resorts were already seeing the effects in mid-November 2026 as several feet of snow fell and some resorts prepared to open early for the season. But El Niño’s supercharged precipitation can spell trouble, too.

I’m an avid skier and snow scientist at Colorado State University. As the U.S. snow season begins amid what’s forecast to be one of the strongest El Niños on record, let’s take a look at what Chile’s very snowy winter might tell North America about what’s to come.

The pros and cons of all that precipitation

El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon that raises global temperatures and shifts weather patterns around the world.

It is defined by rising surface temperatures in the east-central tropical Pacific Ocean. When temperatures there are at least 0.5 degrees Celsius (0.9 Fahrenheit) warmer than average for three months, the world is in El Niño. The August-October average was 2.5 C warmer (36.5 F, making this among the warmest periods on record going back to 1950.

In the U.S., the southern half of the country tends to be wetter than usual during strong El Niños. That happens because the Pacific jet stream shifts southward, steering storms with it. The northern tier of the U.S. tends to be drier and warmer than normal.

That pattern is almost exactly what’s being forecast for the U.S. winter of 2026-27. It’s also what the U.S. Southwest is already experiencing – to the extreme.

Powerful storms supercharged by El Niño in October and November caused widespread destructive flooding in the Four Corners region of New Mexico, Arizona, Colorado and Utah. Fast-melting snow and days of heavy rain flooded the San Juan River and Rio Grande, damaging hundreds of homes.

Recovering from last year’s snow drought

Community water systems and farms across the West need that precipitation after last winter delivered one of the lowest snow years on record for almost the entire western United States.

Major reservoirs in the Colorado River basin dropped during the year to their lowest levels since they were first filled. The two biggest – Lake Powell and Lake Mead – together supply water for about 40 million people and hydropower for hundreds of thousands of people.

The very low snowfall, as well as unusually warm midwinter temperatures that drove sublimation – the evaporation of snow – reduced water stored in the mountains. And that was followed by record-high summer temperatures.

Fall 2026’s heavy rain and snow may help make up for last year and start to alleviate a long-running drought that has been causing water supply problems across the western U.S. for a quarter century.

In a positive sign, Lake Powell rose with the recent rains. Overall, the Super El Niño conditions being forecast for 2026-27 are expected to bring more than average rain and snow this winter across much of the southern and central United States, where it’s also likely to alleviate drought.

What happens in Chile …

Snow scientists like me keep an eye on the South American winter in El Niño years like this because it can give us a sense of what’s coming for North America.

Keep in mind that El Niño has been strengthening over the past few months – including through the South American winter that just ended.

South America saw a huge amount of snow, particularly in the central Chilean Andes. In some areas like Portillo, the snow accumulation was the deepest since the current drought began in 2010, and the deepest in the past 70 years north of Santiago at the top of the Limarí River.

The snow was a boon for Chile’s ski resorts. Valle Nevado got over 24 feet (7.3 meters) of snow and extended its ski season, originally scheduled to end in early October, into early December. Even the extremely dry Atacama Desert saw widespread snow followed by an explosion of spring flowers.

Historically, snowy winters in Chile have meant snowy winters for California’s Sierra Nevada and the southern Rockies, too. The warm El Niño ocean allows the atmosphere to pick up more moisture in this zone than usual, and this brings snowstorms to the U.S. Southwest.

If that pattern holds this winter, the southern and central parts of the West should see well-above-average snowpack and active ski seasons, and those dangerously depleted reservoirs will have a chance to at least partially refill.

Source: The Conversation | Published: 2026-11-20 13:44 UTC

item.title: 50 English Phrases for Plans, Goals, and Progress
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

At the beginning of a new year, many people think about what they want to achieve. Maybe you want to improve your English, develop a new skill, get a better job, or make changes in your personal life.

But how can you talk about your goals, your plans for achieving them, and the progress you’re making? In today’s lesson, you’ll learn 50 useful English phrases for talking about goals, plans, progress, challenges, and success.

These expressions aren’t just for New Year’s resolutions. You can use them all year long when talking about your studies, career, personal projects, and everyday life!

If you want to make LOTS of progress towards fluency, join the Espresso English Academy to improve every area of your English.

Part 1: Phrases For Goals

Let’s start with 10 expressions for describing what you want to achieve.

1. Set a goal

To decide on something specific you want to achieve.

- I’ve set a goal of reading 20 books this year.

2. Aim to

To intend or plan to achieve something.

- I’m aiming to improve my English pronunciation over the next few months.

3. Work toward

To make an effort to achieve something, usually over a period of time.

- She’s working toward getting a promotion at her company.

4. Have your sights set on

To be strongly focused on achieving a particular goal.

- He’s got his sights set on becoming a manager.

5. Set your mind to something

To make a firm decision to accomplish something.

- When she sets her mind to something, she doesn’t give up easily.

6. Make it a priority

To decide that something is especially important and deserves your time and attention.

- I’m making exercise a priority this year.

7. Set a deadline

To establish a date by which something should be completed.

- We’ve set a deadline of March 1 for finishing the project.

8. Set the bar high

To establish a very high standard or ambitious goal.

- The company has set the bar high for this year’s sales targets.

9. Take on a challenge

To accept a difficult task or goal that requires effort.

- I’ve decided to take on the challenge of running a half-marathon.

10. Be determined to

To have a strong intention to do something, even if it’s difficult.

- I’m determined to become more confident when speaking English.

Part 2: Making plans and taking action

Having a goal is one thing. Actually doing something to achieve it is another!

Here are 10 phrases for talking about the steps you take toward your goals.

11. Come up with a plan

To think of or create a plan.

- We need to come up with a plan to attract more customers.

12. Map out

To plan something carefully, including the different steps involved.

- Before starting the project, we mapped out everything we needed to do.

13. Break something down into smaller steps

To divide a large or difficult task into smaller, more manageable parts.

- Learning a language can feel overwhelming, so break it down into smaller steps.

14. Get the ball rolling

To start an activity or process.

- Let’s get the ball rolling by scheduling our first meeting.

15. Take the first step

To begin doing something that will help you achieve a goal.

- Signing up for the Business English Course was the first step toward changing my career.

16. Put something into action

To begin actually doing something you have planned.

- We’ve spent enough time discussing ideas. Now it’s time to put our plan into action.

17. Stick to a plan

To continue following a plan instead of changing or abandoning it.

- It’s easier to stick to a study plan when you have a regular schedule.

18. Follow through on something

To do what you said or planned to do, especially until it’s completed.

- He has lots of great ideas, but he doesn’t always follow through on them.

19. Stay on track

To continue making progress according to your plan or schedule.

- Setting weekly reminders helps me stay on track with my goals.

20. Make time for something

To deliberately find or reserve time for an activity.

- Even with a busy schedule, I try to make time for reading every day.

Part 3: Talking about progress

How are things going? Are you getting closer to your goal?

These 10 expressions will help you describe the progress you’re making.

21. Make steady progress

To improve consistently over time, even if the improvements are small.

- She’s making steady progress toward completing her degree.

22. Improve by leaps and bounds

To improve very quickly and significantly in a relatively short period of time.

- Her English skills have improved by leaps and bounds since she joined the Espresso English Academy.

23. Come a long way

To make a lot of progress compared to where you started.

- Your English has come a long way since you started studying!

24. Be on the right track

To be doing things in a way that is likely to lead to success.

- Your pronunciation is improving, so you’re definitely on the right track.

25. Reach a milestone

To achieve an important stage or accomplishment in a longer process.

- The company reached a major milestone when it opened its 100th store.

26. Make headway

To make progress, especially with something difficult.

- After weeks of negotiations, the two sides are finally making headway.

27. Gain momentum

To begin making progress more quickly or successfully.

- The project was slow at first, but it’s starting to gain momentum.

28. Be well on your way to

To have already made significant progress toward achieving something.

- With six months of consistent practice, she’s well on her way to becoming a great dancer.

29. See results

To notice positive changes or improvements from your efforts.

- If you practice regularly, you’ll start to see results.

30. Pay off

When hard work or effort pays off, it produces good results.

- All those hours of studying finally paid off when she passed the exam.

Part 4: Dealing with challenges and setbacks

Progress isn’t always easy or consistent. Sometimes things don’t go according to plan.

Here are 10 expressions for talking about difficulties, delays, and how to handle them.

31. Hit a roadblock

To encounter a problem that prevents you from moving forward.

- We hit a roadblock when we discovered that the project would cost more than expected.

32. Run into difficulties

To experience unexpected problems.

- They ran into difficulties while developing the new software.

33. Fall behind

To make less progress than expected or planned.

- I fell behind on my reading goal because I was so busy at work.

34. Lose momentum

To begin making less progress or become less motivated.

- After taking a long break, I lost momentum with my exercise routine.

35. Get sidetracked

To become distracted from your original goal or activity.

- I was planning to clean the house, but I got sidetracked by some old photographs.

36. Face a setback

To experience a problem or disappointment that delays your progress.

- The team faced a major setback when their funding was reduced.

37. Get back on track

To return to making progress after a delay or difficulty.

- I missed a week of studying, but I’m ready to get back on track.

38. Push through

To continue working despite difficulties, tiredness, or frustration.

- The final weeks of the project were exhausting, but we pushed through and finished on time.

39. Change course

To make a significant change in your plans or approach.

- Our original marketing strategy wasn’t working, so we decided to change course.

40. Learn from your mistakes

To use past errors or failures to improve your future actions.

- Don’t be discouraged when something goes wrong. Learn from your mistakes and keep going.

Part 5: Achieving goals and looking ahead

Finally, let’s learn 10 expressions for talking about success, accomplishments, and future improvements.

41. Reach your goal

To successfully achieve something you wanted.

- After a year of training, she finally reached her goal of running a marathon.

42. Accomplish what you set out to do

To successfully complete what you originally intended to achieve.

- It took longer than expected, but we accomplished what we set out to do.…

Source: Espresso English | Published: 2026-11-20 17:53 UTC

item.title: The Psychedelic Animated Video for Kraftwerk’s “Autobahn” (1979)
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Ah, yes, “Autobahn.” From the moment the door slams and the ignition starts, prog rockers and pre-new wavers know a journey is afoot. Though Kraftwerk had already made three albums, and the band members still looked like well-meaning, bookish hippies, 1974’s “Autobahn” is considered Year Zero for the denizens of the Electric Café, the four German robots who made human music with machines.

This cel-drawn animation by Roger Mainwood was made in 1979 to promote “Autobahn,” after most of the culture had caught up with the song, and it’s now bopping around pop culture again. By that last year of the ’70s, Omni magazine was a year old, music was sifting through the shockwaves left by Bowie’s Low and Heroes, analog was flirting with digital, and the world was ready to drive on that long, electric highway.

Mainwood’s protagonist is part alien, part human, and he begins looking around in awe in his hip goggles, then sets off for a run straight out of a Muybridge loop, only to wind up floating, flying, sailing and swimming through a landscape indebted to Peter Max, Push Pin Studios, underground comix, and 1930s modernism.

Mainwood had just graduated from London’s Royal College of Art Film and Television School, and was commissioned by John Halas, the Hungarian immigrant who became known as the Father of British Animation, for Kraftwerk’s record label. The label wanted to put out one of the first music Laserdiscs. (Halas, by the way, directed a very UPA-influenced short called “Automania” in 1963). According to Mainwood, he still doesn’t know if the band liked the short or even if they watched it.

Mainwood avoided any direct representation of driving or automobiles, much to his credit, which may be why the film holds its fascination. The animator continued in his field, winding up a producer of several classics of British animation, including The Snowman and the chilling When the Wind Blows. As for the meaning of “Autobahn,” we’ll let Mainwood have the last word:

Thinking back to my thought processes at that time, I remember wanting to specifically not have conventional cars in the film. I wanted a sense of a repetitive journey, and alienation, which I took to be what the music was about…hence the solitary futuristic figure, protected by large goggles, moving through and trying to connect with the journey he is taking. The automobile “monsters” are deliberately threatening (I have never been a big fan of cars or motorways!) and when our “hero” tries to make human contact (with different coloured clones of himself) he can never do it. In the end he realises he is making the repetitive and circular journey alone but strides forward purposefully at the end as he did in the beginning. All of which sounds rather pretentious…but I was a young thing in those days!

You can read more of an interview with Mainwood here.

Note: An earlier version of this post appeared on our site in 2016.

Related Content:

Kraftwerk’s First Concert: The Beginning of the Endlessly Influential Band (1970)

Kraftwerk’s “The Robots” Performed by German 1st Graders in Cute Cardboard Robot Costumes

Ted Mills is a freelance writer on the arts.

item.title: The Directing Genius of Akira Kurosawa Explained
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Generations of Westerners have come to appreciate Japanese cinema through the films of Akira Kurosawa, but many have been shocked to find out that Kurosawa himself isn’t as beloved in Japan as they’d imagined. It’s less that his homeland rejects him than that his work has been regarded there as a somewhat foreign taste. That judgment must have something to it: despite their thoroughly Japanese settings, Throne of Blood, The Bad Sleep Well, and Ran were, after all, Shakespeare adaptations, and Kurosawa spoke openly of structuring his stories in the manner of not just traditional Japanese theater, but also symphonies. Consider, too, the way his films continue to inspire Western remakes, from The Magnificent Seven and A Fistful of Dollars in the nineteen-sixties to Living and Highest 2 Lowest in this decade.

Nor can it be a coincidence that the appreciative voices opening the StudioBinder video on Kurosawa’s genius above belong to Steven Spielberg, Martin Scorsese, and George Lucas. Yet this most internationally celebrated of all Japanese filmmakers can’t, ultimately, have been just a Westerner in disguise, since his work gives viewers around the world something that their domestic movies don’t.

Whatever the extent to which he hybridized the cinematic sensibilities of Japan and Hollywood, he did so through his uncompromising personal involvement in every stage of the process. “The role of the director encompasses the coaching of the actors, the cinematography, the sound recording, the art direction, the music, the editing, and the dubbing and sound mixing,” he once said, expressing his dedication to the ideal of (as no less an American auteur than Jerry Lewis described himself) the total filmmaker.

That Kurosawa understood how to tell a story in a way that transcends cultural boundaries goes without saying; what’s less widely appreciated is the way he did so with a combination of simplicity and complexity. As he put it, “a truly good movie is interesting and easy to understand,” two qualities that often end up in irresolvable tension, at least in the hands of lesser filmmakers. Even among those influenced by Kurosawa, for example, some have mastered immediate visual legibility without ever understanding that sound and music are more effectively used as a counterpoint to, rather than mere intensification of, a scene’s prevailing emotion. How many living directors, for that matter, convincingly approach grand, universal themes without irony or protective distance? If Kurosawa’s films retain a power that seems inaccessible today, it may be because, for him, there was no East or West: there was only cinema.

item.title: 10 English Phrases for Sales, Deals, and Discounts
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Everyone loves to save money – so let’s learn how to talk about it in English!

Black Friday is coming up soon, which means you’re going to see a LOT of sales, deals, and discounts.

That means this is the perfect time to learn some common English expressions for getting a good price, looking for discounts, and even finding out that the thing you wanted is already gone!

OK, let’s learn some phrases for sales and discounts. Our first one is:

1. Everything is on sale / marked down.

When something is on sale, it’s being offered at a lower price than usual.

- “Everything in the store is on sale this weekend.”

Another common expression is marked down, which also means the price has been reduced:

- “All the winter coats have been marked down.”

We can also say exactly how much the price was reduced:

- “This jacket was marked down from $80 to $50.”

One thing to remember: on sale means the price has been reduced, whereas for sale simply means something is available to buy.

2. That’s a great deal.

A deal is an agreement or offer, and when shopping, a great deal means you’re getting something for a very good price.

- “This laptop normally costs $900, but it’s on sale for $600.”

- “Wow, that’s a great deal!”

We also commonly say a good deal or a pretty good deal, but “a great deal” is the best.

By the way, you’ll be able to get a great deal on Espresso English courses during our Black Friday sale, so make sure to sign up for our e-mail list to hear about the discount!

3. You get your money’s worth.

If you get your money’s worth, it means you get enough value or benefit from something to make it worth the amount you paid.

- “I’ve worn this coat for the past ten years, so I definitely got my money’s worth.”

This can actually be used for products of any price – whether less expensive or more expensive. It simply means that the benefits are bigger than the price you paid, so it was worth it, it made sense to spend money on it because your life is much better.

4. It was a bargain.

A bargain is something you buy for a surprisingly low price.

- “I found this dress for only $15. It was a bargain!”

We also often say “a real bargain:”

- “We got our dining room table secondhand for $100. It was a real bargain.”

5. It was a steal.

This one is even more “extreme” than “bargain.”

A bargain is a low price, but a “steal” is something priced so low it almost seems like you’re stealing it, taking it for free.

- “These boots normally cost $150, but I got them for $20. They were a steal!”

Of course, a steal doesn’t mean you actually stole the product! It means the price was so amazingly low that it almost feels like you did.

6. I like to shop around.

To shop around means to look at several different stores or websites and compare your options before deciding what to buy.

- “I don’t buy all my groceries at the same store. I like to shop around and find the best price.”

Shopping around can help you compare not only prices, but also brands, features, quality, and other options.

7. I always stock up on things when they’re on sale.

To stock up on something means to buy a large amount – more than you need right now – so that you’ll have enough for the future.

- “I always stock up on things when they’re on sale.”

For example, if your favorite shampoo is normally $8 but it’s on sale for $4, you might buy four or five bottles. We often stock up on products that we use regularly and that won’t go bad quickly.

8. Here’s a coupon for 10% off.

A coupon is a piece of paper or a digital code that gives you a lower price. And 10% off means the price is reduced by 10%. So if something normally costs $100, it would only cost $90 with the coupon.

Here at Espresso English, we give a MUCH bigger discount than 10% during Black Friday. In fact, we offer the best price on courses available all year, so you do NOT want to miss this sale!

9. Get it while supplies last.

When it comes to physical products, you’ll often see this phrase: while supplies last. This means the offer is available only as long as the store still has that product.

If all the products are purchased, then the offer is over and you can’t buy it anymore. So if you want the product, you might need to act quickly.

10. Sorry, this product is sold out.

If something is sold out, it means all the available products have been purchased, so there are none left to buy.

This can happen to a physical product, like shoes, or to something like tickets to a concert, show, or sporting event – they sell out when all the available tickets have been purchased.

Now you know 10 useful English phrases for talking about sales, deals, and discounts! Can you use a few of them in your own sentences? Give it a try!

Our students say you really get your money’s worth from Espresso English courses, and everything will be marked down – so you can stock up on courses for the entire year if you want!

item.title: Van Gerwen 'preparing for the worst' as he faces Sykes in Grand Slam quarters
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Michael van Gerwen 'preparing for the worst' as he faces Tom Sykes in Grand Slam of Darts quarter-finals

Michael van Gerwen expected to face Luke Humphries in the quarter-finals but will now take on Tom Sykes and knows he needs to be prepared for a real contest; you can watch the Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton live on Sky Sports until November 22

Friday 20 November 2026 18:41, UK

Michael van Gerwen is through to his first premier ranking quarter-final in over a year but he is up against an opponent he probably did not expect.

Van Gerwen put in a stellar display in a battle of two darting juggernauts when he defeated James Wade 10-8 to make it through to the final eight at the Grand Slam of Darts.

The 'Green Machine' battled hard against everything Wade threw at him and, with a late surge and some superb finishing, he got the victory over the line.

Now, he is preparing for a quarter-final in Wolverhampton but instead of the predicted clash with world No 2 Luke Humphries, he is up against the 72nd-ranked player on the Tour in Tom Sykes.

Sykes pulled off a stunning final-leg victory over Humphries to make the quarter-finals on his debut at the major.

The Dutchman was impressed with what he saw from the 'Castleford Tiger' and knows that if he can beat Humphries, then he needs to expect the unexpected.

"Tom did really well against Luke. I didn't expect that, I think no one expected that, because this is the first time he's played such a long format on such a big TV appearance," he said.

"A win is a win and moving forward I think this gives me a lot of confidence.

"I have to face Tom who had a fantastic game against Luke, 100 average, loads of 180s, so I need to make sure I am prepared for anything.

"He is a fantastic player; he's been doing really well lately on the Tour, but now he has to deal with the fact that he's going to be first to 16. He's never been in this situation, so it will be new for him as well.

"But don't get me wrong, if you can beat Luke, he can beat anyone, so I need to make sure I prepare myself for the worst."

Van Gerwen has had well-documented ups and downs in his darting career over the last two years but has had glimpses of the levels everyone knows he can reach, his massive win against Wade the latest.

He admitted that the victory, and the manner of it, helped him overcome some demons about his own game and he is now looking to turn that into consistency.

"Yes, I did (overcome some demons). Of course, when you're not doing what you are capable of, it can be a really frustrating game," Van Gerwen added.

"But then to finally do it and also in the way how I did it, I think that gives me energy also towards the next game.

"I always believe in my own ability, otherwise I wouldn't be here. If I think I can't believe in myself anymore, that's the day I have to stop playing darts.

"But that day is not there, and it won't be there in the next few years, it is as simple as that.

"My consistency is starting to get better, my belief in my own ability starts to get better, if you also look towards the Pro Tours and everything, my game starts to get somewhere, and that's what you want, that's where you put the work in and the effort.

"That is how darts is, and darts can be a really cruel game, but at the moment I am still in so that's a good thing."

item.title: Antonelli fastest but penalty leaves Verstappen on pole
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Antonelli fastest but penalty leaves Verstappen on pole

- Published

Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli was fastest in qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix but a grid penalty will hand pole position to Red Bull's Max Verstappen.

Antonelli, running at the back of the pack of cars in qualifying and maximising his tow, beat Verstappen by 0.258 seconds.

But the new world champion has a five-place grid penalty for using more than permitted number of engine components and will start sixth.

The Italian's team-mate George Russell was just 0.073secs behind Verstappen and will start alongside the Dutchman on the front row.

McLaren's Lando Norris qualified fourth, and will start third, ahead of Red Bull's Isack Hadjar.

Both Ferraris were eliminated in the second session and qualified 11th and 12th with Charles Leclerc ahead of Lewis Hamilton.

Each will be promoted a place by a 10-place penalty for McLaren's Oscar Piastri, who qualified seventh.

Racing Bulls' rookie Arvid Lindblad, sixth fastest, is the last driver to be promoted as a result of Antonelli's penalty.

Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson will start seventh with Alpine's Pierre Gasly eighth and Franco Colapinto ninth.

- Drivers limited to 27 laps for tyres in Qatar

- Published5 hours ago

Antonelli's final run did not start auspiciously as he and Russell became tangled up with the Alpines and Racing Bulls as they sought the best track position to optimise the slipstream effect.

Antonelli ended up the last driver to run and made it to the line with only one second to spare before the chequered flag, one second behind Lindblad.

Normally, being so close to the car in front would be a compromise but in Las Vegas it magnified the tow effect and Antonelli leapt to the front. "That was all the tow," he said over the radio after being told he was on pole.

"Starting the lap, I was only one second behind the car in front and I thought I was screwed," he said. "But the tow is so powerful here."

Verstappen, who has won two of the three Las Vegas Grands Prix, said: "I have been struggling with some weird issues that were also in the car in Brazil and just trying to get my head around how to deal with that.

"In qualifying we managed to make it work. Had a solid qualifying. My first lap in qualifying was pretty much as good as it could be with the tow, so to be on the front row is good for us.

"It was solid in the corners, and you have a bit of dirty air, but it is insane how much you gain on the straights."

Russell had looked in the running for the pole, but was happy with his session despite missing out.

"Overall it's been a very solid session and a solid day," he said.

"I wanted to be on pole but I am probably more pleased with the performance than in Mexico when I was on the front row.

"Kimi did a great job and he probably thought it wasn't going to work out so well being so close but with the tow it worked out."

'Nightmare' for Ferrari

Leclerc and Hamilton were separated by 0.056 seconds and both had tales of woe that explained their early exit - but very different ones.

Leclerc said: "Just a very poor qualifying. We are losing one second in the straights which makes it difficult enough already, and then I did a mistake when I had to put the lap in in Q2, following multiple mistakes we have done as a team and this we need to look at because it builds a lot of frustration that doesn't help.

"But in the end the mistake is on me and I will look at that."

Hamilton added: "It was a nightmare. Just low grip, felt like the tyres weren't working, had some damage on the floor that appeared out of nowhere and was losing 0.3-0.4secs and then had a deployment issue that lost us 0.6secs and with that we were nowhere, and I had no-one ahead of me. That wasn't great. So everything wasn't great.

"We knew we would struggle a bit here but maybe more than we anticipated."

item.title: Antonelli fastest but Verstappen on pole after dramatic Las Vegas qualifying
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Las Vegas GP: Kimi Antonelli fastest but Max Verstappen on pole from George Russell after dramatic qualifying

Kimi Antonelli was quickest in qualifying but a five-place grid penalty for a new engine means Max Verstappen will be on pole from George Russell for the Las Vegas Grand Prix; watch Sunday's race at 4am (build-up from 2.30am), live on Sky Sports F1 and Main Event

Saturday 21 November 2026 05:30, UK

Kimi Antonelli was fastest in qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix but a five-place grid penalty means Max Verstappen will start on pole position from George Russell.

New Formula 1 world champion Antonelli will start sixth due to a grid penalty for exceeding his internal combustion engine allocation and surprisingly went fastest in a hectic end to Q3.

The Mercedes driver only just crossed the line in time to start a final flying lap and was helped by a huge slipstream from the Racing Bulls throughout the lap to beat Verstappen by 0.258s.

- Las Vegas GP: UK schedule and how to watch on Sky Sports

- F1 2026 Calendar | F1 2026 Standings | F1 Gossip Column

- Got the Sky Sports app? Sign up for latest F1 alerts📱

- Not got Sky? Latest Sky Sports deals or stream F1 with no contract 📺

Russell was 0.331s behind Antonelli but the Verstappen-Russell front row cannot be missed when the lights go out at 4am UK time on Sunday (build-up from 2.30am), live on Sky Sports F1 and Main Event, after the pair made contact in final practice.

Neither driver was penalised as Verstappen was given a warning for driving erratically when trying to stop Russell from gaining track position in final practice earlier on Saturday.

McLaren's Lando Norris will start third with Red Bull's Isack Hadjar in fourth and Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad will start in fifth, his highest career grid position.

Oscar Piastri qualified seventh but the McLaren driver has a 10-place grid penalty for exceeding his engine allocation, so will start 17th, so Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson will start seventh instead.

Alpine's Pierre Gasly and Franco Colapinto had great pace throughout qualifying but were caught up in the traffic chaos in Q3 on the out laps, so only qualified ninth and 10th.

Ferrari had a disaster as they struggled in the cold conditions and on the long straights, so both Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton were knocked out in Q2.

It is the first time no Ferrari driver has reached Q3 since the 2024 Canadian Grand Prix and Hamilton was shocked both he and Leclerc did not get through.

Due to the grid penalty for Piastri, Leclerc will start 10th and Hamilton in 11th for Sunday's race.

Penalised Antonelli fastest after 'very weird' qualifying

After the opening day of track action was limited due to rain, final practice was very busy as the teams were keen to get as many dry laps in as possible.

Russell ended up fastest by nearly one second from Antonelli in a Mercedes one-two, so the Silver Arrows were big favourites going into qualifying.

But, as has happened several times this season, things closed up come qualifying and pole position was anyone's guess heading into Q3 as Verstappen was fastest from Gasly in Q2.

The first runs in Q3 saw Verstappen outpace Norris by 0.173s with Russell in third and Antonelli only sixth.

Mercedes sent their drivers out early with Russell ahead of Antonelli, despite Toto Wolff saying the team would back Russell to help him get second in the Drivers' Championship.

Although Antonelli let Russell through on the out lap, he braked hard at the start of the second warm-up lap to try to get a benefit from being behind other cars who were leaving the pit lane for their own out laps.

It led to the two Mercedes, two Alpines and two Racing Bulls all packed together on the out lap and Antonelli ended up at the back of the queue, so was in danger of missing out on a final Q3 flying lap.

The Italian just made it by a few seconds but was around 1.5 seconds behind the Racing Bulls of Lindblad, so was expected to be badly affected by the dirty air.

However, the multiple long straights on the Las Vegas circuit cancelled out the disadvantage of being behind another car in the corners and Antonelli remarkably took pole by a quarter of a second from Verstappen.

"It felt like going back to 60 mini cars where you do the qualifying all together, all super close!" said Antonelli.

"It was a very weird qualifying for me. At first I couldn't get the tyres working, just zero feeling with the car, and also the brake pedal was very long so struggling on the braking.

"But, all in all, it was so unexpected and that last lap I thought I was screwed because I started one second from the car in front, but the tow is so big here that I was able to just gain with that and put it on pole."

Russell improved to beat Norris to third, while the two Racing Bulls drivers moved up to sixth and eighth, but nobody else went quicker on their second Q3 runs.

"I wanted to be on pole but I am probably more pleased with the performance today than I was, let's say, in Mexico a couple of weeks ago when I was on the front row," said Russell.

"But just timing that out lap, getting the slipstream, was just huge. It was pretty crazy, very similar to what we saw in Monza."

Hamilton 'devastated' after double Ferrari elimination

Ferrari did not expect to be competitive in Las Vegas but they did not anticipate both drivers being knocked out in Q2.

Hamilton went off track several times in final practice as he struggled under braking and reported he has "no grip" in qualifying and revealed he suffered some damage.

"I'm devastated. We work hard to do a good job," he told Sky Sports F1.

"I didn't really know where we were going to be today. We knew we would struggle a little bit with these long straights, but I was optimistic going in, I thought the car would be OK.

"But on the first or second lap, we took a hit from something on the floor, some debris or something damaged the floor and we lost a bunch of downforce with it, a few tenths."

Leclerc made a mistake in the middle sector on his final run in Q2 which proved very costly as he missed out on Q3 by one tenth.

"For sure (Q3 was on the cards) but we didn't do a good job. I did a mistake the only lap I was given, basically," Leclerc told Sky Sports F1.

"And at the same time, the execution has been very poor. I don't know. We'll review. I'm very angry now, so I would rather not speak too much. But I think there were plenty of things we could have done much better.

item.title: Cummins to remain captain after 'unanimous support' from Cricket Australia
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Pat Cummins to remain Australia captain, given 'unanimous support' by cricket board amid 'Sandpapergate' fallout

Pat Cummins confirms he will "100 per cent support" forum Cricket Australia has set up following Usman Khawaja's 'Sandpapergate' allegations; CA chair David Boon rejects notion Cummins' integrity has been "compromised" amid varying accounts from players of 2018 ball-tampering scandal

Saturday 21 November 2026 05:28, UK

Pat Cummins will remain as Test and ODI captain after being given "unanimous support" by Cricket Australia, with the skipper confirming he will take part in the independent forum launched following Usman Khawaja's 'Sandpapergate' allegations.

Cummins' position had been under increasing scrutiny since Cameron Bancroft wrote a detail-filled account of the scandal in the West Australian newspaper, backing up Khawaja's claims that every member of the 2018 side was aware of the sandpaper plot.

Bancroft - the player caught on camera trying to alter the condition of the ball in South Africa eight years ago - said he was stirred to break his silence by Cummins' vehement denials of knowledge of the scheme in a press conference last week.

- Pat Cummins faces fresh scrutiny over Sandpapergate claims

- Sandpapergate: News and reaction to ball-tampering scandal

- Listen to latest episode of the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast

After Cricket Australia chair David Boon and CEO Todd Greenberg met Cummins in Sydney on Friday, a statement released on Saturday read: "In the light of the ongoing speculation surrounding the Australian men's team tour of South Africa in 2018, the CA board met to ensure measures are in place to protect the integrity of Australian Cricket and the welfare of all concerned.

"As part of this meeting, the board resolved to express its unanimous support for Pat Cummins as captain given ongoing speculation about his position."

Cummins prepared for 'difficult conversations' in forum

Cummins, who is set to lead Australia in a four-Test series at home to New Zealand from December 9, with the first match in Bancroft's native Perth, said: "Being Australian captain carries with it an awesome responsibility.

"I have and never will take that lightly.

"David (Boon) and Todd (Greenberg) have a very tough job navigating cricket through all of this and I commend them for reaching out to me and to many of the players and staff from 2018.

"I support the forum 100 per cent. I will be there. All of the players and staff I have spoken with are very keen to have their say. There will be a lot of difficult conversations but that is what's needed.

"Otherwise, from this point, captaining the Australian team in Perth will be my focus and priority."

Boon: Cummins' integrity has not been compromised

Boon added: "We've expressed our support to Pat and our concern for everyone impacted by the events of the 2018 tour of South Africa.

"We have learned from that experience and are proud of the team and the culture Pat and other leaders in the team have fostered over the past eight years and unequivocally reject any implication that Pat's integrity has been compromised.

"We are absolutely determined to steward Australian cricket through this very difficult time with diligence and patience and to listen and learn.

"That's what the independent forum we announced this week is about and the board encourages all players and support staff to tell and discuss their stories there.

"We will be publishing the terms of reference in due course."

Source: Sky Sports | Published: 2026-11-21 05:08 UTC

item.title: F1 qualifying results: Las Vegas Grand Prix
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

George Russell led the way in the third and final hour of practice at the Las Vegas Grand Prix Friday evening.

F1 qualifying results: Las Vegas Grand Prix

Who will take pole position for the Las Vegas Grand Prix?

But will the Mercedes driver top the timing sheets during the all-important qualifying hour later tonight?

Russell led teammate Kimi Antonelli and McLaren’s Lando Norris in FP3 Friday evening, with the veteran Mercedes driver posting a lap of 1:34.041, almost a full second ahead of Antonelli, who was 0.911 seconds off the pace. Charles Leclerc and Franco Colapinto rounded out the top five.

Friday’s FP3 session was the only representative session of the weekend so far, as both FP1 and FP2 on Thursday were compromised by wet weather.

The biggest story so far in Las Vegas might just be the list of drivers taking a grid penalty due to new components. Five drivers — Antonelli, Lance Stroll, Oliver Bearman, Oscar Piastri, and Carlos Sainz — have already taken on new components ahead of the Las Vegas Grand Prix and are facing grid drops at the start of the race. Antonelli is facing a five-place grid drop, while Stroll, Piastri, and Sainz are facing ten-place grid drops.

Bearman, who is taking on a fifth Internal Combustion Engine, turbocharger, exhaust, and MGU-K, and as those components all exceed the permitted amount per season, he will start at the back of the grid.

But who will take pole position? We will find out soon enough. Qualifying for the Las Vegas Grand Prix gets rolling at 11:00 p.m. Eastern Time on Friday night, so check back early and often for updates! And as always, download the new SB Nation app, join the F1 Community, and follow the qualifying thread live!

Las Vegas Grand Prix provisional grid

Here are the provisional qualifying results for the Las Vegas Grand Prix. Bear in mind several drivers are taking grid penalties this weekend, as outlined above:

* - Driver will be taking a five-place grid drop

# - Driver will be taking a ten-place grid drop

@ - Driver will be starting at the back of the grid

Las Vegas Grand Prix qualifying

Here is how the qualifying hour unfolded. All updates are listed in Eastern Time.

Q3

12:04: Antonelli goes fastest, but he has the five-place penalty. Verstappen will start up front.

12:01: Bit of chaos as cars jockey for position ahead of the final push laps.

11:56: Verstappen, Norris, Russell, Hadjar, and Piastri the top five after the first cycle of push laps.

11:50: Q3 is underway. Eight cars on the track right away, only the Red Bulls are still parked up.

11:47: Verstappen, Gasly, Russell, Piastri, Norris, Lindblad, Colapinto, Lawson, Hadjar, and Antonelli are the ten drivers through to Q3. Of those drivers, Piastri and Antonelli are both facing a grid drop, so they might be asked to give some tows at the end of Q3 to help Norris and Russell, respectively.

Q2

11:44: Gasly jumps to P1! Leclerc is OUT!

11:42: Clock hits zero and some final laps are underway. Hülkenberg and Bortoleto are both officially out as they are in the garage.

11:38: Five minutes left in Q2 and the six drivers in the drop zone are: Gasly, Colapinto, Hamilton, Sainz, Bortoleto, and Albon.

11:35: Every driver has pumped in a representative lap, and it is Piastri leading the way ahead of Lawson, Norris, Antonelli, and Russell. Big lap from Lawson here in Q2.

11:35: Big lap from Lawson and he jumps to P1 with a 1:35.048, ahead of Verstappen,

11:33: Ten minutes left in Q2, and the times are starting to come in. Hadjar sets the early benchmark with a 1:35.292.

11:29: Hadjar is the first to take to the track, followed by the Alpines.

11:28: Q2 is underway with a green light in Las Vegas.

11:24: From race control, the start of Q2 will be delayed. No reason given as of yet.

11:22: Russell, Antonelli, Leclerc, Norris, Verstappen, Hadjar, Lindblad, Lawson, Piastri, Sainz, Hülkenberg, Gasly, Hamilton, Albon, Colapinto, and Bortoleto are the 16 drivers through to Q2, in that order.

Q1

11:20: Câmara, Pérez, Alonso, Stroll, Bottas, and Bearman are out at the end of Q1.

11:18: Câmara picks up a huge tow from Bearman and gets to P15, but he gets knocked out immediately by Hülkenberg and Bortoleto.

11:16: Three minutes left in Q1 and the drivers in the drop zone are: Pérez, Câmara, Bottas, Alonso, Stroll, and Bearman.

11:15: Bortoleto is now on the track, and all 22 drivers are now in the fight.

11:12: First laps from Alpine and Gasly gets to P9, Colapinto to P11.

11:11: Norris jumps to P1 with a 1:35.109.

11:09: At the halfway point of Q1 and Verstappen leads the way, followed by Russell, Lawson, Antonelli, and Leclerc. Stroll, Bearman, Câmara, Colapinto, Gasly, and Bortoleto are in the drop zone.

Those last three have yet to take to the track.

11:08: To wit: Russell pumps in a 1:35.580 to go top of the table, ahead of Antonelli, Piastri, Hadjar, and Norris.

11:06: Bottas with the early benchmark of 1:38.713. But expect those times to tumble.

11:05: Câmara with a big spin into Turn 1, as the rear axle locks up.

11:04: Only Bortoleto and the two Alpines are yet to leave the garage. Audi seems to be doing some work on Bortoleto’s car, which is cause for concern.

11:02: Air temperature is just 55 degrees, which is chilly by F1 standards. Getting the tires fired up is going to be critical tonight … and it is expected to be colder tomorrow …

11:00: Green light in Vegas, we are underway.

10:59: Bottas and Pérez set to lead the drivers out, followed by the Haas pair of Bearman and Câmara.

10:57: C5, C4, and C3 are the compounds available this weekend, softest in the range from Pirelli.

10:56: “This is a session of consequence,” says Alex Jacques as qualifying is moments away.

10:40: Speculation on the F1TV prequalifying show that Piastri will give Norris a tow at the end of Q1 or even Q2, given that Piastri is taking a grid penalty.

Standing on a snow-covered slope in Switzerland, I joined locals enthusiastically cheering “hopp, hopp, hopp” (Swiss German for “go”) as racers careened downhill on velogemels — wooden, brakeless bikes with sled-like runners instead of wheels. Whizzing past, one by one, competitors feebly attempted to control their speed by digging their heels into the frozen ground.

I had originally come to the Swiss Alps for the world-class skiing, but when I heard about the velogemels, I was eager to try one. As an adventure seeker, I’ll try almost any contraption that gets me down a mountain, and this one sounded stranger than most.

item.title: When Your Winter Trip Has No Snow, Find Your Inner Daredevil Instead.
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

I’ve never understood the appeal of roller coasters or similar thrill rides. The stomach-dropping plunges and screaming passengers who stumble off, then immediately get back in the perpetually long line? No, thank you. I’ve tried enough of them throughout my life to know they’re just not my thing.

So imagine my surprise — or horror, or maybe a bit of both — when I found myself willingly, eagerly even, climbing into an Olympic bobsled, knowing I’d soon be barreling down an icy track at nearly 80 miles per hour, experiencing up to five times the force of gravity. Even more surprising? It turned out to be one of my favorite travel experiences to date.

It happened on a ski trip that barely involved skiing. An unusually warm, dry winter had left the mountains in rough shape, and I’d gone hoping to improve my mediocre technique. Instead, I came home with a new appreciation for the kind of thrill I’d spent most of my life avoiding.

Source: Matador Network | Published: 2026-11-20 17:29 UTC

item.title: Visulahti Wax Museum in Mikkeli, Finland
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

About

Rather than being an impressive, polished wax museum, the Visulahti Wax Museum has become famous for its awkward, outdated, and sometimes unintentionally hilarious figures.

The museum has something of a cult reputation in Finland. Its wax figures are famously questionable in quality: many look surprisingly inaccurate, while some remind you more of a horror movie setting. In 1983, the Wax Museum was established with serious intentions, but nowadays people visit it mainly for nostalgic reasons. You have to approach the museum with a good sense of humour.

The collection rarely gets updated, and the once-popular TV stars are now unfamiliar to the younger audience. The newest figurine is the Finnish president, whose resemblance – or the lack of it – has been widely discussed in the national news.

There are also international stars displayed at the museum, such as Elvis, the Beatles, and Santa Claus. At the end of the tour, a creepy version of Mickey Mouse sings to you with his friends, as you walk out of the building, wondering what you just experienced.

Know Before You Go

Wax Cabinet is open only during the summer season; see the current entry price on the website. Entry is also included with the Visulahti wristband, which gives you access to other activities in the area as well.
