item.title: ‘Now We Have to Deliver:’ New Texas House Member on Her Education Goals
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

‘Now We Have to Deliver:’ New Texas House Member on Her Education Goals

Montserrat Garibay, who came to the U.S. at 12 without citizenship, wants to improve bilingual education, protect Plyler and expand full-day pre-K.

Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter

Democrat Montserrat Garibay, who won Texas House District 49 in this month’s history-making election, told The 74 she has big plans for education when she assumes her new role in January.

Garibay will take the seat vacated by Gina Hinojosa, who successfully challenged Republican Greg Abbott for governor, denying the conservative Trump ally a fourth term and becoming the first Latina to lead the state.

“I’m really proud and grateful,” Garibay said of her own Nov. 3 victory. “I spent the past year listening to people at their doors, and I am ready to take their stories, their needs and what they’re asking us to change to the Capitol.”

And she’s not just celebrating her own success, but that of her party: Democrats took control of the Texas House for the first time in 24 years.

“Seeing Democrats do so well in a state as red as Texas gives me hope and reiterates the power of grassroots organizing,” Garibay said. “I think about the young people we registered who were voting for the first time, the union members who showed up for us, and the volunteers who kept knocking on doors. That’s what democracy looks like to me.”

The 47-year-old is walking into this radically changed landscape as a newcomer, having never run for political office before.

Garibay was born in Mexico City and came to the United States at age 12, unable to speak English — and without citizenship.

She started her post-secondary education at community college before earning her bachelor’s and master’s degrees from the University of Texas at Austin.

She later became the vice president for certified employees with Education Austin, a merged local union affiliated with the American Federation of Teachers, the National Education Association and the AFL-CIO. She also served as secretary-treasurer of the Texas AFL-CIO.

Garibay spent eight years as a bilingual pre-K teacher at the Austin Independent School District before serving in the U.S. Department of Education during the Biden-Harris administration, starting in 2022.

She was first a senior labor relations advisor before taking over as director of the Office for English Language Acquisition. While there, she led the effort to return the Title III program, which funds and supports English learners, to her office from the Office of Elementary and Secondary Education, where it had been for 15 years.

“Bringing it back gave the state and local education leaders a team of 16 career staff with expertise in educating English learners,” Garibay said. “We could answer districts’ and states’ questions, share current research and connect educators with professional development they could use in their classrooms.”

As for her history with the governor-elect, their shared office is not the first time the two have crossed paths: Hinojosa was the first person Garibay voted for — as an Austin school board candidate in 2012 — after she became a U.S. citizen.

She spoke to The 74 a week after the election about the education issues she deems most important. The conversation has been edited for clarity and length.

You came to this country unable to speak English. What was that like for you as a student?

I remember sitting in class and knowing some of the concepts in Spanish but being unable to explain what I knew in English. I was placed in remedial classes. The language I spoke at home — and all the knowledge I carried in that language — was too often treated as a problem.

My ESL teacher, Mrs. Hernandez, changed my experience with school. She gave me challenging work and expected me to do it. She built a relationship with my mother and made school a place where my sister and I felt safe. That combination mattered. I knew I could make mistakes as I learned English, and I knew she expected me to keep learning.

I carried that with me when I became a bilingual pre-K teacher in Austin ISD.

What will be your biggest priorities in education when you assume office in January?

Right now, the way our schools get funded is by daily attendance. We want to make sure that we change that to enrollment. (Chronic absenteeism remains a major challenge for schools across the country. It’s also impacts their funding when allocations are based on daily attendance.)

Why do you want to rein in vouchers?

The 89th Texas legislature under Gov. Greg Abbott approved $1 billion for the launch of the voucher program for school year 2026-27.

The comptroller has already asked lawmakers to double its funding.

First-year records showed that at least 70% of students awarded vouchers had previously attended private school or been homeschooled.

I oppose expanding the program. I want public reporting of who received vouchers, how providers spend the money and what services participating schools provide to students with disabilities and English learners.

My budget priority is to raise the basic allotment and better fund special education and bilingual education in the public schools that serve our communities.

Tell me more about how you might amplify bilingualism.

Being bilingual is a superpower, and in Texas it’s a skill we need every day.

Think about a nurse explaining a diagnosis to a parent or a small business owner serving customers in their own language. I want more Texas students to graduate able to do that kind of work in two or more languages.

In the legislature, I want to expand access to high-quality dual language programs, invest in recruiting and preparing bilingual teachers and strengthen Texas’s recognition of biliteracy through the Seal of Biliteracy (which honors a high school graduate’s proficiency in two or more languages).

I also want school districts, community colleges and employers to work together so students can use their language skills in career and technical education, internships and apprenticeships.

Bilingual students can be the next entrepreneurs in our communities, investing and providing services in multiple languages.

And what will you do to protect Plyler v. Doe, the landmark 1981 Supreme Court decision that guarantees a student’s right to a public school education regardless of their immigration status?

We’re working on a bill right now to make sure we support and protect the access of our students to public education. We’re taking a look at different bills that have happened in New York and different areas.

New York passed a bill that really protected Plyer v. Doe.

Plyler is the law, but we have seen the attacks on it.

Now, with a new governor here in Texas, I think things are going to be different, but I want to make sure that we have those protections no matter what governor we have. That is something that is very dear to me.

Many young immigrants have seen their hopes for college dashed because the government has taken direct aim at the funding that allows them to attend. What might you do about that?

Texas was the first state in our country to offer in-state tuition to qualifying undocumented students. It passed with bipartisan support in 2001, and Gov. (Rick) Perry signed it. It gave students who grew up here and graduated from Texas high schools a chance to pay a rate that made college possible.

A federal court order ended that access in 2025. (The Department of Justice sued 27 states and other entities for offering in-state-tuition. Texas did not fight the administration’s edict.)

I came to Texas undocumented and was the first in my family to go to college. My sister was in the first class of undocumented students receiving in-state tuition.

Education transformed my life. I think about the high school seniors in our district who are now devastated and are trying to figure out how to attend college.…

Source: The 74 | Published: 2026-11-20 15:30 UTC

Original link: https://www.the74million.org/article/now-we-have-to-deliver-new-texas-house-member-on-her-education-goals/

item.title: Opinion: Consent — and the Courage to Speak Up — Must Be Taught Long Before College
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Consent — and the Courage to Speak Up — Must Be Taught Long Before College

Book: Imagine if just one of the frat members implicated in the Cornell rape case had chosen protecting another person over going along with the group.

Get stories like this delivered straight to your inbox. Sign up for The 74 Newsletter

When my 9-year-old son was little, I used to put him in a shirt that said, “Boys will be boys,” but the words were crossed out and underneath it read: “Boys will be good human beings.”

That should be the standard — not just for boys, but for all children. And it starts with parents, caregivers, coaches, teachers and every adult who helps shape and raise a child.

Rape whistles, pepper spray and martial arts can be last-minute defenses against sexual assault. But truly preventing sexual violence means starting early and educating children about body safety, boundaries, consent and what to do when they see or know someone else being harmed.

The emerging story of gang rape allegations at Cornell University shows why those lessons are vital. In a lawsuit, a now-former student says Chi Phi fraternity members pressured her to consume drugs and alcohol until she was incapable of consent, and that seven fraternity members sexually assaulted her while others discussed what was happening live in a group chat. The criminal investigation has since been taken over by the New York state attorney general’s office after local prosecutors did not charge anyone.

This case is yet another call to action: Children must be taught both about consent and to speak up when someone is being harmed, years before they set foot on a college campus.

As a survivor of childhood sexual abuse, the founder of a nonprofit that works with families and schools to prevent it, and a mom of 9-year-old twins, this is deeply personal to me.

There were 57 boys in that fraternity group chat. Fifty-seven chances for the situation to change. Not one spoke up.

That is a failure that starts long before college. Children must be taught that doing the right thing isn’t only about their own behavior. It’s also about what they do when someone else is being harmed — especially when speaking up means going against the group.

That starts with giving children clear, practical lessons they can carry with them as they grow.

My organization helps educators teach children from an early age that they have the right to say no to an unwanted touch. Just as importantly, we teach children to listen when someone says no to them and to respect that refusal. As they get older, that lesson grows with them: A friend, a date, a teammate or someone they’ve been intimate with before does not owe them access to their body. Consent has meaning only when it’s given freely and affirmatively. It can be withdrawn at any time. And someone who is intoxicated, incapacitated or otherwise unable to make that choice cannot give it.

Raising good human beings involves more than teaching children not to hurt someone. They must also be prepared for times when it isn’t their own behavior that is the issue — it’s someone else’s.

Doing the right thing gets harder when the person causing harm is a friend, teammate or someone whose acceptance matters. Kids need to know that loyalty does not mean looking the other way. Being part of a team, fraternity or sorority, friend group or group chat does not mean going along with something you know is wrong. Sometimes doing the right thing means being uncomfortable, unpopular or the odd person out — and doing it anyway.

Speaking up does not always mean confronting someone directly or putting yourself in danger. It can mean creating a distraction, checking in with the person who may be at risk or getting help from a parent, teacher, counselor, coach or another trusted adult. What matters is that friends or witnesses do something, and that they keep telling until they get the two H’s: Heard and Helped. If someone is in immediate danger, call 911.

Imagine if just one of 57 frat members at Cornell had decided that protecting another person mattered more than going along with the group.

That is the kind of child we should all be trying to raise — boys and girls who know what is right and have the courage to act on it.

That’s what it means to be good human beings.

We’d love to hear how The 74’s reporting is helping educators, researchers, and policymakers. Tell us how

item.title: Latest Law School Data Shows Lowest Acceptance Rate Since 2006
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Photo illustration by Justin Morrison/Inside Higher Ed | temniy/E+/Getty Images | Elnur/iStock/Getty Images

With more people applying to law schools, acceptance rates reached a 20-year low in the 2024–25 admission cycle, the AccessLex Institute reported in its annual analysis of legal education data, released yesterday. But the acceptance rate gap between white and Black applicants has continued to widen, as has the gap between male and female applicants.

AccessLex’s annual Legal Education Data Deck summarizes and analyzes data on legal education from several public datasets, including the Law School Admission Council, the National Conference of Bar Examiners, and more. The report aims to highlight trends in law school admissions and matriculation, as well as bar exam results and employment outcomes.

About 76,500 individuals applied for law school in 2024–25, an 18 percent increase from the previous year, leading to an acceptance rate of 65 percent nationwide. That’s the lowest rate since 2006 and follows five straight years in which the acceptance rate hovered around 69 percent.

White applicants were the most likely to be admitted, with 76 percent receiving an offer of admission from a law school, compared to 64 percent of applicants who listed two or more races, 62 percent of Asian applicants, 53 percent of Hispanic applicants, 51 percent of Native American applicants and 41 percent of Black applicants. More white people also apply to law school than those of any other race, making up 43 percent of all applicants. Of the incoming class in fall 2025, 57 percent of students were white.

The gap between admission rates for white and Black applicants increased slightly since 2023, when the Supreme Court banned the use of race in college admissions; at the time, 78.5 percent of white applicants were admitted and 46.3 percent of Black applicants were admitted—a difference of 32.5 percentage points, compared to 35 percentage points in 2024–25. Asian applicants saw the greatest decline in admit rate of any race since 2023: 6.5 percentage points.

The report notes that Black and Hispanic students score above a 160—approximately the 30th percentile—on the LSAT, the admissions exam for law schools, at lower rates than white and Asian students. The American Bar Association used to require schools to use those scores in admissions, but now schools may consider other standardized tests instead, and a handful are permitted to bypass test score requirements altogether. Some legal education access advocates have argued that like many standardized tests, the LSAT unfairly favors white and wealthy students.

“Overreliance on the LSAT score in admissions may exacerbate the underrepresentation of [Black and Hispanic] students in law school,” the AccessLex report states.

The Trump administration has seized on racial disparities in LSAT scores to launch investigations into several law schools, alleging that they discriminated against white and Asian applicants by admitting Black and Hispanic students with lower median scores.

The admissions gap between women and men is also growing. Women have made up a larger proportion of law school applicants than men since 2015, with that share increasing each year; according to the latest data, from the 2023–24 admission cycle, they made up 57 percent of applicants compared to 40 percent for men. Yet men are four percentage points more likely to be admitted, with 72 percent of men and 68 percent of women receiving at least one offer.

Women comprise 56 percent of all J.D. students, the data notes. However, 2025 saw the first increase in the total number of men enrolled in a law program since 2010.

Law schools and other graduate programs historically see high application numbers during economic downturns; the last spike came during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020–21, when about 71,000 students submitted applications—which, at the time, was the highest volume in a decade. Still, the latest numbers haven’t reached the heights of the 2008 recession or the highest recorded figure in AccessLex’s dataset: 110,600 in 2004.

Following the large 2024–25 applicant pool, several colleges celebrated their all-time most selective or high-achieving incoming classes. In a press release from Hofstra University’s Law School celebrated its Class of 2029 for having the highest LSAT scores and grade point averages of any of its first-year classes, as did the University of Iowa. The University of Miami said last year’s admissions cycle was its most selective ever, netting its highest number of applications since 2011.

In its review of post-graduation outcomes, AccessLex reported that disparities in bar-passage rates by race have shrunk compared to 2023, with the pass rate for all groups surpassing 80 percent. Employment rates have stayed relatively stable since 2021.

Source: Inside Higher Ed | Published: 2026-11-20 08:00 UTC

Original link: https://www.insidehighered.com/news/admissions/graduate/2026/11/20/latest-law-school-data-shows-20-year-low-acceptance-rate

item.title: New Rule Changes the Future of Programmatic Accreditation
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Photo illustration by Justin Morrison/Inside Higher Ed | blackngel, Kozlik_Mozlik and tomertu/iStock/Getty Images | DNY59 and sdominick/E+/Getty Images | Thomas Northcut/Photodisc/Getty Images

For years, Republican policymakers have been concerned about what some describe as a “cozy relationship” between accreditors and the trade groups they represent, arguing that it creates a glaring conflict of interest that breeds unnecessary evaluation standards, credential inflation and higher college costs.

Now, as the Trump administration implements new federal regulations and tries to crack down on what it alleges are antitrust violations, experts say certain accreditors could face significant changes. Some agencies are already planning to formally end their scrutinized partnerships in order to comply with the new rule, which takes effect in July.

Earlier this month, the American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA) and its related accrediting body—the AVMA Council on Education—announced plans to become fully separate entities; the Association of Theological Schools is also planning to separate from its accrediting arm, the Commission on Accrediting.

Such quality assurance agencies, known as programmatic accreditors, can help specific types of degree programs—as opposed to entire institutions—access federal student aid and other government grants. But they must meet regulatory standards and be federally recognized in order to do so. Over the years, many programmatic accreditors have also become pivotal in the state licensure process for their given profession. (Students often just have to graduate from a program accredited by a specific agency to qualify for a license, but in some cases the agency also has to be federally recognized.)

For the colleges and accreditors that do require federal recognition to access aid or licensure, the new regulations effectively raise the bar they have to clear to prove “separation and independence” from any related trade groups.

This means that if programmatic agencies want to stay in ED’s good graces, they will no longer be able to depend on the larger, better-resourced professional associations for funding, staff, technology or office space. Nor will they be allowed to accept association members as volunteers on the committees that vote to determine their accreditation standards.

The separate and independent changes also apply to institutional accreditors, which comprehensively evaluate colleges and universities, but those agencies likely won’t have to make as many changes to prove they are independent.

One programmatic agency heavily targeted by the rule change is the American Bar Association’s Council of the Section of Legal Education and Admissions, which Trump’s executive order directly called on to “reform accreditation.” It was also sharply criticized at a recent Education Department panel. Many higher education experts argue the Council works too closely with ABA’s governing board, but the Trump administration has also targeted ABA for culture war issues, including its diversity equity and inclusion standards. So far, the ABA has made a few changes to its accreditation standards, but has not publicly announced any plans to restructure along the lines of AVMA or ATS.

And while both conservative and liberal consumer protection advocates largely agree that ABA and the programmatic accrediting system in general is crawling with antitrust violations, some on the left worry that the Trump administration’s approach to addressing this issue has become overly politicized and won’t be as effective as originally hoped. The rule will force many agencies to reshape their infrastructure or opt out of federal recognition, experts said, but it’s unclear if those changes will truly end the trade group’s influence on accreditation.

“Like what a lot of the Trump administration does, there is a kernel of a good idea buried under a mountain of bad policy here,” said Jeremy Bauer-Wolf, the higher education investigations manager at New America, a left-leaning think tank.

“The idea that there is too much collusion, as the administration puts it, or too much overlap between industry and accreditors is a very real and valid criticism,” Bauer-Wolf added. “But my question becomes: Do you want your posture to be, meet these very specific and sometimes overbearing rules or exit the system? I don’t know if that’s the proper posture.”

‘Consequential Decisions’

No veterinary schools depend on the AVMA’s Council on Education for access to student loans as they are all housed at larger universities with an institutional accreditor that serves as the link. But they do depend on the programmatic agency for access to certain research grants and loan repayment programs. And currently, 49 of the 62 veterinary licensure boards in the U.S. and Canada mention AVMA accreditation and/or federal recognition in their statutes.

These dependencies appear to be a driving factor behind why AVMA and the Council are parting ways, according to a news release that explains the separation, although AVMA also warns that doing so will likely be a costly endeavor.

Currently, AVMA subsidizes about 50 percent of the Council’s accreditation expenses. Under the new rule, that subsidy will no longer be possible, and colleges will have to bear the burden and other new overhead costs through their accreditation dues.

Inside Higher Ed reached out to AVMA for comment but the association declined, saying the new regulations “and their interpretation are still developing.” The group said it could say more after the Education Department releases its Accreditation Handbook “in early 2027.”

Emma Read, CEO of the American Association of Veterinary Medical Colleges, which has also served as a key partner for the AVMA Council on Education, noted that the loss of trade association members voting on accreditation standards will result in a lack of expertise. That absence of insight, she said, could lead to lower quality education and greater logistical challenges for the institutions implementing new policies.

“Who better to understand what it will mean to put a standard in place than the people that actually have to put the standard in place?” Read said. “But we recognize that the department has decided against that. So while our faculty and staff will put ideas forward and propose standard changes … we recognize we won’t have any part in that decision-making.”

Zach Waymer, executive director of the Association of Specialized and Professional Accreditors (ASPA), the association that represents programmatic accreditors, said he’s particularly concerned about the “extremely constrained timeframe” agencies have been given to make those decisions; he is not convinced the rushed implementation of new regulations will have Trump’s desired effect in squashing trade groups’ influence. The rule was finalized in late October.

“These are consequential decisions with financial, operational, and potential legal implications that take time and cost money,” Waymer said.

By sharing resources with trade associations, accreditors have been able to keep costs down and stay “at the forefront of expertise from the field,” he added. It didn’t mean that the trade group itself was making decisions for the accreditor.

“These are time and costs that spill over into programs, institutions, and even, indirectly, students,” he said. “The Department hasn’t demonstrated how these changes will improve educational quality or student outcomes.”

Impact ‘Hard to Gauge’

Not all of the roughly 30 programmatic accreditors currently recognized by the Education Department have decided to formally turn their existing accreditation arms into a new nonprofit like AVMA or ATS. At least seven have opted to withdraw from federal recognition, citing issues with the new accreditation rules.…

item.title: Academy trust pays out after Prevent threat over children’s Palestine badges
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

An academy trust will pay out tens of thousands in compensation to four children who were told they could be referred to Prevent for wearing Palestine flag badges to school.

The school, part of Lion Academy Trust, has issued a formal apology after it sent letters to the children’s parents saying they might be referred to the counter-extremism programme or to local hate crime teams.

The issue dates back to November 2023 when the children’s school, Barclay primary school in Leyton, east London, held a non-uniform fundraising day for Children in Need.

The four children, all British Muslims aged between six and 10 at the time, attended wearing items displaying Palestinian colours or the Palestinian flag, in memory of children who had been killed in Gaza and those who continued to suffer during the conflict, which was ongoing at the time.

One child wore a Children in Need Pudsey sticker featuring a bow tie in Palestinian colours. Another wore a homemade badge bearing the Palestinian flag and colours.

Parents of the four children said they had repeatedly asked the school to apologise for their treatment of the children and had launched a legal challenge when none was forthcoming.

At a hearing at Central London county court on Thursday, the court heard that the academy trust had now made a formal apology to the children and their families and would pay them substantial compensation.

Lawyers for the children alleged direct discrimination, indirect discrimination and harassment on grounds including race, ethnicity, religion and belief, together with breaches of their rights to freedom of expression and freedom of thought, conscience and belief.

Shahid Achhala, the father of one of the children, said: “What happened to our son was deeply disturbing and should never have happened to any child. He was just eight years old, expressing compassion and solidarity with children suffering in Gaza, including members of his own extended family. Instead of being supported and protected by the school entrusted with his care, he was deliberately subjected to mistreatment that caused him considerable emotional distress.

“For almost three years, we have had to fight legally for accountability and an acknowledgment of the wrongs we believe were committed. While we welcome Lion Academy Trust’s apology, we cannot overlook the distress caused to our son and our family, or the fact that this matter could have been resolved long time ago.”

The families were represented by law firm Leigh Day and supported in their legal claim by Prevent Watch, which provides casework support to individuals and families affected by the Prevent duty.

Layla Aitlhadj, a director at Prevent Watch, said: “In this case, parents who were protecting their children’s rights were told that their concerns were ‘false and malicious’. They held firm through three years of pressure. Today the families, and the wider community who stood with them, have been vindicated.”

The academy trust has been approached for comment.

Source: The Guardian Education | Published: 2026-11-20 06:00 UTC

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026/nov/20/lion-academy-trust-children-palestine-badges-prevent-london

item.title: It’s unfashionable to say it, but class still matters – and young people know that | Polly Toynbee
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

This should come as no great surprise: young people are more keenly aware of the significance of social class than those who came before them. The yawning gap in life chances at birth is something they know better than complacent older generations. Class may be unfashionable in the language of politics – long damned by the right as the politics of envy, avoided by many on the left for fear of sounding chip-on-the-shoulder – yet it’s part of the daily experience for young people.

Nearly half of 16- to 34-year-olds in the UK now say class is important to their identity – and not in a good way – according to a new Ipsos poll. That’s nearly twice as many as among the over-55s. Maybe that’s because more young people are better educated at each level, so they know more, with a grounding in reasoned thinking.

More likely this new class consciousness springs from their sharpened experience of life chances among their own generation. They are more likely to think class has become increasingly significant over the past two decades and they’re right: within their own generation, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) has found inequality in the UK is growing more than within other cohorts.

The class antennae of young people have been honed by the obstacles they face that older generations felt less, when class was better disguised by generally rising living standards. What they see around them is the growing inheritocracy – the widening chasm between those who get substantial help from parents at crucial points in their lives and those with no backup.

The IFS has been sending warnings for years: choosing your parents well matters more than your own talents and hard work. Rewards for merit and effort are declining – and young people see it everywhere. Political platitudes about working hard and playing by the rules ignore the evidence they see with their own eyes. For those receiving inheritances in the UK, the gap between expectations at the top and bottom is greatly widening: the bottom fifth are projected to get 5% of their lifetime income from inheritance, while the top fifth, already better paid, could get 29%. The better off are likely to receive it earlier, making it easier to buy a house, take time to choose their job carefully, save less and retire earlier.

As so many young people – many more than the million Neets – struggle to make their way into a career they are qualified for, they can see how class matters far more than money and inheritance. Getting a leg-up from your family background and connections, or just worldly advice from those in the know, is worth everything. The under-35s consider nepotism a serious issue: nearly twice as many are concerned about it as among the apparently socially contented over-55s. This week’s LSE research on cross-class friendships in the US and UK was heartening: they make jokes to get over the awkwardness of revelations of privilege, described by Sam Friedman and Rose Butler as the “omnipresent threat” between them.

How well I recognise that. Admitting to being middle class can be embarrassing. That’s why I have tried in my memoir, An Uneasy Inheritance: My Family and Other Radicals, to be honest about how powerfully privilege is passed down the generations, bequeathing self-confidence and security with second and third chances if you mess up. My family of successful leftwing professionals were all confounded by how to square their advantages with their beliefs – sometimes comically, never denying that privilege, just blushing.

It’s hardly surprising that 40% of those under 35 in Britain think they would benefit from being part of another class. How strange is the social obtuseness or denial of the over-55s, of whom only 14% believe they would have done better if they came from another class. They may be victims of the classlessness myth spread with skill by the right to hide how their wealth soared in the 1980s. Some may be relics of my own youth in the 1960s, a decade rife with the popular social fantasy that we were all classless now, with the same clothes, hair and music, sitting on and smoking the same grass at the Isle of Wight festival, on the same anti-Vietnam demos. The 1960s and 70s did see inequality reducing, yet when I went to university in 1966, only 6% of my cohort did the same.

This class awakening among young people ripples around the world. In Britain, as the wealth divide within the young generation widens, Labour seems to be catching the moment. Andy Burnham and Alan Milburn this week pledged a seismic shift in priorities towards young people, with the recent announcement of the breaking of the triple lock on pensions by 2030 also signalling the way to a generational redistribution.

Most shocking, but barely remarked on in the media coverage of Milburn’s tome of a report, was the massive decline in public spending on young people compared with steep rises for the old. In figures taken from the Intergenerational Foundation, he reports that between 2004 and 2024, pensioners in Britain got 55% more, while the sum per child only rose by 20%. As Milburn writes, this is “neither sustainable nor is it fair”.

To push for redistribution of opportunity, private wealth and public money, this awakening of youth class consciousness needs to organise into active politics.

- Polly Toynbee is a Guardian columnist

item.title: Misty-eyed Burnham gambles on closer ties with EU as he throws down gauntlet to Tories and Reform
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Several sentences into a slightly convoluted answer about where UK-EU relations might go next, Andy Burnham abruptly changed tack. “The important point is that the Britain of today and the EU of today is not the one of 2016,” he said. “Life has moved on in so many ways.”

This is undoubtedly true. But Burnham’s political gamble on closer ties with Brussels hinges on the assumption that most British voters feel this way as well.

Seeking to push his deal on food checks, emissions trading and a new youth exchange scheme, Burnham was at first in full consumer politics mode, saying it would bring cheaper food – with a namecheck for Tesco, Asda and other supermarket chains – as well as lower electricity costs and a claimed 0.5% boost to overall growth.

But as the Brussels press conference went on, the prime minister became more misty-eyed, particularly in describing the youth exchange scheme as a gift to a generation stripped of choices by the 2016 referendum and then Covid. “Hope is a word,” he intoned. “And it starts now.”

For all that Burnham is a skilled political salesman, his oratory is backed up with some helpful political context, matched with cooperative allies.

To begin with, not only politics but polling results are now different. A new constituency-level survey released on Friday showed that of 394 constituencies estimated to have voted leave in 2016, voters in 274 of them would back rejoining the EU – including Burnham’s Makerfield seat.

Standing alongside the UK prime minister in the venue, Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, and António Costa, the European Council president, at times resembled proud parents, beaming at every positive phrase.

They, of course, began work when the EU reset was the personal project of one Keir Starmer. His name was not mentioned on Friday, and it is undeniable that Brussels finds life easier dealing with a UK leader who is both bold and popular.

Speaking to British reporters later in the day, Burnham openly challenged political opponents to rebuff a plan that, he said, could add 0.5% annual growth to the economy in the long term – more, he said, than any other single intervention.

“Why would anybody turn their back on that?” he said, with particular focus on Nigel Farage, who was, soon after Burnham spoke, hosting a retaliatory press conference of his own, 10 minutes’ walk from the EU building.

Even with the tight timing – Farage had to delay his event as the summit timetable slipped – the Reform UK leader drew a decent crowd of reporters. But there will be a sense in No 10 that beyond Farage, most of the formidable Brexit forces of 2016 have melted away.

Kemi Badenoch, who has been advised by her team to talk more about the economy and less about Brexit, spent the day on a visit in Essex. The Conservatives did send out a condemnatory press release about the EU deal, but it focused more on Burnham “reopening the divisions of the past” than the specifics.

More trenchant was a statement from Stay Out, the recently formed Brexit purity group, which floated its argument that rejoining the EU would cost the UK £750m a week.

For all that the dominance of vote leave alumni in Stay Out gives the campaign the slight air of a historic battle re-enactment society, Burnham cannot ignore them. A resonant sidenote of the summit was how he was happy to talk about the specifics of the deal, but not much beyond that.

While it was the PM himself who provoked a debate about a future in which the UK rejoined the EU, the brakes were firmly on in regard to any discussion of such ideas.

Pre-summit talk of possible closer future links with Brussels was replaced by much vaguer language about mutual “brainstorming” on what would come next, with UK officials saying any progress could be months in the making.

Another sign of the caution embedded within Burnham’s ambition was the lineup of UK cabinet ministers who watched as the prime minister, von der Leyen and Costa arrived on Friday morning.

Alongside those you might expect – Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, John Healey, the chancellor, and Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary – was Anneliese Midgley, a close ally of Burnham who has the job of chief whip, No 10’s liaison with Labour MPs.

She was there because a bill setting into UK law the new EU deal will be presented to parliament next week. Most Labour MPs agree with Burnham that the world has changed since 2016. But, as with the voters, he needs to bring them along with him.

Source: The Guardian Politics | Published: 2026-11-20 18:22 UTC

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/nov/20/andy-burnham-uk-eu-brussels-summit

item.title: No one else in Reform is suitable to lead the party, Nigel Farage says
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Nigel Farage has said he does not see another person who could do his job as leader of Reform UK, in a warning shot to potential rivals who might seek to replace him.

The Reform UK leader delivered a message that he was going nowhere despite his worries over his personal safety in the wake of the killing of the Reform politician Ann Widdecombe.

There has been speculation over Farage’s future in light of police and parliamentary investigations of Reform’s financial affairs. The Commons standards watchdog is due to report soon on whether he should have declared a £5m personal gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne before the last election. If he gets a substantial suspension from parliament, he could face a second byelection, contested by other main parties, in his Clacton constituency.

However, Farage sounded a note of defiance in an interview with the Sun, saying: “These are very thoughtful moments, but, you know what, if I’m not here doing this job right now, who else could? Who else would? I don’t see that person. So I’m gonna do it.”

A number of other Reform UK politicians are potential contenders to succeed him, including the party’s economics spokesperson and former Conservative, Robert Jenrick, the home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, and the former leader Richard Tice. Another possibility is the return of Rupert Lowe, who left Reform in acrimonious circumstances and founded his own party, Restore Britain, but who is popular on the online hard right.

The party is going through a difficult period after slipping from first place in the polls to second or third behind behind Labour and sometimes the Conservatives.

Asked by the Sun if he had “blown” his chances of reaching No 10, Farage said: “No, far from it.”

He admitted there had been “self-inflicted wounds” in the past year but said he still had a chance of becoming prime minister.

He told the newspaper that he would fight the next election as Reform leader if he was “still here and fit and healthy”.

He also batted away questions about the £5m, which he has insisted was to pay for his personal security despite the fact the party has been providing this.

“What’s it got to do with you? Drugs, sports cars, desert islands. It’s a gift,” he said, adding that although the party had had “ebbs and flows” and had made mistakes after growing “too far and too fast”, he was confident it was “more than through the worst of it”.

On the prospect of another battle over Europe as Andy Burnham weighs the case for rejoining the EU, the Reform leader said: “If you ask me, have I got the energy and the enthusiasm to do this again? I would say to you, hold my jacket. I’m ready for it.”

He also warned of people taking to the streets with “direct action” if Brexit is reversed.

In a separate interview with the Times while travelling to Brussels, where Burnham was attempting a reset deal, Farage said he believed the issue of Europe would dominate the years to come.

“It’s going to be absolutely huge. It’s going to be much bigger than anyone realises. The genie is out of the bottle; it literally can’t be stopped now,” he said.

He also ruled out joining a new campaign called Stay Out, led by former Tories, suggesting he would make his own case for keeping Brexit.

Source: The Guardian Politics | Published: 2026-11-20 18:11 UTC

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/politics/2026/nov/20/nigel-farage-leadership-reform-uk-party

item.title: EU wants ‘closest possible relationship’ with UK after agreeing Brexit reset deal – live
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Closing summary

- The British prime minister Andy Burnham said his deal with the European Union will add up to £17bn a year to the British economy as he paved the way for even closer ties to Brussels. Burnham said it was a “good day for Britain and a good day for Europe”, as he met EU chiefs in Brussels to announce a package covering food and agriculture exports, emissions trading, and a youth experience scheme which could open the doors for 100,000 young Europeans to temporarily work in the UK, with Britons able to do the same on the continent.

- Burnham said Friday’s deal was “probably the limit” of what could be done before the next national election due by mid-2029, but he envisaged an informal conversation in about a year with the EU about what could be achieved next.

- European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she welcomed Burnham’s willingness to have a broad debate about future relations with the EU. “We are open for brainstorming, and we welcome this brainstorming, so count on us,” she said.

- At the summit, postponed from July after the resignation of Burnham’s predecessor Keir Starmer, the two sides addressed some of the Brexit losses with a package of agreements. The most significant allows cross-border trade in animals, plants and related products, such as sausages or seeds, without the certificates and controls currently required. Britain has estimated this could add up to £5.1bn per year to its economy.

- A further agreement will link the emissions trading systems of Britain and the EU, which would exempt British and EU goods, such as steel, from each other’s border carbon levies. Each side is also set to allow 100,000 young people a year in to work or study for three years.

- However, one potential dampener emerged as the 27-nation bloc and London jostled over linking ultimate implementation of the new deals to Britain agreeing to cut university fees for EU students. Britain prefers to offer only “significantly reduced” fees, and the aim is to resolve the issue within six months.

- Retailers and manufacturers have welcomed Andy Burnham’s new trade deal with the European Union as a “big win” but warned they need “clear and early” guidance from government to aid the transition, Press Association reported. The chief executive of the British Retail Consortium (BRC) called the SPS deal a “big win” for UK retailers but warned that businesses need “at least 18 months” to transition to the new arrangements.

- Nigel Farage, the veteran anti-EU campaigner and leader of the Reform UK party, said the deal “was about the first steps, incrementally, to taking us back into membership of the European Union,” and again predicted an early election next year. Farage told reporters he would campaign to preserve Brexit. “I am ready for this fight,” he said.

- Meanwhile, Denmark’s foreign minister on Friday said Moscow’s defence attache in Copenhagen would be expelled after Russia was suspected of being behind an attempted assassination of a Ukrainian rapper. “We have just summoned the Russian ambassador to the ministry of foreign affairs and notified him of the government’s decision to expel the Russian defence attache from Denmark” within seven days, Lars Lokke Rasmussen told a news conference.

- Students and young workers have taken to the streets in more than 20 European countries in coordinated protests over the surging cost of living and housing, deteriorating learning conditions and rising military spending. Activists from more than 50 groups in countries including Belgium, France, Germany, Greece, Italy, Portugal, Spain and the UK held rallies on Friday, lighting flares, burning cardboard models of tanks and waving placards, many reading “fight for our future”.

item.title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

- Published

The UK and EU have agreed a youth experience scheme which will allow a limited number of 18 to 31-year-olds to work, study or travel in the European Union for up to three years.

Every year, 100,000 Britons will be able to participate in the scheme, with a reciprocal arrangement for 100,000 EU citizens.

A joint EU-UK statement says the scheme is due to launch no later than January 2030.

The numbers for both those coming to and from the EU will be allocated among the member nations according to each country's population.

UK participants will initially be able to apply to travel to one particular EU country but can later switch to a different one, staying in a total of three countries during their three-year stay. However, they must spend 12 months in one country before switching.

Visas issued by the EU or the UK will initially be valid for two years, with an option to extend for one more year.

Neither UK nor EU citizens will be able to access benefits while abroad or bring dependants such as children.

Participants will need to pay an application fee and prove they have enough money to support themselves during their stay.

There are currently no details on what application fees UK citizens will have to pay, but the EU currently charges â¬90 (Â£75) for short-term visas. Numbers vary between countries for longer-term stays.

The UK charges Â£340 for its other youth mobility schemes, in addition to a Â£776 annual health surcharge.

The UK government has not said how much money an EU or UK national needs to have access to in order to take part but for similar schemes the figure is Â£2,530.

There are no details yet on how places on the scheme will be allocated if it is oversubscribed; however previous schemes have used either a first-come, first-served basis or a random ballot system.

The UK already has youth mobility schemes in place with other countries, including 45,000 places for Australians, 8,500 for New Zealanders and 1,000 for Icelanders.

In 2024, 24,400 out of a possible total of 81,100 youth mobility scheme visas were issued by the UK.

Speaking at a joint press conference with EU leaders, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "These opportunities open horizons, and they create friendships that will last a lifetime.

"So it's a very emotional moment because these are the young people that will shape our future."

What about tuition fees?

One sticking point in the negotiations had been tuition fees and the EU's request that Europeans studying at UK universities should pay the same as British students.

A typical undergraduate degree in the UK (excluding Scotland) costs up to Â£9,790 a year for a domestic student, while the cost for international students, including those from the EU, can vary from around Â£11,000 to Â£38,000.

If the UK did agree to reduce fees for EU students, British higher education institutions could lose out financially.

British students at European institutions pay non-EU rates, but these tend to be lower than in the UK, ranging from â¬1,000 to â¬20,000 per year.

The UK and EU have not reached an agreement on the issue, but the joint statement says the two sides will continue working towards a deal and conclude negotiations by May 2027.

The two sides have also agreed to continue discussions about the UK's participation in the Erasmus + programme.

The initiative provides funding for students, teachers, youth workers and sports professionals to study or do work experience in the EU.

The UK left the scheme in 2020 but last year the government re-joined for the 2027/28 academic year only, making a Â£570m contribution to the scheme.

In the statement released on Friday, the EU and UK agreed to explore opportunities "beyond 2027".

What are the criticisms of the scheme?

Some UK politicians had argued that the youth mobility scheme would disadvantage young people in the UK.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said: "I don't think it's fair because it means that more young people are coming here to compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs."

Speaking in the House of Commons on Thursday, Reform UK's Suella Braverman asked: "Why...are the government proposing to open the doors to hundreds of thousands of young Europeans who will come here and work in our shops and restaurants?

"Is that not a total and utter betrayal of young people in this country?"

Defending the government, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden has argued that countries in the EU with greater freedom of movement than the UK had lower youth unemployment rates.

The Labour government has made tackling the large number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) a top priority.

Alan Milburn, in his government-commissioned report into Neets, expressed concern about an "over-dependence" on foreign labour in the last 20 years.

He said the recent fall in net migration had created "an opportunity for employers to reorientate back towards employing young people from their communities".

Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to keep up with the inner workings of Westminster and beyond.

Source: BBC Politics | Published: 2026-11-20 16:07 UTC

Original link: https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6jeqv9nv5eqo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss

item.title: Demography Is the Achilles’ Heel of Dictatorships – Including China
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Chinese rulers already recognized the importance of accurate population data more than 3,000 years ago. Under the Western Zhou dynasty, officials presented the king with such figures in an annual ritual honoring the star believed to govern population counts.

During the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods, Guan Zhong, chancellor of Qi, compared governing without reliable population numbers to crossing a river without a boat or an oar. Qin’s chief minister, Shang Yang, warned that without this information, even a powerful state could be torn apart.

The Qin Empire, whose rise and unification of China in 221 BCE were underpinned by reliable data, punished falsifiers of population figures as harshly as defectors. When the dynasty fell, Xiao He, Liu Bang’s adviser, seized Qin’s population and other state records, helping Liu defeat his rivals and establish the Han dynasty.

Centuries later, the Mongol-founded Yuan dynasty showed how losing reliable population data could bring down an empire. Having lost track of its population and farmland, much of which fell under elite control, the central government lost tax revenue, soldiers, and corvée labor. The state could not even fund Yellow River works, leading hungry and unpaid river workers to join a rebellion. After just 98 years, the dynasty collapsed.

Soviet leaders, by contrast, manipulated population figures for political gain. Joseph Stalin’s agricultural-collectivization campaign, launched in 1929, caused a famine that killed millions of people, yet these deaths were absent from official statistics.

Stalin also claimed the USSR’s population had reached 168 million in 1933 and expected the 1937 census to show a growing, contented population of 180 million. When it counted just 162 million, Stalin regarded the results as a political disaster. Later, the head of the Census Bureau, Olimpiy Kvitkin, and three senior colleagues were arrested and accused by Pravda of seeking to “diminish the numbers of the population of the USSR.” Kvitkin was executed by firing squad, and the census itself was suppressed and branded “harmful.” A new census in 1939 used more politically acceptable methods and reported a population of 170.5 million, but discrepancies prevented publication of the full report.

Russia’s fertility rate fell below replacement level as early as the 1960s. But, as demographer Anatoly Vishnevsky put it, officials concealed the problem through elaborate “games.” By the 1980s, low fertility was shrinking the country’s working-age population. Oblivious to this, Soviet leaders invested heavily in foreign ventures like the war in Afghanistan.

The People’s Republic of China, having based its system on the Soviet model, adopted the practice of manipulating statistics. During the Great Leap Forward, local officials were all too happy to inflate grain-yield figures to meet Mao Zedong’s objective of “surpassing Britain and catching up with America.” Qian Xuesen, the “father of Chinese rocketry,” gave these claims a veneer of scientific legitimacy. The inflated harvest figures helped keep the campaign going for three years, contributing to tens of millions of starvation deaths.

Manipulated statistics also shaped China’s population policy. In 1979, Chinese leaders floated the idea of a one-child policy but lacked scientific backing for it. Rocket scientist Song Jian, a protégé of Qian, filled the gap with seemingly rigorous projections that China’s population, unrestricted, could skyrocket to 4.3 billion by 2080. The one-child policy was formally adopted several months later, in September 1980.

Around 1991, China’s fertility rate had fallen below replacement level, yet fertility and birth statistics were revised upward to sustain the government’s claims of overpopulation. The 2000 census counted just 13.8 million infants, while official birth figures for that year stood at 17.7 million. In a 2002 paper, a senior family-planning official argued that if the census was accurate, China would no longer need its family-planning policy. Yet as late as 2014, Zhai Zhenwu, then-president of the China Population Association, warned of an intolerable baby boom, projecting that a two-child policy would push the fertility rate to 4.5 births per woman and annual births to nearly 50 million.

The longer the government relied on bogus population figures, the more difficult it became to admit that it had been manipulating them. To do so would have dealt a massive blow to the government’s credibility. It would have meant acknowledging that the one-child policy was a colossal error and revealing that foreign investors and governments had based their China strategies on false data.

In a recent monograph in Contemporary China Review, I present extensive evidence that China’s official population figures are overstated by at least 130 million, with the largest discrepancies concentrated among people born after 1990. For years, these inflated population figures drove projections that China’s economy would far surpass the United States’ and strengthened Chinese leaders’ belief that the balance of power was shifting in their favor. As early as 2011, an internal report urged the Communist Party’s leadership to abandon Deng Xiaoping’s strategy of “hiding its capabilities and biding its time.”

Party doctrine reflected this growing confidence. In 2012, then-President Hu Jintao articulated his “Three Confidences” in China’s path, theory, and system. China had already begun moving away from Deng’s strategy of integration with the West, adopting a more assertive foreign policy. Current President Xi Jinping completed the “Four Confidences” in 2016, adding culture to Hu’s original three. Soon enough, officials began invoking the slogan “the East is rising and the West is declining.”

In the United States, rosy assessments of China’s economic strength have long fueled misguided “Thucydides trap” narratives and heightened strategic anxiety. But policymakers in both countries have failed to recognize China’s demographic Achilles’ heel, even as its shrinking workforce has been sapping its economic momentum.

Copyright: Project Syndicate, 2026.

Source: The Diplomat | Published: 2026-11-20 15:53 UTC

Race & Ethnicity

A monthly digest of the Center’s latest research on race and ethnicity · Subscribe ↗

The Dating Attitudes of Single Black Adults

Black adults are more likely than other U.S. adults to be single (42% vs. 29%). About half of Black singles say they’re currently looking for a relationship or casual dates, though that share is higher among men than women.

Majorities of both Black men and women looking for a romantic relationship say it’s important for a good spouse or partner to be caring and compassionate, romantic, to help with household chores, and to believe in God.

- Also read: Many Black Adults Say Close Relationships Influence Their Views About Being a Black Man or Woman

- More from this survey: For Many Black Americans, Family Extends Beyond Birth and Legal Ties

- This is the second report in a series from our National Survey of Black Americans. Earlier this year we published a report exploring family which, for many Black Americans, extends beyond birth and legal ties.

Everyday Americans: Asians in the U.S. Today

Our new book, Everyday Americans, co-published with Third State Books, offers a uniquely in-depth portrait of Asians in the U.S. based on findings from our landmark study. Why did we write it?

Now 24 million strong, this group is the fastest growing racial and ethnic group in the United States, and the only group that is majority immigrants or children of immigrants.

We heard about a wide variety of challenges Asian Americans face, such as linguistic diversity, hidden heritage and circumstances at odds with the model-minority stereotype. And these challenges aren’t universal for all Asians in the U.S. Your experience likely differs depending on your origin country. The book, which features interviews with prominent members of the community, such as actress and director Joan Chen, Billboard’s Mike Van and Poshmark’s founder and former CEO Manish Chandra, along with every day individuals that participated in various parts of the Center’s project, offers one of the most in-depth portraits available of Asian America.

Stay tuned for post-election analysis from the Center, but in the meantime, here are a few interesting pieces from our portfolio:

item.title: Gemini Notebook's New Interactive Site Builder Is Much More Useful Than I Expected
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Gemini Notebook, Google's AI tool for study and research, already lets you do a lot with your notes: You can turn them into flashcard quizzes, interactive podcasts, video explainers, mind maps, and infographics, as well as interrogating the sources you've collected through AI-powered prompts and responses. Now there's something new. You can also build interactive websites from your notebooks.

That might not immediately seem like the most obvious fit, turning your research notes into a mass of HTML code. But it gives you another way to look at your material and to get insights from it. Here's how it works, what you could potentially do with it, and how impressively it worked when I put it to the test on some early 20th-century Irish literature.

Creating websites in Gemini Notebook

Website building is rolling out now for Gemini Notebook's web app for all users, and is "coming soon" to the mobile app. You won't see a website option in the Studio panel alongside Audio Overview, Reports, Quiz, and the rest; instead, you type something along the lines of "make me a website" in the prompt box.

To make a website, you need sources, so I set Gemini Notebook to collect information about James Joyce's 1914 collection of short stories, Dubliners. As I studied Dubliners many years ago (I highly recommend it), I was hoping I'd spot any AI errors and hallucinations, and be able to properly assess the quality of Gemini Notebook's analysis.

With a suitable amount of information absorbed into the AI brain, I got Gemini Notebook to make me a website. Google doesn't give too much official guidance here, but says you should add "a description of what you want to build for work or study," so if you have a particular style or angle in mind, include it.

Here was my prompt: "Build a website using all the sources and information collected so far. Make it an interactive guide to the individual stories in Dubliners, as well as the overarching themes and context. I want to use it as a study aid to explore different aspects of the story collection."

The finished website pops up in the Studio panel, and in my case it took around five minutes to put something together from 26 different sources. Click on the website, and it opens in a new window—you can use it from there, open it in a separate tab, or download the code to your computer.

I was honestly impressed by how much Gemini Notebook managed to pack into a single website: I got plot summaries, analysis, critical context, and some of the main themes and motifs outlined. There was an interactive quiz at the bottom of the page to test my knowledge, and even a graphic I could click through to reveal different elements of how the stories fit together.

Everything was well laid out and functional, albeit with the standard "sheen" you get from anything made by AI (which tends to always pick the same colors and fonts). I wouldn't have necessarily thought that I needed a website if I was still studying Dubliners today, but I can definitely see how it would have helped.

Different ways you could use Gemini Notebook-generated websites

For something like my project, a website really works well as a study aid, since it offers a different way of interrogating the information. You can already do that in the main chat, and with tools such as the audio and video overviews, but this is different. It's a bit like having a mini-Wikipedia focused just on whatever you're researching.

The interactive elements that are included—so in my example, I could click from story to story, and theme to theme, within the same page—make a site more engaging than a standard report document and a static wall of text, and should help the information stick if you're trying to study it.

I can also see how this might be useful for sharing data with others. Maybe you need to analyze monthly report figures, or you want to chart how your organization has developed a product over time—perhaps an interactive website will relay that information in a more compelling way than a slide deck or PDF.

Maybe you have a notebook stuffed with details of a big family vacation. Putting together a website through Gemini Notebook would give your family a hub that they could use to easily check up on the details of the trip—where you're going and when, what you'll see there, what they need to pack, and so on. Another idea might be a family tree, if you have ancestry data and sources packed together in a notebook. Putting together a website would be a great way to visualize it, and, again, it's something you could share with relatives. If there were updates to the data you've collected, you could generate a new website.

Bear in mind that you can do a lot with your prompt. My website turned out the way it did because that's what I asked for, and if you need more interactivity or specific types of sections, then you can ask. Based on my follow-up prompts, you can also specify colors and certain layout choices, though it's not quite a full-scale website builder.

It looks like these sites are single-page creations, though they do have interactive elements and sections that change as you click around. It might be better to think of them as mini apps rather than sites. As of yet, there's no built-in option for publishing a site online or sharing it with others, so you need to download the HTML and do that manually.

Source: Lifehacker | Published: 2026-11-20 17:00 UTC

item.title: This Note-Taking Pebble Ring Is so Simple, and I Love It
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-condensed version. This text was produced by an LLM from the original article and may omit details. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Refinement was skipped, so the body is an excerpt of the original.)

Pebble’s $75 ring, the Index 01, has one job: It lets you record voice memos. That seems like it would be underwhelming, and the idea was ridiculed by some of Pebble’s fans when the product was first announced. But I’ve been wearing it for a few weeks, and folks: I love it.

In this era where every tech product is trying to also be every other tech product, I appreciate the Index’s simplicity. This is a ring with no heart rate sensors or even charging pins, just a microphone, a button to activate it, and a light to let you know that it’s working. The audio is processed on your device; no need to send anything to the cloud.

To buy the Index 01 ring, you get yourself a sizing kit (either buy one for $10 or 3D print it yourself), order the ring, and pair it with the Pebble app on your phone. I use an iPhone rather than an Android, which means I can’t use certain features like setting timed reminders or connecting to Beeper, but it’s still an incredibly useful little device. The Index has no charger, since it uses a disposable battery that Pebble estimates will last about two years.

How to use the Index 01 ring

The simplest way to use the Index is to wear it on your index finger (hence the name, get it?) and press the button with your thumb. Speak a quick note while holding the button in, and the ring will flash to let you know it got the message. A moment later, you’ll get a notification saying that it added (whatever you said) to your “Notes to self” note.

To take this further, you can create different notes and ask the ring to add what you say to a specific note. You can also double-click the button to ask a question. The answer will appear in the notification you get on your phone or watch a moment later. (The ring does not speak to you.)

All the notes you leave yourself appear as plain text in the Pebble app, fully editable. If you tap on each one, you can see a timestamp from when you left the note, and you can replay the voice recording if the transcription doesn’t make sense. (Why is there a “pencil sharp pepper” on my packing list? Ohh, that’s a pencil sharpener.) You can also add notes by typing them, which I find useful when starting a to-do list or a packing list.

It’s incredible how useful a simple timestamped note can be. I used to do something similar with my “notes to self” chat in Signal, but the Index makes it even easier since I won’t get distracted by opening my phone. For example, I make a note on the Index whenever I take a medication, so that tomorrow morning I will be able to check whether I already took, say, a long-acting allergy pill. (You do not want to accidentally double up on those.)

How I used the Index 01 on a road trip

There’s one thing that, for years, I wished for a simple tool to help me do. It’s trivial, which makes it extra frustrating that I have not been able to find a good solution. I would simply like to note when I leave for a road trip, and when I start and end each stop. This way I can tell how long the driving took as a portion of the whole trip, and how long my stops tend to be so I can plan them better next time.

You’d think this would be easy, but every existing tool drove me nuts in a different way. Stopwatches only store a single number, so I can’t break down how long each stop was—and if I miss a button press, I’m screwed. Sending myself a Signal text is probably my best option, but if I’ve just parked my car after three hours of driving, the second I pick up my phone I’m going to see all the notifications that arrived while I was on the road, and I’ll forget to actually send that text.

But this is exactly what the Index does well. I don’t even need to open my phone or look at my watch. Pressing the button with my thumb means I can do this one-handed without having a microphone always listening. (It’s also a great way to jot down the random things I think of while driving.)

The Index worked perfectly for my travel log, and I even used it for a workout after I got to my hotel room that night. I’d do 10 pushups, then tell the ring “add 10 pushups to my workout.” I’d do 20 crunches, and add that as well. I left the workout note open on my phone and could glance over and see what I had already done, since my messages got added to the note as I went.

I didn’t need a workout app for any of this, or a special-purpose travel app. I can just leave myself a dang note, and the note-taking app can remember when I left the note and, if I choose, play back exactly how I said it. It’s gloriously simple. Good job, Pebble.

Source: Lifehacker | Published: 2026-11-20 16:15 UTC
